articles.title: 'Cyber incident' forces UK Gov to take some services offline
articles.body:
- Regular benefit and pension payments are not affected and will be paid as normal, the department says
- Gemma, 34, says she has just £30 left in her bank account and worries her payments could be cut if she fails to fill out her universal credit journal - but DWP confirms people in situations like hers will not be sanctioned
- Our correspondent says cyber incident has become a catch-all term used in the early stages of what often ends up being a cyber attack - here's the difference
Close form
Are you affected?
Get in touch
To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser.
This video can not be played
Media caption,
Watch: What has happened to online pension and benefits services?
Live Reporting
Edited by Manish Pandey and Matt Spivey
Millions lose access to online benefits and pension services after 'cyber incident'published at 18:40 GMT
- 18:40 GMT
- Jamie Whitehead Live reporter
- Image source, PA Media
- Millions of people haven't been able to access online benefits and pension services, as the government says its system has been hit by what it calls a "cyber incident".
- The Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) says its digital services - including for pension, universal credit and Pip applications - were taken down as a "precaution", while assuring claimants regular payments would be paid.
- Downing Street hasn't ruled out "malicious" activity, and says there is no evidence of data loss in the incident, with investigations into the cause ongoing.
- Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden described the incident as "serious", with the DWP working with the National Cyber Security Centre to get things running again.
On any particular day, there can be problems with processing some paymentspublished at 18:29 GMT
- 18:29 GMT
- Michael Buchanan Social affairs correspondent
- The DWP processes around 2.5 million payments each day, worth about £1.3bn.
- On any particular day, there are problems with a small proportion of them.
- And while it’s logical that anyone who has a problem today is linking it to the cyber incident, the DWP are emphasising that they currently have no information to suggest regular payments are being affected.
- They also say that anyone who fears a benefit sanction as a result of being unable to upload information to their digital journal today should not worry as they will not be penalised due to the DWP suspending their online services.
'Focus on readiness', but it's 'a way of life' - the reaction we've heardpublished at 18:21 GMT
- 18:21 GMT
- Image source, Reuters
- The DWP said it took down some online services as a "precaution" after identifying the "cyber incident". Here is the response:
- From those in the field:
- Haroon Malik, a fellow at the Chartered Institute of Information Security, said it's "very uncommon" for governments to be taken offline by cyber incidents and it needs to focus on "readiness" and accept that this is going to happen "more and more".
- Trevor Dearing, a senior director at cybersecurity company Illumio, said the longer-term goal should be tighter controls: "Millions rely on DWP services, and the goal must be that an attack happens and the public doesn't notice."
- Beverley Griffiths, senior lecturer in security and resilience at Buckinghamshire New University says cyber incidents are now "a way of our life", but that the public should be reassured "resilience plans" are in place.
- And those who rely on the services:
- Meanwhile, some people have expressed frustration about services being taken down - Craig in Scotland told the BBC he was offered a trial job tomorrow but cannot get a suit, tie and shoes without his advance universal credit payment.
- Meanwhile single mum-of-four Samantha has said she relies on the payment and has "just enough money in my account to do a food shop".
- The DWP has said that regular benefit and pension payments have not been affected by the cyber incident.
- This is a service that lets you report a death to most government organisations in one go.
- It informs HM Revenue & Customs (HMRC), the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP), the Passport Office, the Driver and Vehicle Licensing Agency (DVLA), the local council and more.
- The reason for the outage seems to be because "Tell Us Once" is managed by the DWP, despite connecting with many other government departments.
- When you try to use the service online this afternoon, the DWP outage message appears.
Cyber incidents now 'a way of our life', security and resilience lecturer sayspublished at 17:10 GMT
- 17:10 GMT
- An expert in security and resilience says the UK will likely continue to see cyber incidents occur.
- "This is the world we live in now," Beverley Griffiths, senior lecturer in security and resilience at Buckinghamshire New University, tells the Press Association.
- "And you know they [the public] should take comfort in the fact that these departments, these organisations have got resilience plans in place - they are responding."
- Griffiths doesn't think the public should be too worried, but says "there is a lot going on in the world at the moment".
- She feels the "more complex we are", the more gaps and weaknesses we have, adding that it is almost like living with the weather.
- "It is a way of our life," Griffiths adds.
- Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden describes the outage as a "serious cyber incident", with investigations into the cause ongoing - Downing Street has not ruled out "malicious" activity.
What are the DWP's online services used for?published at 16:48 GMT
- 16:48 GMT
- Image source, Geography Photos via Getty Images
- Let's take a look at universal credit, as an example. Recipients can use their online account to:
- See when their next payment is due and how much they'll get
- Send messages to their work coach or case manager
- Report changes in their circumstances to ensure they receive the correct amount
- Receive notification of appointments - including where and when to attend
- Inform the DWP what they are doing to find work by recording information in the online journal
- The issue is broader than just universal credit, though:
- When you try to use the DWP website to see if you can apply for other benefits like personal independence payments (PIP), it takes you through to an error page which flags "temporary disruption"
- The same is true when you click on the application page for Jobseeker's Allowance
- If you've reached the age where you can first apply to receive state pension, you can usually do that using the DWP website too. But anyone clicking the "apply now" button will also find themselves landing on an error page
'I have just enough money in my account to do a food shop'published at 16:24 GMT
- 16:24 GMT
- James Gregory Live reporter
- Samantha Reah, a single mum-of-four from Cardiff, was expecting her monthly Universal Credit payment to enter her bank account today.
- But when she looked this morning, her £1,600 payment wasn't there - meaning several of her usual outgoing payments had bounced.
- She tells me she's been on Universal Credit since 2021 and there has never been a missed payment, but when she called the Department of Work and Pensions, an adviser told her it was nothing to do with the outage.
- "I have just enough money in my account to do a food shop," Samantha says, adding she has a cleaning business "which is the only job I can do at the moment".
- "So I rely on the payment today - it's my payday."
- She says that she was told by the DWP adviser that the payment could come into her account by 20:00 GMT today at the latest, but that if she still hasn't received it she will have to wait until Monday.
- "I can't wait and see," Samantha says. "Even my Tesco mobile has bounced today so I don't have enough mobile data.
- "I'm panicking - it's going to be a long and stressful weekend."
- The DWP have told the BBC regular payments are not affected and that if customers have any issues with their payments, they should call on their benefit phoneline.
- The NCSC leads the UK's defence against cyber threats and helps individuals, businesses and public sector organisations protect their online services and devices.
- It offers proactive guidance for defending against such threats and also provides incident response when they do occur.
- This can include determining the extent of the incident, managing its impact, restoring systems and working to increase security to prevent it happening again.
- The NCSC is part of the Government Communications Headquarters (GCHQ) and works closely with international allies, law enforcement and the UK’s intelligence and security agencies, including MI5 and MI6.
More than 15,000 reports of gov.uk problems since yesterday eveningpublished at 15:41 GMT
- 15:41 GMT
- By Kayleen Devlin
- More than 15,000 reports of problems with the gov.uk website were submitted to outage monitoring website Downdetector between yesterday evening and lunchtime today.
- Downdetector tells BBC Verify that more than 1,300 reports about the UK government’s website were received between 19:20 and 21:00 GMT yesterday. Typically, they would expect around one report or fewer every 15 minutes.
- While Downdetector does not track individual government departments and cannot establish how many complaints related specifically to DWP services, it represents a significant surge of reports on the gov.uk domain over an extended period of time.
- Around two-thirds concerned login problems, with reports coming from across the UK.
- A DWP spokesperson tells BBC Verify that the department became aware of the cyber incident on Thursday, but declined to give an exact time.
- The spokesperson says there is currently no evidence of personal data being compromised or payments being affected. Whether anyone gained unauthorised access to DWP systems remains under investigation.
What to know about the Department for Work and Pensions cyber incidentpublished at 15:25 GMT
- 15:25 GMT
- Adam Goldsmith Live reporter
- Image source, Press Association
- 'Serious cyber incident': The Department for Work and Pensions has been hit by a "serious cyber incident" but there's no evidence anyone's data has been compromised, according to Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden.
- Who or what is to blame? We don't yet know what's behind the outage, but the prime minister's spokesperson says there is currently "no evidence to suggest a malicious actor has targeted other government departments".
- But sanctions will be waived: The DWP says nobody will be sanctioned for being unable to update their job-seeking journals if they've been affected by the outage - like Gemma who told us she's worried her payments might be reduced.
- 'Done the right thing': Despite the inconvenience for people seeking to use the DWP site, some experts say taking it offline was the correct protocol to stop a potential attack from escalating.
- The DWP has "extremely old computer systems": According to its most senior official Sarah Healey, who told a Parliamentary committee earlier this month that the department's cyber-security and resilience measures are "critical".
Sanctions will be waived if you’re affected todaypublished at 14:58 GMT
- 14:58 GMT
- Kevin Peachey Cost of living correspondent
- Millions of people in the UK receive universal credit and, for many, part of the deal is attending mandatory appointments and staying in touch with your work coach or case manager.
- For example, this includes updating a journal with the information on how you’re looking for work. Failure to do so may mean sanctions – when benefit payments are stopped for each day the sanction is in place.
- Gemma, in St Neots, has been in touch to say: “I can't update my journal in the universal credit site so I'm worried that I could be sanctioned for it and I have a video call on Monday and I'm worried that I may miss it due to this.”
- However, the DWP has confirmed that nobody will be sanctioned if their access has been affected by the cyber incident.
- "As we work to resolve this cyber incident as quickly and safely as possible, customers who do not attend or cannot update their circumstances will not be sanctioned. Sanctions already processed earlier will still apply," a DWP spokeswoman said.
'I'm worried universal credit payments could be cut if I can't fill out journal'published at 14:54 GMT
- 14:54 GMT
- Jacob Phillips Live reporter
- Image source, Handout
- A woman who relies on universal credit is concerned she could have her payments cut if she is unable to fill out a journal showing she has been applying for jobs.
- Gemma Barnes tells me she has just £30 left in her bank account which she needs to buy food.
- But she is worried she will have to spend £6 on Monday to travel to her nearest job centre if services continue to be disrupted, instead of attending a weekly catch-up session via a video link.
- The 34-year-old says she's worried her payments could be reduced if it appears like she has not been filling out her journal, which shows the DWP that she has been applying for jobs.
- Gemma explains any delay in her payments could leave her unable to pay household bills.
- "With it being so close to Christmas I need [that money] at the moment," she adds, explaining she has to often rely on items in the reduced food section to make ends meet.
- Gemma, who lives in St Neots in Cambridgeshire, says she has been trying to access the universal credit website "all of today and since last night as well" but she has not been able to get through to the site.
Cyber incident or cyber attack - what's the difference?published at 14:21 GMT
- 14:21 GMT
- Joe Tidy Cyber correspondent
- The Department for Work and Pensions says it is dealing with a "cyber incident" and is not saying much else about what’s happening inside the IT networks of this vast government department.
- The term has become a catch-all one used frequently in the early stages of what often ends up being a cyber attack.
- The reason organisations often use the term "cyber incident" rather than "cyber attack" or "data breach" is that in the opening stages of an incident they may not yet know:
- Whether an attacker successfully gained access
- Whether data was stolen
- Whether the event was malicious, accidental, or merely suspicious activity
- How widespread the impact is
- From a communications perspective, "cyber incident" is also often the safest legally and technically accurate phrase while teams try to figure out what’s going on.
- As a reminder, an investigation is under way into the incident. Downing Street has said that "currently there is no evidence of customer data loss".
Protecting public is 'constant challenge for government' - Pat McFaddenpublished at 14:06 GMT
- 14:06 GMT
- Image source, UK Pool
- A bit more from Pat McFadden's update on the cyber incident at the DWP.
- Asked about comments from the chair of the Science and Technology Committee (which you can read in our previous post) that the disruption should be "a wake up call", McFadden says they are "constantly working to protect our systems".
- "When we get an incident like this, the most important thing to do is to protect the public," he says, adding protecting the public's data is a "constant challenge for government".
- McFadden adds working to secure key systems is a "critical part of the UK's resilience".
Disruption 'should be a wake up call', says Science and Technology Committee chairpublished at 13:59 GMT
- 13:59 GMT
- Image source, Getty Images
- Image caption,
- Dame Chi Onwurah says the government must be transparent about any impact on people's services and data
- The chair of the Science and Technology Committee says the
disruption at the DWP today "should be a wake up call".
- In a statement, Dame Chi Onwurah says the committee has
"repeatedly warned that the government cannot achieve its digital
transformation of public services without addressing weaknesses in its digital
infrastructure and improving standards of data hygiene."
- "Public bodies hold citizens' data on trust, and that
demands the highest standards," she continues.
- Onwurah also says that people rely on the DWP systems for
what she calls some of the most essential services the state provides
adding: "They should be able to trust that the tech and data
underpinning them are secure and resilient."
- "Whilst the government has set out a vision for a
modern digital state, it needs a credible delivery plan with clear
responsibilities, milestones and metrics against which progress can be
judged," she continues, adding that the government must provide clarity
about what has happened.
- The Science and Technology Committee scrutinises government
policy, with a broad remit to consider science and technology.
Outage is a 'serious cyber incident' - work and pensions secretarypublished at 13:44 GMT
- 13:44 GMT
To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser.
- This video can not be played
- We've just heard an update from Pat McFadden, the work and pensions secretary, who describes today's outage as a "serious cyber incident".
- He says they were aware of an issue yesterday and the department "did the right thing" to take down their services in order to protect the public's personal details.
- McFadden adds there's no evidence that anyone's data has been compromised, and says payments will be made as usual.
- The department is working with the national cyber security centre to get systems up and running, he says, adding investigations into the cause are ongoing.
Government must be 'laser focused' as it prepares for similar incidents, says expertpublished at 13:18 GMT
- 13:18 GMT
- Jacob Phillips Live reporter
- A cyber security expert says it's "very uncommon" for government services to be taken offline because of cyber incidents.
- While it’s still unclear what the nature of the incident is, Haroon Malik, a fellow at the Chartered Institute of Information Security, tells me the Department for Work and Pensions wouldn’t have taken services offline unless something serious had happened, or there was a heightened risk that something was about to happen.
- Malik says the government should rehearse similar scenarios to make sure it's well prepared, and have detailed plans in place for when services go down.
Some universal credit users say they have not received paymentspublished at 12:56 GMT
- 12:56 GMT
- Image source, Handout
- Image caption,
- Mother Evie Merison says: "I can't imagine how stressful it must be for other disabled people who claim universal credit"
- The Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) said earlier that regular benefit and pension payments had not been affected by the cyber incident.
- But some people who receive universal credit have contacted the BBC to say they have not yet received their payments.
- Georgina Howarth, 30, says she has had to ask her mother for money to help buy food after not receiving her universal credit payment.
- "I've been on the phone to them [DWP staff] every hour since 8am," the Plymouth resident says. "They said they can't even get on the system."
- A mother in Bedford also says she did not receive her expected Universal Credit payment this morning.
- Evie Merison says: "I have a weekly shop to do on Sunday and bills coming out by Monday. What am I meant to do?"
- Craig in Scotland says he has cancelled a trial shift because he did not receive an advance Universal Credit payment he was going to use to buy work clothes.
- Meanwhile, Ian Marr in Leeds says he has not received his pension payment or heating allowance today.

articles.title: Stanford Physicist Uses AI to Tackle Quantum Gravity Problem
articles.body:
Stanford Physicist Uses AI to Tackle Quantum Gravity Problem
Insider Brief
- Stanford physicist Venkatesa Chandrasekaran proposed a quantum theory of gravity that uses the paths of light to calculate how spacetime can fluctuate.
- The approach yielded a finite result for a graviton-pair calculation that diverges under an approximation and reproduced a known quantum correction to black hole entropy.
- Chandrasekaran said he developed several calculations and proofs through months of work with OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra, using about 400 million tokens.
A Stanford physicist has proposed a quantum theory of gravity that uses the paths of light to get a finite answer for a calculation that can otherwise run to infinity.
If the approach holds up, it could help reconcile quantum mechanics, which governs the behavior of matter and energy at small scales, with Einstein’s general relativity, which describes gravity as the curvature of spacetime. The study also reproduces a known quantum correction to the entropy of a black hole.
In a preprint posted on arXiv, Venkatesa Chandrasekaran calculated what happens when two gravitons, the hypothetical quantum units of gravitational waves, are created and then disappear. The calculation gave a finite answer even after accounting for waves of arbitrarily short wavelength. An approximation applied to the same calculation produced an infinity.
Chandrasekaran said in the paper’s acknowledgments that he developed several of its calculations and proofs through months of back-and-forth work with GPT-6 Astra, an OpenAI model. He put the total at about 400 million tokens, the units of text AI models process, and said OpenAI provided the computing resources.
The work addresses a problem of reconciling general relativity with quantum theory, a problem that, as mentioned, has vexed top physicists for decades. General relativity treats gravity as the curvature of spacetime. In plain terms, quantum theory allows physical quantities to fluctuate. If spacetime itself fluctuates, the geometry that ordinarily tells physicists where and when something happens also becomes part of what they have to calculate.
Chandrasekaran’s proposal uses the boundaries of finite regions of spacetime to set up those calculations. The boundaries follow paths that light could take, and their shape can change with the gravitational field. That gives the calculation a way to specify where something happens even as the geometry changes.
The study also finds that a region bounded this way, with a specified maximum size, can hold only a finite number of mutually distinguishable quantum states. In a separate calculation for a large black hole, the approach recovered both the standard relationship between a black hole’s entropy and its surface area and a previously calculated quantum correction.
It’s important to note that the paper is theoretical and presents no experimental test.
Using Light to Set the Boundaries
To calculate how gravity behaves when spacetime itself can fluctuate, Chandrasekaran starts by defining the region he wants to study. He uses the paths light can take between two events to set its boundaries.
One way to envision this is to imagine a flash going off and a detector set to record light at a particular moment later. Light spreading out from the flash marks one boundary. Tracing the possible paths of light backward from the detector at that moment marks the other. The two boundaries enclose a region called a causal diamond. Any point inside it can receive a signal from the flash and send one in time to reach the detector.
In general relativity, gravitational waves can distort those boundaries. The paper treats the surface where they meet as part of the system and locates quantities relative to it. Chandrasekaran first solves the classical equations that constrain which combinations of boundary data are possible. He then applies quantum rules to the remaining variables, which include the two ways a gravitational wave can be polarized.
To describe a larger stretch of spacetime, the paper joins regions along shared boundaries. It matches the gravitational data on the two sides and sums over the quantum states that can occur at an intermediate stage. Chandrasekaran shows that these intermediate sums converge within the construction. In fact, they converge even when the set of possible states is infinite.
The order of operations matters, as the graviton-pair calculation shows.
In practice, physicists often start with a rough answer and refine it by adding corrections based on the strength of the interaction.
In this example, expanding in Newton’s gravitational constant before adding the contributions from different wavelengths produces a term that grows without bound. Keeping the constant at its physical, nonzero value and doing the sum first gives a finite answer. At very short wavelengths, contributions that would otherwise drive the divergence partly cancel.
Counting States Inside a Black Hole
For the state-counting result, Chandrasekaran imposes a maximum size on a macroscopic causal diamond using what he calls a gravitational clock. The clock is a distance-like reading defined along the paths of light. Gravitational radiation changes that reading by affecting how neighboring light paths converge. Putting an upper limit on the reading also restricts which wave states can fit within the region.
The study concludes that a causal diamond with a fixed size limit can contain only a finite number of distinct quantum states. That means the area where the two light cones meet can take only certain values, with gaps between them.
The black hole calculation uses a surface where a bundle of outward-directed light rays momentarily stops spreading. The local gravitational data are enough to identify that surface and begin counting states on its interior side.
By summing over interior states, Chandrasekaran recovers the leading term in the Bekenstein-Hawking formula, which makes a black hole’s entropy proportional to its horizon area. Entropy describes how much microscopic information is compatible with the same large-scale description.
For a large, nonrotating black hole, the study also found a small adjustment to the standard entropy formula that grows slowly as the black hole’s surface area increases. The result matches an earlier calculation by physicist Ashoke Sen that held the black hole’s mass fixed and accounted for small variations in its spin.
Next Steps
A lot of work remains.
The four-dimensional theory covers gravity in a vacuum, where gravitational waves can propagate. Extending it to include matter would widen its scope. The calculation also recovers Einstein’s equations in the low-energy limit for initial quantum states concentrated around a classical geometry. It calculates the first quantum correction in that regime, including how fluctuations in gravity in turn affect the average geometry.
One question Chandrasekaran leaves for future work is whether different choices in building the quantum state space lead to equivalent theories for the same range of clock readings. Another test would be to carry the black hole and low-energy calculations beyond the first quantum correction.
For a deeper, more technical dive, please review the paper on arXiv. It’s important to note that arXiv is a pre-print server, which allows researchers to receive quick feedback on their work. However, it is not — nor is this article, itself — official peer-review publications. Peer-review is an important step in the scientific process to verify results.

articles.title: European Commission Declares Browser Competition a Digital Markets Act Priority
articles.body:
In comments to Politico regarding our open letter, the European Commission acknowledged the letter and noted that browsers are “effectively the entry point to the web” and one of the main ways publishers reach readers. They went on to say that “browser competition is one of the priorities of the Digital Markets Act”. The EU Commission also stated it is in talks to ensure rival browsers “can effectively compete” with Safari on iPhones and iPads.
Share and join the conversation: Mastodon, LinkedIn, Bluesky and X.
An Extraordinary Coalition in Defence of the Web
The letter has garnered incredible support. We want to say a massive thank you to all the organisations, businesses and individuals that have stepped forward to defend the web's ability to compete fairly as an open platform for consumers and businesses alike.
What is particularly extraordinary is the sheer diversity of the coalition, ranging from human rights, consumer rights, software freedom advocacy organisations to Europe's major publishing associations, prominent startup organisations, independent browser vendors and technology companies.
The breadth of this support demonstrates that browser and web app competition is not simply an issue for browser vendors, but one that affects the entire digital economy and society more broadly.
Signatories to the letter include, among many others:
Civil Society, Consumer Rights and Software Freedom
- Open Web Advocacy (OWA) An international coalition of software developers and technology experts advocating for an open, competitive and interoperable web.
- European Digital Rights (EDRi) Europe's largest network of digital rights organisations, bringing together over 50 organisations to defend fundamental rights and freedoms in the digital age.
- Norwegian Consumer Council One of the leading national consumer rights organisation internationally recognised for its groundbreaking work on digital consumer protection. Behind the viral video A Day in the Life of an Enshittificator.
- ARTICLE 19 An international human rights organisation dedicated to defending freedom of expression and access to information worldwide.
- Free Software Foundation Europe (FSFE) The Free Software Foundation Europe is a charity that empowers users to control technology. The FSFE helps individuals and organisations to understand how Free Software contributes to freedom, transparency, and self-determination.
- European Citizen Action Service (ECAS) An international, Brussels-based non-profit organisation whose mission is to empower citizens in order to create a more inclusive and stronger European Union by promoting and defending citizens’ rights.
- Bits of Freedom A Dutch non-profit advocacy group focused on digital rights such as the right to privacy and communication.
- Digitalcourage A German civil rights organisation with decades of experience defending privacy, individual freedoms and democratic values in the digital age.
- Croatian Alliance of Consumers (UPH) A consumer federation in Croatia established to unite consumer protection groups and advocate for consumer rights.
- Blueprint for Free Speech An international human rights charity dedicated to defending freedom of expression, protecting whistleblowers and strengthening press freedom worldwide.
Publishers and Journalists
- European Publishers Council (EPC) A coalition of Europe's leading media groups committed to defending freedom of expression, editorial independence and media pluralism, safeguarding the economic foundations of independent journalism and ensuring that publishers can compete fairly alongside digital gatekeepers.
- European Federation of Journalists (EFJ) Europe's largest organisation representing journalists, defending the professional rights and editorial independence of over 296,000 journalists through 76 associations and unions across 44 countries.
- European Magazine Media Association (EMMA) The representative voice of more than 15,000 publishing houses producing over 50,000 magazine titles across Europe, advocating for a free, diverse and economically sustainable publishing sector.
- European Newspaper Publishers’ Association (ENPA) Europe's largest representative body of newspaper publishers, bringing together 14 national associations across 14 European countries to defend press freedom and the sustainability of independent journalism.
- News Media Europe (NME) A major voice of Europe's news media industry, representing over 2,700 news brands across print, digital, radio and television.
- Global Forum for Media Development (GFMD) A global network of over 200 member organisations across more than 80 countries, uniting media organisations, journalism support groups and civil society to strengthen independent journalism and defend media freedom worldwide.
- Association of European Journalists in Belgium (AEJ Belgium) An independent association bringing together journalists and EU correspondents to defend press freedom, democratic transparency and independent journalism.
Competition and Economic Policy
- Open Markets Institute Europe A competition policy think tank advancing antitrust enforcement, tackling concentrated corporate power and promoting open, competitive markets across Europe.
- Balanced Economy Project An international non-profit organisation tackling excessive corporate power and working towards a fairer, more democratic economy.
- Enforce (Irish Council for Civil Liberties) A specialist initiative advancing digital rights through strategic litigation, regulatory enforcement and technical expertise.
- Innovate Europe Foundation An independent think tank bringing together European technology and business leaders to strengthen Europe's technological sovereignty, innovation and competitiveness.
- Rebalance Now A German non-profit organisation advancing competition policy and tackling monopoly power through research, advocacy and regulatory engagement.
- iconomy A Berlin-based consultancy and venture builder supporting European technology startups and fair competition in digital markets.
Industry Associations, Startups and Investors
- European DIGITAL SME Alliance Europe's largest network of digital SMEs, championing innovation, competitiveness and digital entrepreneurship.
- Y Combinator A world-leading startup accelerator that has helped launch and scale some of the world's most successful technology companies, including Stripe, Airbnb, DoorDash, Reddit and Dropbox.
- France Digitale A leading European startup association, advancing entrepreneurship, investment and technological innovation.
- German Startup Association A leading voice for Germany's startup ecosystem, advocating for innovation and entrepreneurship.
- Coalition for App Fairness A global coalition advocating for fair competition, consumer choice and open digital marketplaces.
- Movement for an Open Web (MOW) A business coalition that has played a role in challenging Google's dominance of digital advertising through competition complaints and regulatory action.
- European Games Developer Federation A leading representative of Europe's video game development industry, promoting innovation and competitiveness.
- Little Tech Association An organisation supporting technology startups, entrepreneurship and fair competition in digital markets.
Browsers
- Mozilla The non-profit-backed organisation behind Firefox, working to build an open, accessible and competitive internet.
- Vivaldi An independent European browser developer with an emphasis on user choice, privacy and customisation.
- Brave A privacy-focused browser and search engine developer.
- The Tor Project A non-profit organisation developing technologies that protect online anonymity, privacy and freedom from censorship.
Search Engines
- Ecosia A search engine that dedicates its profits to climate action, reforestation and environmental restoration worldwide.
- Qwant A European search engine with a focus on user privacy and European digital sovereignty.
- Kagi An independent, subscription-based search engine offering high-quality, advertisement-free search.
Software, E-Commerce and Online Services
- Shopify One of the world's leading commerce platforms, powering millions of businesses globally and powering hundreds of thousands of online stores across Europe.
- Fastmail A leading independent email provider delivering privacy-focused email, calendar and productivity services to individuals and businesses worldwide.
- Cryptee An Estonian technology company providing end-to-end encrypted document editing, photo management and cloud storage.
- Pelican Party Studios An independent Dutch video game studio developing innovative multiplayer browser games, including the popular Narrow.one.
- Soundslice An innovative web-based music education platform combining interactive sheet music, audio and video to transform how musicians learn, practise and teach music.
- Krellian A technology company developing open standards and web-based technologies to make buildings smarter, safer and more sustainable.
Web Development, Infrastructure and Developer Communities
- Vercel A leading cloud infrastructure and web development platform behind Next.js, powering hundreds of thousands of websites across Europe and millions worldwide.
- Clearleft A digital design consultancy with a longstanding contribution to web standards, accessibility and user experience.
- QuirksMode.org A resource for browser compatibility research, web standards and cross-browser development.
- London Web Standards An established web developer community promoting open web standards and organising the renowned State of the Browser conference.
- RUMvision An innovative web performance monitoring platform helping businesses deliver faster and more accessible web experiences.
- meet.js A Polish JavaScript developer community advancing technical knowledge, collaboration and innovation through conferences and meetups.
See the Full List Of Signatures
The Commission Must Now Act
We welcome the Commission's recognition that browser competition is a priority under the DMA. However in the more than two and a half years after Apple's obligations came into effect, not a single browser vendor has been able to upgrade its existing EU users to its own browser engine.
The extraordinary breadth of this coalition demonstrates both the importance of the web as a competitive platform and the scale of the opportunity being denied to European consumers and businesses.
Apple cannot be allowed to indefinitely frustrate the objectives of the DMA through successive rounds of ineffective compliance. The Commission must now move beyond dialogue, commence formal enforcement proceedings and compel Apple to remove the remaining barriers to effective browser and web app competition.
The web has waited long enough.
A free and competitive web on iOS
Europe is rallying.
Add your voice.
Tell the European Commission: it’s time to enforce the DMA and let the web compete.
Sign the letter
Unlock the Web on Mobile

- European Magazine Media Association (EMMA) The representative voice of more than 15,000 publishing houses producing over 50,000 magazine titles across Europe, advocating for a free, diverse and economically sustainable publishing sector.
- European Newspaper Publishers’ Association (ENPA) Europe's largest representative body of newspaper publishers, bringing together 14 national associations across 14 European countries to defend press freedom and the sustainability of independent journalism.
- News Media Europe (NME) A major voice of Europe's news media industry, representing over 2,700 news brands across print, digital, radio and television.
- Global Forum for Media Development (GFMD) A global network of over 200 member organisations across more than 80 countries, uniting media organisations, journalism support groups and civil society to strengthen independent journalism and defend media freedom worldwide.
- Association of European Journalists in Belgium (AEJ Belgium) An independent association bringing together journalists and EU correspondents to defend press freedom, democratic transparency and independent journalism.
Competition and Economic Policy
- Open Markets Institute Europe A competition policy think tank advancing antitrust enforcement, tackling concentrated corporate power and promoting open, competitive markets across Europe.
- Balanced Economy Project An international non-profit organisation tackling excessive corporate power and working towards a fairer, more democratic economy.
- Enforce (Irish Council for Civil Liberties) A specialist initiative advancing digital rights through strategic litigation, regulatory enforcement and technical expertise.
- Innovate Europe Foundation An independent think tank bringing together European technology and business leaders to strengthen Europe's technological sovereignty, innovation and competitiveness.
- Rebalance Now A German non-profit organisation advancing competition policy and tackling monopoly power through research, advocacy and regulatory engagement.
- iconomy A Berlin-based consultancy and venture builder supporting European technology startups and fair competition in digital markets.
Industry Associations, Startups and Investors
- European DIGITAL SME Alliance Europe's largest network of digital SMEs, championing innovation, competitiveness and digital entrepreneurship.
- Y Combinator A world-leading startup accelerator that has helped launch and scale some of the world's most successful technology companies, including Stripe, Airbnb, DoorDash, Reddit and Dropbox.
- France Digitale A leading European startup association, advancing entrepreneurship, investment and technological innovation.
- German Startup Association A leading voice for Germany's startup ecosystem, advocating for innovation and entrepreneurship.
- Coalition for App Fairness A global coalition advocating for fair competition, consumer choice and open digital marketplaces.
- Movement for an Open Web (MOW) A business coalition that has played a role in challenging Google's dominance of digital advertising through competition complaints and regulatory action.
- European Games Developer Federation A leading representative of Europe's video game development industry, promoting innovation and competitiveness.
- Little Tech Association An organisation supporting technology startups, entrepreneurship and fair competition in digital markets.
Browsers
- Mozilla The non-profit-backed organisation behind Firefox, working to build an open, accessible and competitive internet.
- Vivaldi An independent European browser developer with an emphasis on user choice, privacy and customisation.
- Brave A privacy-focused browser and search engine developer.
- The Tor Project A non-profit organisation developing technologies that protect online anonymity, privacy and freedom from censorship.
Search Engines
- Ecosia A search engine that dedicates its profits to climate action, reforestation and environmental restoration worldwide.
- Qwant A European search engine with a focus on user privacy and European digital sovereignty.
- Kagi An independent, subscription-based search engine offering high-quality, advertisement-free search.
Software, E-Commerce and Online Services
- Shopify One of the world's leading commerce platforms, powering millions of businesses globally and powering hundreds of thousands of online stores across Europe.
- Fastmail A leading independent email provider delivering privacy-focused email, calendar and productivity services to individuals and businesses worldwide.
- Cryptee An Estonian technology company providing end-to-end encrypted document editing, photo management and cloud storage.
- Pelican Party Studios An independent Dutch video game studio developing innovative multiplayer browser games, including the popular Narrow.one.
- Soundslice An innovative web-based music education platform combining interactive sheet music, audio and video to transform how musicians learn, practise and teach music.
- Krellian A technology company developing open standards and web-based technologies to make buildings smarter, safer and more sustainable.
Web Development, Infrastructure and Developer Communities
- Vercel A leading cloud infrastructure and web development platform behind Next.js, powering hundreds of thousands of websites across Europe and millions worldwide.
- Clearleft A digital design consultancy with a longstanding contribution to web standards, accessibility and user experience.
- QuirksMode.org A resource for browser compatibility research, web standards and cross-browser development.
- London Web Standards An established web developer community promoting open web standards and organising the renowned State of the Browser conference.
- RUMvision An innovative web performance monitoring platform helping businesses deliver faster and more accessible web experiences.
- meet.js A Polish JavaScript developer community advancing technical knowledge, collaboration and innovation through conferences and meetups.
See the Full List Of Signatures
The Commission Must Now Act
We welcome the Commission's recognition that browser competition is a priority under the DMA. However in the more than two and a half years after Apple's obligations came into effect, not a single browser vendor has been able to upgrade its existing EU users to its own browser engine.
The extraordinary breadth of this coalition demonstrates both the importance of the web as a competitive platform and the scale of the opportunity being denied to European consumers and businesses.
Apple cannot be allowed to indefinitely frustrate the objectives of the DMA through successive rounds of ineffective compliance. The Commission must now move beyond dialogue, commence formal enforcement proceedings and compel Apple to remove the remaining barriers to effective browser and web app competition.
The web has waited long enough.
A free and competitive web on iOS
Europe is rallying.
Add your voice.
Tell the European Commission: it’s time to enforce the DMA and let the web compete.
Sign the letter
Unlock the Web on Mobile

articles.title: Here are the best Black Friday deals you can grab for $30 or less
articles.body:
What can you get for $30 these days? When it comes to tech, you might be surprised. Even as gadgets get more expensive, $30 can still go a long way, especially on Black Friday. For just $8, for instance, TP-Link’s Tapo smart plug will let you control the Christmas tree lights from your phone. You can also grab a decent pair of ANC-equipped earbuds for under $20, or spend even less on a clever set of rechargeable AA batteries. And it’s not just gadgets that are on sale: you can even sign up for a year of Disney Plus and Hulu for $4.99 ($8 off) a month.
Here are the best Black Friday deals you can grab for $30 or less
From smart plugs to noise-canceling earbuds, there’s plenty of discounted tech for those on a tighter budget.
Below, we’ve rounded up the best Black Friday deals for $30 or less, from charging accessories and smart home tech to earbuds, streaming subscriptions, games, and more. Whether you’re looking for practical stocking stuffers or want to treat yourself without spending too much, these are the deals that won’t put a (huge) dent in your wallet.
Apple AirTag (second-gen)
Apple’s latest AirTags feature an upgraded ultra-wideband chip for more precise location tracking, a noticeably louder speaker, and an expanded Bluetooth range. Read our review.
Disney Plus, Hulu Bundle
You can get an ad-supported Disney Plus and Hulu bundle for $4.99 a month ($8 off) for an entire year. Both streaming services feature a deep catalog of new and classic TV shows and movies, including The Simpsons, Andor, Toy Story 5, and The Fantastic Four: First Steps.
SwitchBot Bot Rechargeable
Do you ever wish you could turn on your coffee maker or hit the light switch without getting up? The SwitchBot Bot lets you do that. All you need to do is stick the inexpensive contraption on a standard button or rocker switch, which will allow you to control or schedule your pet feeder, garage door, and a wide range of other devices from your smartphone.
Octobuddy Classic
Who needs magnets when you have suction cups? Octobuddy’s cheap silicone mount works with most phones to provide hands-free flexibility whenever necessary. It features 24 single-sided cups, which allow you to stick your phone to a mirror, window, or any other surface you think will provide that perfect TikTok angle.
Kodak Charmera Keychain Digital Camera
The Chamera is not a good camera, but that’s not the point. Kodak’s charming, keychain-friendly tchotchke lets you snap lo-fi memories on a whim, with an ultra-small 1.6-megapixel sensor, a built-in LED flash, and the tiniest amount of storage.
Hoto 3.6V Electric Screwdriver Kit Pro
Hoto’s rechargeable screwdriver is ideal for small repairs. It offers three torque modes, a rotational speed of up to 220RPM, and a helpful circular LED to illuminate dark spaces. The durable case also holds all 25 steel bits and an extension bar for getting into hard-to-reach places.
Zepath USB-C Li-ion AA Batteries
Rechargeable AA batteries are handy until it’s time to charge them. Most wall chargers let you refill four, maybe six, at once. Zepath’s clever solution is to ship them in an easy-to-use USB-C charging case that charges eight simultaneously. The batteries themselves are long-lasting, too.
HBO Max
An HBO Max Basic subscription provides access to shows like A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms, The Last of Us, and The Pitt, as well as films like Superman and Weapons. You can get a year of the monthly ad-supported subscription for $5.49 a month (about $6 off) until December 1st.
Wuben G5 rechargeable flashlight
The Wuben G5 flashlight is as small as a Zippo lighter, yet far more versatile, with a bright, rotatable light that can shine in numerous colors. It features USB-C charging and has an adjustable clip.
LifeStraw Sip
The original LifeStraw was designed for those heading into the backcountry. The new LifeStraw Sip? Not so much. The reusable steel straw is geared more toward travelers than outdoor enthusiasts, though fortunately it still manages to remove about 99.99 percent of microplastics, bacteria, and parasites from your drinking water.
Peacock
Peacock is a great way to catch up on a wealth of content from NBC’s various networks, whether you plan to rewatch The Office or catch up on all things Bravo. A Premium subscription also grants access to films from studios like Universal Pictures and DreamWorks, along with live sports and a host of Peacock Originals.
Anker 621 Magnetic Battery (MagGo)
Anker’s 621 Magnetic Battery is a slim, 5,000mAh charger that can attach magnetically to the back of any MagSafe-ready iPhone.
TP-Link Tapo Matter-Certified Smart Plug Mini
TP-Link’s Wi-Fi smart plug lets you remotely control lamps, fans, and other appliances using your phone or voice commands. It supports Matter, so it works with all major smart home platforms to set schedules and timers to automatically turn devices on or off.
Paramount Plus (monthly subscription)
Paramount Plus Premium provides access to live sports as well as movies and shows from both platforms, including Tales of the Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles, a host of Yellowstone spinoffs, Star Trek shows, Sonic the Hedgehog 3, Twin Peaks, Dexter, and more.
Amazon Fire TV Stick 4K Plus
Amazon’s last-gen Fire TV Stick 4K Plus streams in 4K and supports Dolby Atmos, Dolby Vision, and Alexa Plus. It also ships with the redesigned Fire OS and, unlike more recent models, still lets you sideload Android TV apps.
CMF Buds 2A
With 12.4mm drivers, active noise cancellation, and an IP54 rating, the CMF Buds 2A offer high-end features at an affordable price. You can also customize the sound, adjust ANC levels, and find the earbuds using the Nothing X app.
Twelve South AirFly SE
Twelve South’s entry-level Bluetooth transmitter delivers up to 25 hours of continuous use and lets you connect up to two pairs of headphones to an in-flight entertainment system, making it a great travel companion no matter where you’re going.
Catan (6th Edition)
In Catan, up to four players strategically compete and trade for resources. The iconic board game ends when one player reaches 10 “victory points,” which is achieved by constructing a sprawling civilization of roads, settlements, and cities using sheep, ore, wheat, and wood.
Azul
Azul is a game in which you arrange patterned tiles in order to create the most beautiful tapestry possible. Arranging tiles in a strategic sequence will help you build your score while limiting your opponents’ ability to grow theirs.
Halo: Campaign Evolved
Halo: Campaign Evolved lets you revisit the original Halo: Combat Evolved campaign with better graphics, updated controls, and improved sound. The well-crafted remake also adds three new missions starring Master Chief and Sgt. Johnson, which take place before the main campaign. Read our review.
Anker 140W 2-in-1 USB-C to USB-C Cable
No one should have to deal with a rat’s nest behind their desk when devices like Anker’s 2-in-1 USB-C cable exist. The handy USB-C cable splits at the end, giving you the ability to charge up to two devices from a single port. That means you can split power between a phone and tablet or juice a 16-inch MacBook Pro to 50 percent in just 20 minutes using a single port.
The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt Remastered
The Witcher 3 lets you explore the war-torn Northern Kingdoms as Geralt of Rivia while preparing to face the mysterious Wild Hunt. The recent remaster adds improved visuals, smoother combat, and better movement, cementing the game’s status as one of the best RPGs of all time.
Iniu P55-E2 Power Bank (10,000mAh)
Iniu’s P55-E2 Power Bank is an ultra-slim three-port USB charger that’s capable of fully recharging an iPhone 16 twice. It supports charging speeds of up to 45W via a USB-C port, which can deliver fast recharging for a range of gadgets.
Glocusent Bookmark Style Reading Light
Glocusent’s clip-in reading light features five brightness levels and multiple color temperature settings, ranging from a soft, warm glow that’s great for late-night reading to a brighter light that’s perfect for daytime use. The slim USB light easily slips into your pocket, too, so you can read anywhere, from a cozy bed to a dimly lit train.
LIFX Everyday Smart Light Bulbs (two-pack)
LIFX’s dimmable, color-changing bulbs offer Wi-Fi connectivity, simple setup, and Matter compatibility, so they work with any major smart home platform. The company is currently trialing a Thread beta that will bring the option to add Thread connectivity to all its Matter devices.
ChomChom Roller Pet Hair Remover
The ChomChom is a reusable roller that works great for removing unwanted pet hair from furniture, allowing you to skip lint rollers, vacuuming, and other cleaning tools in a pinch.
Apple TV (six-month subscription)
Apple TV offers ad-free streaming of original shows and movies, including shows like Severance, Silo, Slow Horses, and Pluribus. The service also features a rotating selection of films, along with live Formula 1 races and Major League Soccer matches.
Anker Zolo Magnetic Wireless Charger
Anker’s Qi2 charging pads support wireless charging speeds of up to 15W, and their 5-foot cable shouldn’t feel constricting if you need to move the charger around.
Blink Mini 2K Plus
Blink’s Mini 2K Plus is a small plug-in security camera that lets you monitor your home or pets with 2K video, motion detection, and color night vision. It also offers two-way audio, a built-in siren, and Alexa support; however, some features, including person and vehicle detection, require a Blink subscription.
Loop Quiet 2 earplugs
Attending a live concert? You can protect your hearing with Loop’s Quiet 2 earplugs. They pack up to 24dB (SNR) of noise reduction and come with four eartip sizes, allowing them to accommodate a range of ear shapes.
Crunchyroll
Crunchyroll is an anime-centric streaming service that offers ad-free access to shows like One Piece, Jujutsu Kaisen, The Apothecary Diaries, and Black Clover, with new episodes available shortly after they air in Japan.
Logitech Pop Mouse
Logitech’s Pop is a cute, simple wireless mouse with an ambidextrous design and the ability to switch between up to three devices. It supports customization through the Logi Options Plus app and can last for several months on a single charge.
Logitech G502 Hero
Logitech’s G502 Hero has most of the same features as one of our top choices among gaming mice, the G502 Lightspeed, except it’s wired. If you’re okay with that, this is an excellent mouse that you can usually find for $50 or less.
Ugreen Nexode 240W USB-C Cable with Digital Display
The proliferation of miniature screens continues with Ugreen’s latest Nexode USB-C Cable, which features a full-color LCD screen on one end that displays current power draw (up to 240W). It also supports 480Mbps data transfer speeds and, unlike similar power meter-equipped cables, lets you turn off the screen when needed.
Tile Pro
The Tile Pro is the company’s loudest Bluetooth tracker, one that benefits from a 500-foot range. It also features a user-replaceable battery, unlike some other Tiles, and works with both iOS and Android devices.
Anker Nano Travel Adapter (5-in-1, 20W)
Anker’s jack-of-all-trades travel adapter packs enough ports to refill your devices during some downtime. It features one AC outlet, two USB-C ports (one tops out at 20W), and two USB-A ports. It’s not the fastest wall charger, but it’s a solid choice when you can find it at a discount.
Kobo Remote
The Kobo Remote lets you turn pages on a compatible Kobo e-reader with the click of a button, so you can keep reading without reaching for the screen. It connects directly over Bluetooth and features a curved, handheld design that doesn’t require clipping anything onto your e-reader.
Ring Indoor Cam (second-gen)
The second-gen Ring Indoor Cam lets you keep an eye on your place in 1080p, with support for motion detection alerts, a live feed, and color night vision.
Workpro EDC Folding Utility Knife
Workpro’s EDC is a lightweight folding utility knife with a side-mounted button that lets you flick it open and closed with one hand. It uses standard utility blades, which you can easily replace using a spring-loaded plate, making it handy for breaking down cardboard boxes and other tasks.
Lamicall’s cord organizers use magnetic clasps to keep cables in place, preventing them from slipping behind desks, shelves, and other furniture when unplugged.
Nalgene Narrow Mouth water bottle (16-ounce)
Nalgene’s lightweight, 16-ounce water bottle features a narrow opening for sipping, a leakproof lid, and a slim design that fits in cup holders. It’s made from durable, BPA- and BPS-free plastic, with measurement markings along the side and dishwasher-safe construction.
Fanttik S1 Electric Screwdriver
This tiny cordless driver comes with five double-ended bits for most basic around-the-house projects and Ikea-level builds.

articles.title: Five Non-Leadership Books for Leaders
articles.body:
Foundation Trilogy (Isaac Asimov) — There was a decade when I read through this trilogy1 every year or so. Asimov is a fine writer, but his characters are… flat. Their dialogue is equally flat… it’s like reading two LLMs argue about the meaning of life. Empty of heart.
What I appreciate about Asimov’s writing is that most of it is very logical. Characters feel like dispassionate observers of their situation. Describing their fate painfully logically. The fate of the galaxy is quite literally being litigated, but they could just as easily discuss the pros and cons of breakfast for dinner.
It is the Vulcan-like absence of emotion that is required during the hardest parts of being a leader. Everyone is mad — often justifiably — and everyone is looking straight at you with those angry eyes. As a human and as a new manager, your instinct is to prepare for combat, but this is usually the wrong initial response. The longer you listen, gather intelligence, and read the room, the better chance you have to respond coherently.2
Boyd: The Fighter Pilot Who Changed the Art of War (Robert Coram) — Let’s clear the air first. John Boyd was not a good person. You can skip the last quarter of the book where his conduct toward his family and others is described at length. John Boyd is not a person to be admired, but his ideas are worth studying.
This is a book about the decisions that Boyd made, both as a decorated fighter pilot and then as a consultant advising on how fighter planes were built. His contribution — the OODA loop:
- Observe. Figure out where you are.
- Orient. Apply your experience, knowledge, and impressive collection of prior disasters to this situation.
- Decide. Choose your next move to the best of your ability.
- Act. Deploy the decisions and, yup, go back to Observe.
It’s a loop.
This is the barest and simplest of explanations, but like all of these recommendations, the point is not to take my word for it; the point is to soak in the book and see what you discover.
The 48 Laws of Power (Robert Greene) — You were promised non-leadership leadership books, yet… isn’t this a leadership book?
It is not. Ok, maybe a leadership history book. Greene captured and aggregated the leadership philosophies of Machiavelli, Sun Tzu, and others. The laws are pithy: “Never Outshine the Master” or “Win Through Your Actions, Never Through Argument”.
I built a leadership training program where I plopped this book into the reading list without context. I was curious: “What would new leaders find in this book?”
Their first question was, “Is this real?”
Sort’a.
“Is this how I should act as a leader?”
Definitely not.
“Why did you have us read this?”
The #1 answer to most questions I am asked regarding leadership is, “Well, it depends.” It depends on the people involved, their level of experience, the state of their relationship, the culture of the team and the company, and a lot more. Those who provide one-line answers to leadership questions are giving a possibly useful starting point, not an answer.
Universal Principles of Design (William Lidwell, Kritina Holden, Jill Butler) — There’s a moment in your leadership career when you are going to be up against another team whose craft is unfamiliar and that you are dependent on. Design is one of those teams that I spent much of my early career thinking, “Really need this team and pretty sure they can perform magic.”
It’s not magic. It’s just hard work.
There are a great many books to help you begin to dissect the craft of design, but Universal Principles of Design gave me my first working model for all the different work that goes into design, as well as a remedial initial understanding. Remedial, not because the work is simple, just my starting understanding. If you build things, you will build better things when you understand all the different ways it can be built.3
Accidental Empires (Robert X. Cringely) — I’m including this mostly because I’m still sad that Cringely recently passed away. Like Robert B. Parker, Cringely had an outsized influence on my writing. This book is leadership-adjacent because while many of his stories are exaggerated or perhaps straight-up not true, many are.
I admire many of the leaders that you admire, but I also know that every single one of them is deeply flawed. It’s comforting to tell the stories of your heroes, but I believe every time you tell that story, it becomes more about how you feel about the story rather than what actually occurred. I suspect Cringely’s exaggerations and stretches of the truth are simply that. He wrote about Silicon Valley rumors where the more incendiary the rumor, the more copies of InfoWorld sold.
Accidental Empires is a good education in storytelling, but it is also a solid reminder that even though the stories are suspect, these are most certainly deeply flawed humans making incredibly important decisions that affect you… daily.
Applied Judgment
In the new world where you can have your robot read the article, the book, or the website, you can feel empowered by asking the robots to give you a summary — the key bits of important information. It’s satisfying, but it’s just information. You’ve done nothing with it. You’ve confused the act of understanding with the act of acquisition.
What are the critical bits of information in each of these five books? It depends entirely on you. Foundation might bore you with a manner of logical thinking you already have. Same with the insights on decisions that Boyd suggests. 48 Laws of Power resonated with me because, at the time, I was developing as a senior leader, and I was baffled by the actions of other senior leaders. Actions that were clearly described in 48 Laws of Power… not specifically, but broadly. The way I applied my learnings to that situation, using the story of that law of power, is likely totally different from how you’d act in the same situation.
I return to each of these books frequently because the information conveyed by the stories didn’t just resonate with me; it changed me. Universal Principles of Design made the seemingly unapproachable craft of design understandable. It allowed me to see how small choices greatly affect both the usability and the feeling of a thing. I return to Accidental Empires (like Microserfs) regularly to remember the stories of how it started and who was responsible.
And that they are just humans. Working hard. Deeply flawed. Acting and applying judgment from what they’ve learned and read.
- You don’t need to read the whole trilogy to get the vibe. ↩︎
- The whole Robot Series is worth a read and introduces the Laws of Robotics, which are worth a think in this day and age. ↩︎
- Love this. ↩︎

Attorneys General Jones and Rayfield File Suit Against SpaceX, Parent Company of X, xAI, and Grok, Over Creation and Promotion of Child Exploitation and Non-Consensual Images on Platform 
Virginia and Oregon Attorneys General seek accountability for harms and significant new protections for consumers 
***Read the full filing here***
RICHMOND, Va. – Today, Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones took a significant step in holding operators of X and its AI tool, Grok, accountable for knowingly failing to protect Virginians, while falsely promoting the safety of its platform and AI tool.
In the lawsuit, the Commonwealth of Virginia alleges that SpaceX, the telecommunications and space transportation conglomerate that operates the social network X and its artificial intelligence company, xAI (now called “SpaceX Super Intelligence”), and developed the Grok family of large language models, failed to prevent Grok from generating sexualized images of people, including children, without their knowledge or consent—while simultaneously promoting the safety of the social media platform and AI tool. The Grok-generated content includes non-consensual intimate imagery (NCII), other non-consensual sexualized images, and Child Sexual Abuse Material (CSAM). Today’s suit was filed in collaboration with Oregon Attorney General Dan Rayfield, who filed a separate but similar action.
“This lawsuit is about seeking justice for the millions of Virginians who maintain accounts on X and were misled by the company’s false reassurances that their data and images would be safe on the platform,” said Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones. “When xAI allowed Grok’s creators to sideline consent to turn a profit, they prioritized growth and engagement over safety, and they deceived the public about it. Today’s filings are the first step towards holding this company accountable.”
With a single existing photograph, Grok could, and did, fabricate a realistic image or video of a person nude, or partially nude, or engaged in sexual activity, all without the individual’s knowledge or consent. This violation is not acceptable.
The company ignored industry-standard safeguards so xAI could distinguish itself in the AI arms race. Grok’s ability to generate sexualized content was leveraged as a promotional opportunity. These exploitations of Virginian’s safety enabled the widespread creation and distribution of sexualized images through Grok’s integration with X.
“SpaceX allowed Grok and the X platform to create, host, and share unacceptable and dangerous content—and in fact knowingly designed a product without the obviously necessary safeguards in place,” said Attorney General Rayfield. “It’s no surprise that Grok and X became a haven for perpetrators using AI to create and share child sexual abuse material. The lack of needed safety measures was considered a feature, not a bug, which they promoted as ‘spicy mode.’”
In his filing, Attorney General Jones shows that SpaceX and its subsidiaries marketed Grok as an AI companion with a “rebellious streak,” knowing that its video and image generation technology would be used to produce CSAM, non-consensual intimate images of adults and children (NCII), and other sexualized imagery. In fact, X and its subsidiaries created and promoted a “spicy mode” that specifically allowed for the creation of nude and otherwise sexualized images.
A study by the Center for Countering Digital Harm (“CCDH”) estimated that, between December 29, 2025, and January 8, 2026, Grok created and posted on X approximately three million sexualized images, including approximately 23,000 images that appeared to depict children. That’s an average pace of roughly 190 sexualized images per minute, and one sexualized image of a child approximately every 41 seconds. Nearly 30% of the sexualized images of children identified by CCDH in its study remained publicly accessible in posts on X a week or more after they were identified—and even many of those that were “removed” could still be accessed via separate URLs.
SpaceX and its subsidiaries publicly assured consumers that robust protections were in place to prevent Grok from creating CSAM, NCII, and other sexualized images. In reality, millions of people — including in Oregon and Virginia — were nevertheless exposed to harmful content and the risk that their own images could be manipulated into sexually explicit content without their consent.
“Time and again, xAI and X told consumers they were being protected from abuses. That was false. Instead, the tool permitted users to routinely create and circulate non-consensual intimate imagery and sexualized images, and child sexual abuse material (CSAM), causing harm to individuals and children,” added Attorney General Jones. “Companies that deploy powerful tools don’t get to ignore consumer safety and call it innovation. The law applies to everyone, and this office will hold big tech accountable when they break the law.”
“Like the other technology companies that we’re holding accountable, xAI not only knowingly endangered kids and our communities, but they also lied to our faces about non-existent safety measures,” added Attorney General Rayfield.
Attorney General Jones’ lawsuit was filed in the Circuit Court for the City of Richmond. Attorney General Rayfield’s lawsuit was filed in Multnomah County Circuit Court.
Published on: November 23, 2026
###

The company ignored industry-standard safeguards so xAI could distinguish itself in the AI arms race. Grok’s ability to generate sexualized content was leveraged as a promotional opportunity. These exploitations of Virginian’s safety enabled the widespread creation and distribution of sexualized images through Grok’s integration with X.
“SpaceX allowed Grok and the X platform to create, host, and share unacceptable and dangerous content—and in fact knowingly designed a product without the obviously necessary safeguards in place,” said Attorney General Rayfield. “It’s no surprise that Grok and X became a haven for perpetrators using AI to create and share child sexual abuse material. The lack of needed safety measures was considered a feature, not a bug, which they promoted as ‘spicy mode.’”
In his filing, Attorney General Jones shows that SpaceX and its subsidiaries marketed Grok as an AI companion with a “rebellious streak,” knowing that its video and image generation technology would be used to produce CSAM, non-consensual intimate images of adults and children (NCII), and other sexualized imagery. In fact, X and its subsidiaries created and promoted a “spicy mode” that specifically allowed for the creation of nude and otherwise sexualized images.
A study by the Center for Countering Digital Harm (“CCDH”) estimated that, between December 29, 2025, and January 8, 2026, Grok created and posted on X approximately three million sexualized images, including approximately 23,000 images that appeared to depict children. That’s an average pace of roughly 190 sexualized images per minute, and one sexualized image of a child approximately every 41 seconds. Nearly 30% of the sexualized images of children identified by CCDH in its study remained publicly accessible in posts on X a week or more after they were identified—and even many of those that were “removed” could still be accessed via separate URLs.
SpaceX and its subsidiaries publicly assured consumers that robust protections were in place to prevent Grok from creating CSAM, NCII, and other sexualized images. In reality, millions of people — including in Oregon and Virginia — were nevertheless exposed to harmful content and the risk that their own images could be manipulated into sexually explicit content without their consent.
“Time and again, xAI and X told consumers they were being protected from abuses. That was false. Instead, the tool permitted users to routinely create and circulate non-consensual intimate imagery and sexualized images, and child sexual abuse material (CSAM), causing harm to individuals and children,” added Attorney General Jones. “Companies that deploy powerful tools don’t get to ignore consumer safety and call it innovation. The law applies to everyone, and this office will hold big tech accountable when they break the law.”
“Like the other technology companies that we’re holding accountable, xAI not only knowingly endangered kids and our communities, but they also lied to our faces about non-existent safety measures,” added Attorney General Rayfield.
Attorney General Jones’ lawsuit was filed in the Circuit Court for the City of Richmond. Attorney General Rayfield’s lawsuit was filed in Multnomah County Circuit Court.
Published on: November 23, 2026

articles.title: Norse Atlantic suspends all flights as it faces potential collapse
articles.body:
Norse Atlantic suspends all flights as it faces potential collapse
The Norwegian low cost carrier Norse Atlantic Airways has suspended all flights as it rushes to resolve what it warned is a critical financial situation.
The airline said if no solution can be found, it intends to file for bankruptcy.
It uses a fleet of 12 Boeing 787 aircraft on long-haul routes from a number of European airports, including London Gatwick, Rome and Oslo.
Prior to the suspension of flights, it was advertising services from London to Orlando, Cape Town, Bangkok and Phuket.
Flight disruption
One aircraft was meant to depart London for Orlando this morning, while another was meant to arrive from Cape Town this evening.
The suspension has also affected Pakistan International Airlines, which had been leasing aircraft and crews from Norse Atlantic.
PIA was forced to cancel services from London to Islamabad and from Manchester to Lahore last night.
In a statement on social media, PIA said all UK flights from today would be operated by aircraft from its own fleet.
Londoner Fred was due to fly to Cape Town with Norse Atlantic next week for a friend's wedding, but has decided to change his plans.
"Yesterday the exact same flight I was going to get was cancelled, so I was worried" he told the BBC's Your Voice. "I sent an email to Norse and have had nothing back".
He decided to rebook with a different airline, which cost him an extra £1,000.
Another traveller, Claire from Herefordshire, is currently on holiday in South Africa with her daughter.
"We are due to fly home on Sunday and are now looking at a really expensive flight back," she said.
"We have tried contacting Norse but have been given an automated response saying someone will get back to us within three business days."
Advice for passengers
Consumer group Which? advised Norse Atlantic customers to not cancel their flights as the airline has not collapsed. Doing so removes passengers' right to a refund.
Rory Boland, Which? travel editor, said: "If Norse does go bust, whether you get a refund depends on how you booked and paid. If you booked directly with Norse, you may be able to claim a refund via your credit card provider, or possibly your debit card."
Those stuck abroad should contact insurers, while those with package holidays reliant on Norse Atlantic flights should contact their tour operator, he added.
Low-cost, long-haul
Norse Atlantic Airways was set up in 2021 as a low-cost long-haul carrier.
It entered the market as a successor to Norwegian, which withdrew from long haul routes as a result of the Covid pandemic.
But it has struggled to make money, and its problems worsened this year, as fuel prices rocketed due to the war in Iran.
Unlike many other European carriers, Norse Atlantic does not hedge its fuel bills by buying supplies in advance at fixed prices.
This left it fully exposed when prices soared, with the cost of fuel roughly doubling at one point. Prices remain significantly higher than they were before the conflict began.
In the first half of the year Norse Atlantic made a loss of $94.6m.
In a statement to the Oslo Stock Exchange on Wednesday, the airline said its financial situation was critical, and it needed to find short term funding to continue its operations.
After suspending flights, the company said it was in discussions with investors regarding a possible takeover that "would include a financing solution".
However, it said if short term funding could not be found quickly, "it is the Board's intention to file for bankruptcy".
Norse Atlantic had been looking for a buyer since July.
Its potential collapse follows the failure of Spirit Airlines in May. The US-based low cost carrier was another airline left exposed when jet fuel prices soared, as US airlines typically do not hedge their purchases.
If Norse Atlantic were to fold, it would be another major setback for the low-cost long-haul model, which has typically proved popular with passengers but difficult to sustain financially, especially on transatlantic routes.
Additional reporting by Rozina Sini
