articles.title: New York and California Age Gating Rules Go into Effect in the New Year
articles.body:
Come January 2027, everyday social media browsing in two of the country's largest states will look noticeably different. In California, AB 1709 (2026), AB 1043 (2025), and SB 976 (2024) are slated to take effect on January 1, 2027. Meanwhile, state attorney general regulations for New York’s Stop Addictive Feeds Exploitation (SAFE) for Kids Act take effect on January 25, 2027.
EFF has opposed these laws across legislatures, regulatory proceedings, and the courts. The core problem is simple: age-gating mandates trade away everyday user privacy and free expression under the guise of safety, while pushing platforms to gather even more personal data on users.
What California’s Rules Say
Three interlocking California laws take effect on January 1, 2027, reshaping how platforms handle age checks and design features for young users. First, SB 976 (2024) requires verifiable parental consent before platforms can offer algorithmic feeds or nighttime notifications to anyone under 18. Second, AB 1709 (2026) goes even further by outright banning "addictive features," including personalized recommendation algorithms, autoplay, and endless scroll, for users under 16, even with parental permission. Third, the Digital Age Assurance Act (AB 1043, 2025) mandates age-assurance checks across devices (operating systems) and apps, serving as the enforcement backbone for those restrictions. Together with the California Attorney General’s proposed rules on SB 976, which outline age-gating methods, accuracy, circumvention, and parental consent, these laws force platforms into a two-tier design that walls young people off from basic content-discovery tools, puts everyone's privacy at risk to prove their age, and has already drawn First Amendment lawsuits from social media companies against both SB 976 and AB 1709.
For example: rather than minimizing corporate surveillance and data collection by passing stronger privacy laws, the SB 976 regulations encourage companies to evaluate behavioral patterns, collected user data, digital interactions, and metadata to estimate age (Sec. 561(a)(2)), alongside location data collected for other purposes (Sec. 565). Good privacy laws should discourage collecting that information in the first place, not reward broader tracking.
At the same time, these age assurance rules build in steep error rates and weak safeguards. They acknowledge that age-verification tools can misclassify young people as adults, allowing false-positive rates of up to 8% for 16-year-olds and 15% for 17-year-olds (Sec. 561(c)(4)(iv)). Yet the rules set no benchmarks at all for false negatives, meaning adults (especially 18- to 20-year-olds) are likely to be wrongly flagged as under 18. They also recognize demographic bias in facial recognition, yet offer no concrete fix, vaguely telling companies to take mitigating measures like correcting dataset imbalances (Sec. 563(a)(6)). While users can appeal wrong age estimates, the rules set no firm deadlines, meaning mistakes can drag on without a prompt fix, blocking user access (Sec. 564). Worse, requiring platforms to let users report others they suspect are under the age of 18 (Sec. 567) invites targeted harassment by bad actors, while rules telling companies to account for users trying to “conceal or misrepresent” their California location (Sec. 565) risk penalizing everyday VPN users.
What New York’s Rules Say
Along the same lines as the California regulations, New York’s SAFE for Kids Act restricts personalized recommendations and nighttime notifications (between midnight and 6am) without required consent, and mandates that platforms run age assurance and determine user location. If a user does not verify their age or is estimated to be under-18, they will either be relegated to an account with no personalized recommendations and nighttime notifications (if the platform creates one), or prohibited from accessing the platform/service.
As we detailed in our December 2025 comments to the New York Attorney General, age-verification mandates inevitably chill access to online speech. And the final regulations introduce several troubling specifics.
The New York regulations use broad definitions for "age estimation," "age inference," and "age verification" (700.1(h)–(j)) that push companies to collect and retain more personal information from users. Even where privacy protections apply to that information, users cannot sue or enforce those rights themselves, since enforcement rests solely with the Attorney General (700.8). Worse, the rule’s definition of deletion appears to let companies "de-identify" age-assurance data and keep using it in that form, potentially feeding AI model training and creating re-identification risks if leaked or stolen. At the same time, platforms are required to hold onto records (including a user's age status and compliance data) for five years, increasing the risk of misuse or breaches (700.7(b)).
Echoing the problems in California, location and accuracy regulations bring further privacy and security risks. The regulations demand that operators must weigh all reliable location information and take reasonable steps to detect user efforts to “conceal or misrepresent” being in New York, which expands location tracking and threatens VPN use (700.2(d)(2)). On accuracy, the rules permit up to a 15% false-positive rate for 17-year-olds (700.1(b)), yet just like the California rules, say nothing about false negatives—meaning adults, especially 18- to 20-year-olds, are likely to be wrongly flagged as under 18. When that happens, the appeals process can take longer than 10 days, leaving misclassified adults locked out of standard features (or platforms altogether) for over a week.
What This Means for Users in NY and CA
Under both states' regimes, many users will be pressed to hand over personal information just to access standard features like personalized feeds or notifications, while social media companies are encouraged to monitor (and monetize) user behavior even more closely. Because these laws define "addictive feeds" so broadly that the label covers virtually every basic recommendation tool (including feeds built from who you follow, posts you like, or topics you say you are interested in), platforms face a stark choice: either build stripped-down versions of their apps without algorithmic feeds, likes, or notifications, or simply boot any account suspected of belonging to someone under 18. Either way, all users, and especially young people across both states, risk being shut out of major online spaces as they exist today.
When young people lose accounts or get pushed into stripped-down experiences, they lose contact with friends, support groups, community organizing, local news, creative audiences, and ways to speak out on current issues. U.S. law has long recognized that people under 18 have their own constitutional rights to speak and receive information, and sweeping age gates directly interfere with those rights.
At the same time, lawmakers often sell age-verification mandates as a way to rein in Big Tech, yet the opposite happens in practice. Megacorporations like Meta and Google have the resources to build expensive age-estimation systems and absorb steep fines (such as $50,000 per violation in California) while they figure out compliance. Smaller platforms and independent communities such as Bluesky or Dreamwidth, however, cannot afford those legal risks or engineering costs. As we have already seen in states like Mississippi, crushing compliance burdens push smaller sites out of the market and drive users back toward the biggest corporate giants. Instead of holding Big Tech accountable, these rules entrench its dominance; leaving everyone with fewer community options, less innovation, and a more centralized surveillance machine.
Help Us Help You
Legislative and regulatory action are setbacks, but they do not settle the debate. If these rules affect you in California, New York, or anywhere else: keep a record while the details are still fresh, and share it with our team at agegates@eff.org.
Take screenshots and note the date, time, service, and what you were trying to do; write down what you lost (whether that means an account, a club or volunteer group, contact with friends, local news, or a favorite creator) or note if you chose to walk away from a service rather than submit an ID or personal data. You do not need to hand over sensitive information to show that these rules burdened you. If you hit an age check or parental-consent snag, save what the platform asked for, whether it worked or failed, any privacy promises or laws cited, and any appeal attempts.
If these restrictions get in your way, email EFF at agegates@eff.org and tell us what happened. Tracking real-world lockouts, age-check failures, and infringements on free speech puts us in a stronger position to challenge the worst of these restrictions in legislatures and the courts. At the same time, we will keep fighting for laws that actually make people safer online by curbing corporate surveillance and giving parents, youth, and all internet users meaningful choice and control.

articles.title: Nvidia CEO's comeback fuels debate on misogyny or impunity for rich and powerful
articles.body:
NEW YORK (AP) — Just over a year ago, the chief executive officer of an Ohio tech company was forced to resign when he was caught on video embracing an employee at a Coldplay concert. The CEO of McDonald's was among several pushed out over a consensual relationship at the height of the #MeToo movement.
Now the stunning reinstatement of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang despite similar allegations of sexual misconduct is fueling fears of a resurgence of impunity for the rich and powerful.
Huang resigned from Nvidia after he admitted to having an extramarital affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy, and following reports that he was involved with a second woman who was his subordinate. Huang has acknowledged that he violated the company's code of conduct, which warns against personal relationships that may create conflicts of interest.
But in an extraordinary turnaround following a pressure campaign from Huang's tech allies and President Donald Trump, Nvidia's board voted unanimously Monday to reinstate him. The board said it had received assurances from the U.S. government that Huang was not a national security concern, but there was no mention of the sexual misconduct allegations at the center of the scandal.
WATCH: How Trump may have profited from Huang's return to Nvidia
Trump, however, did address Huang's personal conduct
The president, who has a history of marital infidelity and has faced allegations of sexual assault he says are false, predicted the scandal would only help Huang's reputation.
"Sex sells, fellas," Trump declared in an interview on CNBC.
He also posted a doctored image of Huang raising a red bra in triumph, a pose that parodied a famous photograph of Trump himself moments after he survived a 2024 assassination attempt in Butler, Pennsylvania.
The White House did not immediately respond to a request by The Associated Press for comment Wednesday.
'Horrible message to men everywhere'
Trump's response reinforces the impression "that there is a class of men who see violence against women, coercion of women as a currency of power," said Cheyenne Hunt, an attorney who founded the advocacy group Reckoning Action after her role in bringing to light the sexual assault allegations that brought down Democratic Sen. Eric Swalwell and Maine Senate candidate Graham Platner.
"This sends a horrible message to men everywhere that it's open season on their direct reports," Hunt said.
READ MORE: What Trump told PBS News about Jensen Huang before Nvidia reinstatement
Randall Peterson, a professor of organizational behavior at the London Business School, said the #MeToo movement had reinforced the idea that company leaders who engage in relationships with subordinates "are in serious trouble because you cannot rule out coercion. You just cannot."
Peterson said the messaging now is that "you are at risk, as in the days before #MeToo."
"I'm sad about that," he said. "I thought we had moved on from that."
An apologetic but jubilant comeback
Huang, for his part, apologized to his employees a day after returning to Nvidia, saying he had made mistakes and was in daily therapy, according to a livestreamed meeting reviewed by The New York Times. He also warned that his reinstatement didn't mean other employees could violate the company's code of conduct, saying that "sometimes, it's appropriate to forgive" and "sometimes it's not."
He also addressed a report by The Times about his management style that included publicly berating and threatening violence against employees. He acknowledged he had sometimes gone too far and promised that the company's human resources department would henceforth collect feedback about his conduct.
The saga, however, has "made very clear that Huang is untouchable," said Ann Lipton, a University of Colorado Boulder law professor who specializes in corporate and securities law.
WATCH: How Trump may have profited from Huang's return to Nvidia
"It suggests that if you've had a certain amount of success, then you should be able to get away with pretty much whatever you want," Lipton said.
That's especially true in the male-dominated tech industry, she added, citing Meta founder Mark Zuckerberg's comment last year that corporate culture needed more "masculine energy."
The Nvidia scandal has brought scrutiny to the independence of its 10-member board and a corporate culture centered around hero-worshiping its celebrity CEO.
Thousands of people, including former and current employees, had signed a petition calling for Huang's return. Nvidia's collapsing stock had fueled fears that the AI bubble would pop and, for Huang supporters, bolstered their argument that his vision, connections and deal-making skills were indispensable to the entire industry.
WATCH: What's next for Nvidia and Jensen Huang after Trump's intervention
Nvidia's shares rocketed up 31.5% upon his reinstatement on Monday — although they have since fallen — and employees chanted Huang's name as he returned to headquarters. The company did not respond to requests for comment for this story.
Freada Kapor Klein, an investor and activist in equity and access issues around tech, said Nvidia and other successful tech startups "become cult-like. And people get addicted almost to being part of this inside powerful club."
While America has a history of industries idolizing big names like Henry Ford or Andrew Carnegie, tech culture adds to that by "glorifying geniuses. And so there is something extra special about technological prowess, more than or on top of just business success," Klein said.
Speaking up in the face of impunity
Women make up just 21% of Nvidia's global workforce and an even smaller share of its managers and leaders, according to the company's latest sustainability report, which touts its efforts to achieve gender pay parity as well as establish employee resource groups for women and other groups, and family-supporting policies such as generous paid parental leave.
The company's code of conduct, meanwhile, says employees "must report" suspected violations and offers extensive guidelines and reassurances about protection against retaliation.
Huang's triumphant return, however, is exactly the sort of outcome that silences victims of sexual misconduct, said Fatima Goss Graves, president and CEO of the National Women's Law Center, which runs the Time's Up Legal Defense Fund, a program to support workers facing sexual harassment.
Still, she said the legacy of the #MeToo movement continues to inspire women to speak out about sexual harassment and misconduct, adding that public scandals like the one at Nvidia sometimes provoke outrage that leads to an uptick in complaints to Time's Up and other organizations.
Goss Graves noted that on the same day Huang was reinstated, Democratic Rep. Jimmy Gomez of California resigned from Congress after the House Ethics Committee released a report finding "substantial evidence" that he made unwelcome sexual advances toward a House staffer and subjected the staffer to unwanted sexual contact, the latest in a string of lawmakers or candidates brought down by misconduct allegations in recent months.
Meanwhile, Trump's role in getting Huang's job back drew immediate bipartisan fire and the CEO is expected to testify next week before the Senate Banking Committee.
"What comes next really matters," Goss Graves said. "If everybody shrugs their shoulders and says some people are too important to be held accountable, then we will have a problem."
Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue.

articles.title: ‘The Book of the Human Body’ Surveys 2,000 Years of Remarkable Anatomical Inquiry
articles.body:
‘The Book of the Human Body’ Surveys 2,000 Years of Remarkable Anatomical Inquiry
As long as humans have been around, we’ve been curious about existential questions like, Why are we here? And how do things work? That goes for our own bodies, too. But in our era of modern science and medicine, it’s difficult to imagine a time when physicians weren’t familiar with all of the bones in the skeleton, how a baby grows inside a womb, or how the cardiovascular system works. Even the profession that comes to mind when we think of a doctor didn’t really emerge until the past few centuries. During the medieval period, barber-surgeons were the primary medical practitioners (yes, the people who cut hair also conducted surgeries).
As medicine morphed into a scientific and intellectual pursuit, academies cropped up starting in the late 1700s, such as the College of Philadelphia—the first medical school in the U.S.—and the Edinburgh School of Surgery in Scotland. Ethics were, let’s say, malleable. In Edinburgh, a legal shortage of fresh cadavers used for study in the early 1800s spawned a shady underground trade in bodies, many of which were dug up from new burials in the dead of night. And then there were the famous serial murders committed by William Burke and William Hare, who cashed in by selling well over a dozen of their victims’ corpses to anatomist Robert Knox for use during his lectures. Suffice it to say, some scholars really wanted to understand our innards.
Slated for release in January, The Book of the Human Body delves into the art and science of anatomy, disease, reproduction, and more. Published by TASCHEN, the two-volume set compiles more than 950 images from over 75 rare books and manuscripts from around the world. From ancient analyses to medieval studies to modern diagrams, the anthology surveys the breadth of eras and cultural influences that have shaped our understanding of our physical selves.
Authored by medical historian Richard Barnett, the book celebrates universality and unquenched curiosity. Despite sleeping, breathing, and walking around in our bodies every day, we are often still mystified by much of what makes them work. Throughout history, that sense of wonder has remained constant. Barnett says, “Whatever they might represent, whatever they might express, these extraordinary images have lost none of their power to shock or captivate, to teach or inspire.”
Illustrations include a silk manuscript dated to 168 B.C.E., discovered in a tomb in southern China, which features 44 figures engaged in exercises of “self-cultivation,” plus excerpts from Andreas Vesalius’s anatomical atlas, Fabrica, published in 1543. “In all of these examples, the illustrations stand out not only as objects of medical understanding, but as conspicuous works of art in their own right,” the publisher says.
Pre-order your copy on Bookshop.

articles.title: Scientists Used Seabirds To Track Hidden Ships
articles.body:
Scientists Used Seabirds To Track Hidden Ships 19
			
		 	
				Scientists equipped seabirds with audio recorders and GPS trackers to detect fishing vessels that were not broadcasting their locations through the Automatic Identification System (AIS), according to a new study published in Science Advances. They found that unseen vessels accounted for about 32% of vessel-related audio detections in the North Atlantic and 12% in the Mediterranean. "The one petrel in the study interacted with vessels in the South Pacific, but its geolocation device was damaged, so it was not possible to calculate how many ships it encountered had their trackers off," adds 404 Media. From the report:  Many vessels are required to continuously signal their location using the Automatic Identification System (AIS), which openly broadcasts a ship's location, similar to flight tracking. But AIS can be disabled for legitimate reasons -- such as evading pirates -- or with more nefarious motivations, such as concealment of illegal fishing activities.  The new study was not designed to interrogate why any particular vessel switched off its AIS tracker. However, the discovery that seabirds are regularly interacting with unseen ships can shed light on broader efforts to monitor commercial fisheries, while also revealing new insights about seabird behavior, especially their risk of becoming "bycatch" when they are fatally trapped in fishing gear.
Unseen vessel activity "is concerning, or at least important, regardless of whether it's legal or illegal," said Jonathan Rutter, a postdoctoral research fellow at the University of Oxford who led the study, in a call with 404 Media. He added that the recordings were not intended to be used for law-enforcement or surveillance, but that this line of research could become a "powerful tool for improving risk assessment" by recording seabird-vessel interactions that would otherwise be off the map.

articles.title: Our favorite headphones and earbuds are cheaper than ever for Black Friday
articles.body:
If you haven’t already caved and bought a fresh set of wireless earbuds, over-ear headphones, or bone conduction headphones this year, Black Friday is rewarding you with a colossal amount of deals, including discounts on the best models available. Apple, Beats, Soundcore, Sony, Nothing, and other major brands are offering some of the best prices we’ve seen on many of their products, whether you’re on a tight sub-$100 budget or willing to spend more (but still want a great deal). We’re seeing some surprisingly great sale prices, especially on noise-canceling earbuds like the AirPods Pro 3 and Soundcore Liberty 5 Pro.
Our favorite headphones and earbuds are cheaper than ever for Black Friday
We’re seeing the lowest prices to date on the AirPods Pro 3, Sony’s XM4C, and even bone conduction headphones.
Bose QuietComfort Headphones Gen 2
Bose’s second-gen QuietComfort Headphones build on the original with better sound quality and support for lossless audio over USB-C. They also offer improved noise cancellation and are more comfortable thanks to their lack of “eardrum suck.”
Shokz OpenRun
The standard OpenRun are a lighter option than the newer OpenRun Pro 2, with a streamlined wraparound design, up to eight hours of battery life, and an IP67 rating for better water resistance. However, they don’t offer the same bass performance or USB-C charging.
Beats Studio Pro
The latest Beats Studio Pro feature improved noise cancellation, sound quality, and comfort. They also support lossless audio over USB-C and offer native support for a range of iOS and Android features like other Beats headphones. Read our review.
Apple AirPods Max (second-gen)
We consider the second-gen AirPods Max a worthy successor to the original. The over-ear headphones boast fantastic sound and a few useful features that first-time buyers will likely love. But first-gen owners aren’t missing out on much. Read our review.
Soundcore Liberty 5 Pro
The Liberty 5 Pro are Soundcore’s most impressive wireless earbuds yet. At this price, they’re a steal, thanks to their superb call quality and a slew of other features typically reserved for higher-end models. Read our review.
Nothing Headphone (1) Pro
Nothing’s first attempt at pro-grade headphones is a hit. The 1 Pro are comfortable, with great sound from its triple-driver design, and they support Auracast. Their ANC isn’t quite at the level of pricier competitors, but they’re a solid value at the Black Friday price. Read our review.
Sony WH-1000XM6 headphones
Sony’s best wireless headphones yet in terms of sound quality and active noise cancellation (plus the return of a foldable design from the XM4), the XM6 also bring a higher price tag. Despite the current (lowest yet) deal, they’re $208 more than their predecessor, the XM5. Read our review.
Nothing Headphone 1
Nothing’s first over-ear headphones have a retro transparent design and high-end features like active noise cancellation, spatial audio with head tracking, and plush ear pads. They also feature a paddle button that allows you to control music playback. Read our review.
Beats Studio Buds Plus
The Studio Buds Plus are priced correctly for the moment. The comfort, sound, ANC, and battery life are fantastic for $90 (and that transparent option is stellar), though some might be best served by spending $60 more for the feature-rich AirPods Pro 3. Read our review.
Beats 360 headphones
The Beats 360 are ANC headphones for people who prefer headphones over earbuds at the gym. They’re Beats’ first IP-rated cans, with ear cushions that you can easily remove for cleaning (or style points). They also stay in place during most exercises, while still delivering solid bass. Read our review.
Sony WH-1000XM4C
Sony’s XM4 noise-canceling headphones were so good, the company brought them back with a few minor improvements. They still offer great ANC, a timeless foldable design, and performance nearly on par with Sony’s newer flagships at a fraction of the cost. If you don’t need a folding design, opt for the XM5, which are $20 less. Read our review.
Nothing Headphone A
Nothing’s second over-ear headphones may not offer everything found on the pricier Nothing Headphone 1, but you do get physical controls, good sound, and more than five days of battery life per charge. Their design is also a bit more discreet, for better or worse. Read our review.
Shokz OpenRun Pro 2
You can keep your favorite jogger or cycler safe while they pump up the jams with these specialized headphones. Shokz’s halo-shaped earpieces pulse sound through the wearer’s jawbone, keeping their ears open. A separate speaker greatly improves bass, while splash resistance and long battery life make them ready for any adventure.
Powerbeats Pro 2
The Powerbeats Pro 2 are some of the best earbuds for fitness. Their ear hook design is comfortable, keeping them snug while you work out, and they have IPX4 water resistance. Like the AirPods Pro 3, they have heart rate monitoring built in. Read our review.
Nothing Ear (a)
Former Verge reviewer Chris Welch praised this model as being able to go toe to toe with Apple in terms of sound quality, even if they can’t match it with as many features. Still, at $55, you’re getting a fantastic value here. Read our hands-on.
CMF Buds Pro 2
Most companies strictly remove features to cut costs. CMF, Nothing’s sub-brand, kept noise cancellation and great sound in its Buds Pro 2, and added a volume-adjusting dial to its charging case. Novel, yet affordable.
Sennheiser Momentum 5 Wireless headphones
The Momentum 5 support higher-res audio than their predecessors, if you’ve got the right device to connect them to. They carry forth the design and fantastic battery life, but with a Black Friday price cut that cancels out the $50 increase from the last-gen model.
AirPods Pro 3
Apple’s AirPods Pro 3 deliver the best noise cancellation and sound quality of any AirPods yet, along with a more comfortable, secure fit and improved water resistance. They also feature built-in heart rate tracking for workouts and support live translations for a handful of languages. Read our review.
Shokz OpenFit Pro
Open-style earbuds aren’t just for the sporty; they’re an entirely different way to listen that keeps you environmentally aware without the plugged-up feeling of traditional buds. The OpenFit Pro take a balanced approach, with seamless open-ear performance and even a touch of noise reduction to dampen the din on crowded commutes.
CMF Headphone Pro
The market is flooded with surprisingly cheap yet good over-ear headphones with active noise cancellation. The Headphone Pro by CMF are certainly some of the best-looking out there, and they come in multiple colors.
Sony WH-1000XM5
Despite having been succeeded by the WH-1000XM6, the 2022 XM5 are still an excellent set of headphones. Their active noise cancellation effect is one of the best out there — competitive with the latest models from Bose and Apple — and the sound profile is tighter and more balanced than the older Sony headphones.
JBL Tour One M3
JBL’s Tour One M3 noise-canceling headphones come with a touchscreen-equipped wireless transmitter that lets you wirelessly listen to audio from in-flight entertainment systems and other devices without Bluetooth. They also offer solid active noise cancellation and last up to 70 hours on a charge.
Samsung Galaxy Buds 4 Pro
Samsung’s latest high-end earbuds are great, with better ANC and a more consistent sound profile than their predecessor. But unless you plan to pair them with a Galaxy phone, they’re tough to recommend for iPhone or Pixel owners. Read our review.
Google Pixel Buds Pro 2
Significantly smaller and lighter than their predecessors, the Pixel Buds Pro 2 also offer stronger noise cancellation, a crystal clear transparency mode, and lengthy battery life. Read our review.
Bose QuietComfort Ultra Headphones (second-gen)
The latest-gen QuietComfort Ultra Headphones support lossless audio over USB-C and terrific sound with a bit of fine-tuning. They also include a battery-saving feature that powers them down when you lay them flat on your desk. Read our review.
Pixel Buds 2a
Google’s latest pair of wireless earbuds features crisp sound, a comfortable design, and solid active noise cancellation, which is great considering the budget-friendly price tag. They even offer built-in support for Gemini and, unlike the entry-level AirPods, a purple option! Read our review.

articles.title: Credit card skimming scripts using WebRTC found on popular shopping sites
articles.body:
Credit card skimming scripts using WebRTC found on popular shopping sites
All the sites we contacted took action; but the larger consumer web ecosystem should be prepared to mitigate these attack vectors
A card-skimming script was planted on the online stores of Lascana, Samsonite, American Tourister, Revolve and FWRD in the week before Black Friday. After our reports to affected companies, all have had the script removed (on November 24th or 25th) ahead of Black Friday. We observed it in action on one of the five websites: Lascana, where it sent our test card's details to a 3rd party. We believe the script was built to take a card number, expiry and security code, along with a user's name, address, phone and email, and send them to malefactors as a user entered their payment credentials. It did this before the store checked the payment, so a card could be taken even if the order was declined or cancelled, and nothing would look wrong to the shopper. Across all of these sites, we do not know how many, if any, shopper details or payment credentials may have been captured.
Which sites were affected
On November 24, we notified all of the named parties in this article and others, including: Amazon Web Services about the storage buckets serving the script, Cloudflare about the services the malefactor used, the domain registrars, the pixel vendor, the consent-banner provider and the affected retailers and platforms. Lascana replied to us and removed the Quorum pixel from their site by November 24th at 15:48 UTC. Quorum confirmed the identified malicious code was removed from their pixel tracker, and they restored the clean marketing pixel as of November 24th at 21:09 UTC.
Revolve provided this statement on behalf of REVOLVE and FWRD: “On November 25, InfoHawk notified our team of a potential security issue impacting mobile and tablet versions of our websites which we resolved the same day. We appreciate the outreach, and are actively investigating the issue to determine any potential impact.”
* Quorum is an ad-attribution platform that links ad views to store visits and online sales (quorum.inc).
† Seers is a cookie consent management platform and data privacy compliance company (seers.ai).
How the attack works
This attack uses WebRTC, the technology that allows you to make video calls in your web browser. WebRTC lets a web page open its own channel to another party and pass data (e.g. audio/video packets) over it. It has likely been used (both to load the skimmer and to send the stolen card details out) because security rules and monitoring tools often do not watch this communications channel as closely. For example, Meta briefly used WebRTC in a creative way in 2025, according to researchers looking at the technology as a compromise vector. This form of attack appears to target mobile devices, and we only saw the server enable the skimmer on checkout pages, so desktop checks and homepage scans would likely not see it. The skimmer's traffic appeared to run through Cloudflare's relay, so it would blend in with the WebRTC traffic and hide its true endpoint.
The skimmer and card details both traveled over WebRTC
    How the kit is designed to work on a store page, in 7 steps. Only step 4 is
    an ordinary web request, which a connect-src rule can block;
    steps 5 to 7 run over the WebRTC data channel, outside
    connect-src.
  
- 
      Store page Bootstrapping the attack The loader gets onto the page through a consent-banner setting, a retailer CDN file, a shared marketing pixel or the store's own HTML.
- 
      Store page Loading scripts from S3 buckets 
          It loads Insds.js or gtage.js from an Amazon
          S3 bucket.
- 
      Store page Targeting the attack to mobile checkouts 
          It runs only on small or touch screens. The Samsonite version runs on
          /checkout only.
- 
      Web request · connect-src can block it Establishing the WebRTC connection 
          GET /_cf/ice fetches the relay details, and POST /_cf/rel sends the WebRTC offer, to a brand-named northbridgeads[.]com host.
- 
      WebRTC data channel · outside connect-src Data exchange via TURN relay 
          Every exchange that returned relay details used
          turn.cloudflare.com. The malefactor's answers listed only
          Cloudflare relay addresses; through that relay it sends code and
          receives data.
- 
      WebRTC data channel · code in Attack code is loaded and executed 
          The skimmer arrives in chunks over the channel, is checked against a
          SHA-256 digest, then run with eval.
- 
      WebRTC data channel · data back Data goes back the same way At Lascana's checkout‡, the skimmer sent our test card details this way.
‡ This was the only example of live card details being sent off-site that we captured.
Worried that your card was compromised?
Check your recent statements for charges you don't recognize, especially on debit cards. Call your bank or card issuer right away, report the fraud and ask for a new card number. Follow up with a written dispute within 60 days of the statement that shows the charge.
Our understanding of US federal law is that your liability for unauthorized credit card charges is capped at $50, and is generally zero if only your card number was stolen, as in a skimming attack like this one. Debit cards have weaker protections that depend on how quickly you report, so act fast. For more information, see “Additional resources” below.
What site owners should immediately do
connect-src rule that lists only the hosts you use.
  That blocks the two web requests the script needs before WebRTC opens. Without them the skimmer never arrives, whichever file was tampered with.
What security teams should look for
We saw the skimmer delivered in three different ways across five websites run by different companies, and all of them appear to rely on the same attacker infrastructure. That makes it likely that other sites are affected too, so we encourage online retailers to check their own sites for the signs below.
- 
      Script sources: search page source, tag managers, consent-banner
      settings and CDN files for scripts from
      <brand>-static.s3.amazonaws[.]com (files Insds.js, gtage.js). We believe this is the
      malicious code.
- 
      Tracking pixels: if you load
      qscripts.s3.amazonaws[.]com/pscript.js, check its last line
      for one of the above CDN buckets, and if present, remove the tracking
      pixel. We recommend reviewing all similar tracking pixels and their
      exposure to sensitive fields or actions on your website.
- 
      Seers banners: If you have integrated Seers, open your banner
      config
      (cdn.seersco.com/banners/<account>/<domain>/cb.js)
      and check that every URL field holds only a URL. In the affected configs,
      the privacy-policy link field also held a hidden image, whose onerror event handler loaded the malicious code.
- 
      Checkout traffic: on a phone-sized touch screen, at the payment
      step, look for /_cf/ice and /_cf/rel requests to *.northbridgeads[.]com and a relay-only WebRTC connection
      used by the malicious code. Desktop checks miss it.
- 
      Strings: KghRtc, rtc-signal-v1 and quickfetch are referenced in the malicious code and may
      warrant further investigation if present.
The industry is not ready for the scale of supply chain attacks coming
This attack takes advantage of a few critical design decisions in websites that, if improperly configured, allow malicious actors to broadly deploy and trigger exploits across the open web.
- Websites load third-party code, often through a tag manager, from servers they don't control. The vendor can change that code at any time, and it can pull in further third-party code the site never reviewed.
- That code runs as an ordinary script with the same rights as the site's own code. It can read and rewrite the page, watch what users type, and load more code.
- Login, personal-information and payment pages often load the same marketing scripts as the rest of the site. Card fields should sit in an isolated payment frame, and third-party tags should be kept off these pages entirely.
Loading third-party tracking pixels on checkout, payment and login pages is far too common a practice today. Each pixel can run whatever code its vendor's file holds, including a skimmer, and whoever controls that file can change it without the site noticing. Every site should review which tracking pixels load on pages that take payment or sign-in details, who can change those files, and whether they need to be there at all.
A similar weakness was exploited at scale on 16 November 2026. An attacker reportedly used a flaw in Optimizely's Web Experimentation product to add malicious code to customers' projects, and Optimizely's own servers delivered it to visitors of 178 organizations' sites, including Zoom, the BBC and CNN, with no change to those sites' own code.
Additional resources
- Mastercard, "What is digital skimming? Your guide to staying safe while shopping online". Published October 10, 2024, it explains how criminals sneak malicious code into e-commerce websites to steal the payment data of customers who use their cards there.
- Visa, "Why hackers are prioritizing account data attacks in digital payments". This describes how hackers inject malicious code onto the checkout pages of merchant websites to harvest payments account data and personally identifiable information (PII) entered by customers.
- Visa Zero Liability
- Mastercard Zero Liability
- CISA/FBI E-Skimming fact sheet. It explains how cyber criminals introduce skimming code on e-commerce payment card processing web pages to capture credit card and personally identifiable information and send the stolen data to a domain under their control. It's from 2020, but it's still the clearest government explainer.
- FBI Internet Crime Complaint Center

          S3 bucket.
- 
      Store page Targeting the attack to mobile checkouts 
          It runs only on small or touch screens. The Samsonite version runs on
          /checkout only.
- 
      Web request · connect-src can block it Establishing the WebRTC connection 
          GET /_cf/ice fetches the relay details, and POST /_cf/rel sends the WebRTC offer, to a brand-named northbridgeads[.]com host.
- 
      WebRTC data channel · outside connect-src Data exchange via TURN relay 
          Every exchange that returned relay details used
          turn.cloudflare.com. The malefactor's answers listed only
          Cloudflare relay addresses; through that relay it sends code and
          receives data.
- 
      WebRTC data channel · code in Attack code is loaded and executed 
          The skimmer arrives in chunks over the channel, is checked against a
          SHA-256 digest, then run with eval.
- 
      WebRTC data channel · data back Data goes back the same way At Lascana's checkout‡, the skimmer sent our test card details this way.
‡ This was the only example of live card details being sent off-site that we captured.
Worried that your card was compromised?
Check your recent statements for charges you don't recognize, especially on debit cards. Call your bank or card issuer right away, report the fraud and ask for a new card number. Follow up with a written dispute within 60 days of the statement that shows the charge.
Our understanding of US federal law is that your liability for unauthorized credit card charges is capped at $50, and is generally zero if only your card number was stolen, as in a skimming attack like this one. Debit cards have weaker protections that depend on how quickly you report, so act fast. For more information, see “Additional resources” below.
What site owners should immediately do
connect-src rule that lists only the hosts you use.
  That blocks the two web requests the script needs before WebRTC opens. Without them the skimmer never arrives, whichever file was tampered with.
What security teams should look for
We saw the skimmer delivered in three different ways across five websites run by different companies, and all of them appear to rely on the same attacker infrastructure. That makes it likely that other sites are affected too, so we encourage online retailers to check their own sites for the signs below.
- 
      Script sources: search page source, tag managers, consent-banner
      settings and CDN files for scripts from
      <brand>-static.s3.amazonaws[.]com (files Insds.js, gtage.js). We believe this is the
      malicious code.
- 
      Tracking pixels: if you load
      qscripts.s3.amazonaws[.]com/pscript.js, check its last line
      for one of the above CDN buckets, and if present, remove the tracking
      pixel. We recommend reviewing all similar tracking pixels and their
      exposure to sensitive fields or actions on your website.
- 
      Seers banners: If you have integrated Seers, open your banner
      config
      (cdn.seersco.com/banners/<account>/<domain>/cb.js)
      and check that every URL field holds only a URL. In the affected configs,
      the privacy-policy link field also held a hidden image, whose onerror event handler loaded the malicious code.
- 
      Checkout traffic: on a phone-sized touch screen, at the payment
      step, look for /_cf/ice and /_cf/rel requests to *.northbridgeads[.]com and a relay-only WebRTC connection
      used by the malicious code. Desktop checks miss it.
- 
      Strings: KghRtc, rtc-signal-v1 and quickfetch are referenced in the malicious code and may
      warrant further investigation if present.
The industry is not ready for the scale of supply chain attacks coming
This attack takes advantage of a few critical design decisions in websites that, if improperly configured, allow malicious actors to broadly deploy and trigger exploits across the open web.
- Websites load third-party code, often through a tag manager, from servers they don't control. The vendor can change that code at any time, and it can pull in further third-party code the site never reviewed.
- That code runs as an ordinary script with the same rights as the site's own code. It can read and rewrite the page, watch what users type, and load more code.
- Login, personal-information and payment pages often load the same marketing scripts as the rest of the site. Card fields should sit in an isolated payment frame, and third-party tags should be kept off these pages entirely.
Loading third-party tracking pixels on checkout, payment and login pages is far too common a practice today. Each pixel can run whatever code its vendor's file holds, including a skimmer, and whoever controls that file can change it without the site noticing. Every site should review which tracking pixels load on pages that take payment or sign-in details, who can change those files, and whether they need to be there at all.
A similar weakness was exploited at scale on 16 November 2026. An attacker reportedly used a flaw in Optimizely's Web Experimentation product to add malicious code to customers' projects, and Optimizely's own servers delivered it to visitors of 178 organizations' sites, including Zoom, the BBC and CNN, with no change to those sites' own code.
Additional resources
- Mastercard, "What is digital skimming? Your guide to staying safe while shopping online". Published October 10, 2024, it explains how criminals sneak malicious code into e-commerce websites to steal the payment data of customers who use their cards there.
- Visa, "Why hackers are prioritizing account data attacks in digital payments". This describes how hackers inject malicious code onto the checkout pages of merchant websites to harvest payments account data and personally identifiable information (PII) entered by customers.
- Visa Zero Liability
- Mastercard Zero Liability
- CISA/FBI E-Skimming fact sheet. It explains how cyber criminals introduce skimming code on e-commerce payment card processing web pages to capture credit card and personally identifiable information and send the stolen data to a domain under their control. It's from 2020, but it's still the clearest government explainer.
- FBI Internet Crime Complaint Center

articles.title: Rayshader 1.0: Exit the Matrix
articles.body:
Be sure to read to the end for what I can guarantee is the most exciting and cinematric R package bibliography you’ve ever seen. Everything you see in the below blog post was rendered in R with the rayverse.
Eight years ago, rayshader started as a small experiment in making beautiful maps in R. The first version was based on a simple question: what if we combined raytracing and cartography? I had always been interested in learning both about mapping and pathtracing, and what better way than to combine the two ideas into a single R package? The big “aha!” moment came when I applied that method with interactive 3D terrain for the first time and took it for a spin.
The surface was no longer just a shaded map: it felt tangible and real, a 3D rectangle twirling like a Little Debbie cosmic brownie on a microwave turntable. The combination of cartographic hillshading and 3D raytraced terrain looked spectacular in a way that, at the time, mostly lived in bespoke Blender scenes or other advanced 3D modeling tools. And unlike Blender, you didn’t need to learn a whole new ecosystem to visualize your data in 3D: it lived in the same place your data did (R!), which allowed for a gentler learning curve.
But as time went on and the package and userbase expanded, I had a nagging feeling: rayshader was still too hard.
Not always, of course: plenty of people were using it, quite effectively. Simple use cases were fine: pass in a matrix, add a few layers, call plot_3d(), and suddenly you had a cool-looking 3D landscape. If that’s all you needed: great! But if the story you were trying to tell was about data within the landscape–well, that’s where the friction began to burn.
Beauty is table stakes
I built rayshader for people who wanted to make data beautiful without leaving R. Beauty has a real purpose in the world: it draws people’s eyes. It doesn’t matter how accurate or well-constructed your map is if the reader swipes on by: in the market for human attention, beauty and form are table stakes.
Journalists understood that quickly, and were some of rayshader’s earliest adopters.
The Wall Street Journal’s The Future of Arctic Shipping used detailed shipping, bathymetric, and ice coverage data to explain the complexities of the Northern Sea Route. The piece was recognized by the Information is Beautiful Awards, which described it as a deeply researched story built from shipping, bathymetric, and ice coverage data. It appeared only a few months after I released rayshader: talk about an introduction! Bloomberg’s 2024 Gaza rebuilding story, Gaza Reduced to 42 Million Tonnes of Rubble. What Will It Take to Rebuild?, used R, rayshader, and rayrender as part of the visual system for communicating the scale of destruction and debris in Gaza. And in June 2022, a rayshader 3D flood visualization appeared on the front page of The Sydney Morning Herald, inset into coverage of the Lismore flooding.
That last one stuck with me (and not only because a rayshader map was featured “above the fold” in a major newspaper!). Rayshader had started as a way to make beautiful data visualizations in R, but here it was being used in deadline journalism to help explain a disaster to a general audience. The package had left the domain of “fun engaging social media posts” and entered the visual language of public-interest reporting.
But getting a reader to stop scrolling is only half the problem. Working with journalists taught me how much friction stood between having the data and making the final product. A newsroom deadline is a very good detector of bad API design. If adding buildings takes half a day of coordinate fiddling, that feature might as well not exist. If a 3D path requires a hand-rolled coordinate transform pipeline, nobody is doing that 30 minutes before a deadline. If a pathtraced render looks great but takes too long to converge, it is not going to make it to print. Especially if the editor needs a slight tweak: “Oh, sure–just give me 8 hours to re-render the animation.” Ha. Nope.
Working with journalists taught me how much friction stood between having the data and making the final product.
The problem wasn’t so much with rayshader itself: it was how much spatial bookkeeping and manual fiddling you had to do to get data into rayshader before you could do all the fun stuff. And at the root of all that bookkeeping was the humble matrix, rayshader’s original choice for representing terrain.
The problem with matrices
Rayshader used matrices to represent terrain because it simplified a lot of the work that went into turning a bunch of elevation values in a 3D object. But most real data does not arrive nicely packaged as a plain rectangular numeric array. It arrives as georeferenced rasters, polygons, lines, and points. It arrives cloaked in an unknown coordinate reference system. It arrives in meters, feet, yards, degrees, or German legal metres. Choosing the matrix as the base input made it easy for me, the developer, by putting the spatial problem (mostly) on the user.
Is there an… illegal german metre?
Convert the raster to a matrix. Save the extent. Transform the vector data. Save the CRS. Crop the linework. Pass the heightmap again. Pass the extent again. Wait, is the extent format lat/long/lat/long or lat/lat/long/long? I never remember–whatever, try both. The first choice is (somehow!) always wrong. Pass zscale again. Resize the overlay. Pass the CRS again. Check whether the map is oriented correctly. No? Surprise! Errant minus sign. Yuck.
This was not just annoying for beginners. It annoyed me, and I wrote the damn thing: now that’s a usability red flag! The new version of rayshader includes a series of changes that gets rid of all of this overhead and allows you to focus on presentation instead of the data processing.
rayshader has gained object permanence
The big change in rayshader 1.0 is this: rayshader no longer has short-term amnesia. Rayshader now keeps track of all the spatial details from your underlying map so you don’t have to worry about it any more.
This changes the user experience from:
Transform and pass in your data into an aligned matrix coordinate system, and rayshader will render it in beautiful 3D.
To:
Transform and Pass in your data into an aligned matrix coordinate system, and rayshader will render it in beautiful 3D.
The black diamond learning curve is now a gentle bunny slope. Terrain can stay a spatial raster. Road can stay a spatial line and will automatically be converted to the correct coordinate system when plotting. Buildings can be passed in as spatial polygons and will automatically be cropped to the underlying map’s extent.
A rayshader scene now extracts and caches the important metadata from the input data: heightmap, extent, CRS, zscale, vertical exaggeration, and rendered-object metadata. That cache lets downstream render_*() calls do the thing users always wanted them to do: simply drop data into the scene.
Most of the functions can now add to the scene simply by passing the data, plus an optional argument that specifies altitude or height, either directly or through a column in an sf object. The rest of the arguments then focus on how you want to style the data.
For example, let’s load in some road and elevation data and see what the new API looks like. The code below defines the helpers and loads the data into R. There’s no rayshader in it, so you have absolutely no obligation to read it :).
Data loading code (boring, you can skip)
microsoft_building_links_url =
  "https://minedbuildings.z5.web.core.windows.net/global-buildings/dataset-links.csv"
worldcover_base_url =
  "https://esa-worldcover.s3.eu-central-1.amazonaws.com/v200/2021/map"
# Helper function to get buildings from world-wide building dataset
get_microsoft_building_footprints = function(
  scene,
  n = Inf,
  cache_dir = file.path(tempdir(), "microsoft-building-footprints"),
  links_url = microsoft_building_links_url,
  zoom = 9
) {
  dir.create(cache_dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
  links_file = file.path(cache_dir, "dataset-links.csv")
  if (!file.exists(links_file)) {
    download.file(links_url, links_file, mode = "wb", quiet = TRUE)
  }
  links = utils::read.csv(
    links_file,
    colClasses = c(
      Location = "character",
      QuadKey = "character",
      Url = "character",
      Size = "character",
      UploadDate = "character"
    )
  )
  tile_links = links[
    links$QuadKey %in% scene_quadkeys(scene, zoom),
    ,
    drop = FALSE
  ]
  if (nrow(tile_links) == 0) {
    stop(
      "No Microsoft building footprint tiles found for this scene.",
      call. = FALSE
    )
  }
  buildings = lapply(
    tile_links$Url,
    read_microsoft_building_tile,
    cache_dir = cache_dir
  )
  buildings = do.call(rbind, buildings) |>
    sf::st_make_valid() |>
    sf::st_transform(sf::st_crs(scene))
  buildings = suppressWarnings(sf::st_intersection(buildings, scene))
  buildings = suppressWarnings(
    sf::st_collection_extract(buildings, "POLYGON", warn = FALSE)
  )
  buildings = buildings[!sf::st_is_empty(buildings), ]
  if (nrow(buildings) == 0) {
    stop(
      "No Microsoft building footprints intersected this scene.",
      call. = FALSE
    )
  }
  buildings$footprint_area_m2 = as.numeric(sf::st_area(buildings))
  if (is.finite(n) && nrow(buildings) > n) {
    buildings = buildings[
      order(buildings$footprint_area_m2, decreasing = TRUE),
    ]
    buildings = buildings[seq_len(n), ]
  }
  height = if ("height" %in% names(buildings)) {
    buildings$height
  } else {
    rep(NA_real_, nrow(buildings))
  }
  height[!is.finite(height) | height <= 0] = NA_real_
  height[is.na(height)] = runif(sum(is.na(height)), 6, 18)
  buildings$height_m = height
  keep_cols = intersect(
    c("height_m", "confidence", "footprint_area_m2"),
    names(buildings)
  )
  buildings[, keep_cols]
}
lonlat_to_bing_tile = function(lon, lat, zoom) {
  lat = pmax(pmin(lat, 85.05112878), -85.05112878)
  tile_count = 2^zoom
  x = floor((lon + 180) / 360 * tile_count)
  y = floor(
    (1 - log(tan(lat * pi / 180) + 1 / cos(lat * pi / 180)) / pi) /
      2 *
      tile_count
  )
  data.frame(
    x = pmax(pmin(x, tile_count - 1), 0),
    y = pmax(pmin(y, tile_count - 1), 0)
  )
}
bing_tile_to_quadkey = function(x, y, zoom) {
  vapply(
    seq_along(x),
    function(i) {
      paste0(
        vapply(
          seq.int(zoom, 1),
          function(bit) {
            digit = 0L
            mask = bitwShiftL(1L, bit - 1L)
            if (bitwAnd(x[i], mask) != 0L) {
              digit = digit + 1L
            }
            if (bitwAnd(y[i], mask) != 0L) {
              digit = digit + 2L
            }
            as.character(digit)
          },
          character(1)
        ),
        collapse = ""
      )
    },
    character(1)
  )
}
scene_quadkeys = function(scene, zoom = 9) {
  bbox = sf::st_bbox(sf::st_transform(scene, 4326))
  tiles = lonlat_to_bing_tile(
    lon = c(bbox[["xmin"]], bbox[["xmax"]]),
    lat = c(bbox[["ymax"]], bbox[["ymin"]]),
    zoom = zoom
  )
  tile_grid = expand.grid(
    x = seq(min(tiles$x), max(tiles$x)),
    y = seq(min(tiles$y), max(tiles$y))
  )
  unique(bing_tile_to_quadkey(tile_grid$x, tile_grid$y, zoom))
}
read_microsoft_building_tile = function(url, cache_dir) {
  tile_file = file.path(cache_dir, basename(url))
  if (!file.exists(tile_file)) {
    download.file(url, tile_file, mode = "wb", quiet = TRUE)
  }
  geojsonl_file = tempfile(fileext = ".geojsonl")
  on.exit(unlink(geojsonl_file), add = TRUE)
  writeLines(
    readLines(gzfile(tile_file), warn = FALSE),
    geojsonl_file,
    useBytes = TRUE
  )
  sf::st_read(geojsonl_file, quiet = TRUE)
}
# Load the data using the helpers above.
library(terra)
library(sf)
library(dplyr)
library(elevatr)
library(tigris)
options(tigris_use_cache = TRUE)
bbox_ll = c(
  xmin = -119.03,
  ymin = 37.60,
  xmax = -118.94,
  ymax = 37.67
)
target_crs = "EPSG:32611"
scene_ll = sf::st_as_sfc(
  sf::st_bbox(bbox_ll, crs = sf::st_crs(4326))
) |>
  sf::st_as_sf()
scene = sf::st_transform(scene_ll, target_crs)
dem = elevatr::get_elev_raster(
  locations = scene_ll,
  z = 12,
  clip = "bbox"
) |>
  terra::rast()
names(dem) = "elevation_m"
scene_crop = sf::st_transform(scene_ll, terra::crs(dem))
dem_crop = terra::crop(dem, scene_crop)
roads = tigris::roads(
  state = "CA",
  county = "Mono",
  year = 2024,
  class = "sf"
)
water = tigris::area_water(
  state = "CA",
  county = "Mono",
  year = 2024,
  class = "sf"
)
buildings = get_microsoft_building_footprints(scene, n = 3910)
- Transform to a UTM CRS (so everything is in meters)
- Pass in our lat/long bounding box
Pretty straightforward… just kidding, loading geospatial data is always a pain. Nothing I can do about that! But the real question is: how complex is visualizating all this data once it’s loaded?
# Run once in the R console to install rayshader from my R-universe.
if (interactive()) {
  install.packages(
    "rayshader",
    repos = c("https://tylermorganwall.r-universe.dev", "https://cloud.r-project.org")
  )
}
library(rayrender)
library(rayshader)
# Plot in 3D
dem_crop |>
  height_shade() |>
  plot_3d(window_size = c(1500, 500))
# Data
render_roads(roads)
render_water(water)
render_buildings(buildings)
# Camera angle
render_camera(fov = 80, phi = 40, theta = 135, zoom = 0.25)
render_highquality(
  datetime = as.POSIXct("2025-12-21 09:00:00", tz = "America/Los_Angeles"),
  iso = 5
)
rgl::close3d()
Not complex at all! You call the function named after the type of data… and it renders the data in the scene. Any additional arguments are just for styling the data to your liking.
And the payoff is not just less typing: it lets us get to the fun part of 3D data visualization faster. The coolest part of rayshader has always been building strikingly beautiful 3D landscapes from your data. But the third dimension raises the cognitive cost of entry: before you can play director and cinematographer, you have to build the set. When every point, path, and polygon needs the user to track the CRS and extent info themselves and transform the data appropriately, many users never get to the stage where they can experiment with lighting and composition, styling the data (costume design!), or focus on editing the overall narrative.
But also, less typing!
The third dimension raises the cognitive cost of entry: before you can play director and cinematographer, you have to build the set.
This release automates almost all of the behind-the-scenes work. The boring parts–CRS juggling, extent passing, heightmap repetition, matrix conversion, and other bookkeeping–stay in the package internals. The user is then free to jump to the enjoyable creative roles: the executive producer of the analysis, the production designer of the world, or the sound designer of a multi-sensory data experience.
Spatial data: free yourself from the matrix!
Rayshader now accepts many more spatial inputs for the heightmap. The plot_3d() function can now accept a heightmap as a matrix, a terra::SpatRaster, a raster object, or a raster filename. When the input is spatial, rayshader extracts and caches the extent and CRS. If zscale is not supplied, rayshader derives it from raster cell resolution. If the raster is geographic longitude/latitude, rayshader estimates the meter-per-cell scale at the raster center. The data was always there; it just had to be piped around to the right place! Now I do the plumbing for you.
Let’s look at an example. The same DEM and main-road data feed both versions below. The difference is who’s now doing the spatial bookkeeping (hint: it’s not you).
Data load
bbox_ll = c(
  xmin = -119.03,
  ymin = 37.60,
  xmax = -118.86,
  ymax = 37.74
)
target_crs = "EPSG:32611"
scene_ll = sf::st_as_sfc(
  sf::st_bbox(bbox_ll, crs = sf::st_crs(4326))
) |>
  sf::st_as_sf()
scene = sf::st_transform(scene_ll, target_crs)
dem = elevatr::get_elev_raster(
  locations = scene,
  z = 12,
  src = "aws",
  clip = "bbox",
  tmp_dir = tempdir()
) |>
  terra::rast() |>
  terra::project(target_crs, res = 30) |>
  terra::crop(terra::vect(scene))
roads = tigris::roads(
  state = "CA",
  county = "Mono",
  year = 2024,
  class = "sf"
) |>
  sf::st_make_valid() |>
  dplyr::filter(MTFCC == "S1200")
Old workflow
scene_extent = terra::ext(dem)
scene_crs = terra::crs(dem)
heightmap = raster_to_matrix(dem)
zscale = 30
heightmap |>
  height_shade() |>
  plot_3d(
    heightmap = heightmap,
    zscale = zscale,
    extent = scene_extent
  )
render_path(
  roads |>
    sf::st_transform(scene_crs),
  extent = scene_extent,
  heightmap = heightmap,
  zscale = zscale,
  crs = scene_crs
)
render_highquality()
- 1
- Pull the raster extent out into a separate object.
- 2
- Pull the raster CRS out into a separate object.
- 3
- Convert the spatial raster into the matrix rayshader expects.
- 4
- Manually specify the zscale
- 5
- Color the elevation matrix before constructing the terrain.
- 6
- Re-specify all the inputs to plot the scene in 3D.
- 7
- Manually transform the vector layer at the point where it enters the scene.
- 8
- Repeat the scene metadata again when adding a path.
- 9
- Pathtrace the scene with rayrender.
new workflow:
dem |>
  height_shade() |>
  plot_3d()
render_path(roads)
render_highquality()
- 1
- Keep the DEM as a spatial raster.
- 2
- Create a hillshade.
- 3
- Pass the hillshade into plot_3d(). Let the cached heightmap, CRS, extent, and derived zscale carry forward into the scene.
- 4
- Pass the lines; rayshader transforms and filters it against the cached scene.
- 5
- Pathtrace the scene with rayrender.
Internally, rayshader still converts the raster to something it can render. Externally, the scene remembers enough to let the render_*() functions just work.
There is now also a cleaner division between physical scale and visual exaggeration. zscale now describes the relationship between horizontal and vertical units, while vertical_exaggeration describes the stylistic exaggeration. For spatial rasters, rayshader can derive zscale from the raster itself, placing the data at its physical scale. You can then adjust vertical_exaggeration to emphasize the terrain without changing the underlying unit conversion.
And this spatial data directionality can now be reversed. spatialize_image() turns a rayshader image, matrix, RGB array, or RGBA array back into a georeferenced terra::SpatRaster. It can inherit the cached extent and CRS from the active scene, convert rayshader’s linear color values to sRGB, and optionally append the source heightmap as an additional raster layer. So rayshader’s output can now feed back into other GIS software, rather than just assume rayshader is the final destination itself.
library(rayshader)
# Color cells below sea level before exporting the RGB raster.
rgb_raster = montereybay_spatial |>
  sphere_shade(vertical_exaggeration = 15) |>
  add_water(montereybay_spatial < 2, color = "dodgerblue4") |>
  spatialize_image(
    include_alpha = TRUE,
    include_height = TRUE
  )
terra::writeRaster(
  rgb_raster,
  "../images/2026/rayshader-100/monterey-georeferenced.tif",
  overwrite = TRUE
)
terra::plotRGB(rgb_raster, r = 1, g = 2, b = 3)
This release lets rayshader fit into a real spatial workflow: spatial input, then rayshader styling, followed by spatial output. So you can generate beautiful hillshades and terrains in R, and then bring them into other spatial software like QGIS or ArcGIS. Work in the GIS interface you already know, render the terrain in R, and drop the result right back into your map.
A watershed moment for rayshader water
Rayshader’s water was always a bit of an afterthought: it was good for rendering an ocean with bathymetry data, but it didn’t really work if the water was localized to one portion of the map. A lake halfway up a mountain shouldn’t require flooding everything below it to see the water, but rayshader’s old water meshing method assumed one water level for the whole map. Which was perfect if all you needed was that one large body of water: set a level and fill the scene to that height. Separate lakes, reservoirs at different elevations, and imperfect shorelines called for something more flexible.
Now water can arrive as a raster or a polygon, high in the mountains or below sea level. render_water() uses the terrain and coordinates already stored in the scene to properly place and render the water in a sane way.
The old single-level behavior remains available as water_render_method = "legacy", as it is much faster and is perfectly suited for coastlines and topobathymetry data.
Water can follow grid cells with water_render_method = "raster" or preserve polygon boundaries with the default, water_render_method = "polygon". Both draw a watertight mesh at the footprint and elevation you supply, even when that means an exposed vertical water wall where the supplied shoreline doesn’t quite meet the terrain. Fast, flexible, and suitable for the rare case where you need to visualize Moses crossing the Red Sea.
Another (much cooler, IMO) option is water_render_method = "optimized". It fits a closed shoreline to the actual 3D terrain mesh, adjusting the water elevation to match the supplied area. Using the elevations beneath your water footprint to seed candidate levels, the optimizer searches for a contour that comes as close as possible to the supplied water area without spilling out of the terrain. The animation below shows how candidate levels change the flooded area.
If no closed water body is possible—for example, the supplied water would flood the entire map—rayshader falls back to raster water.
A different problem arises when a DEM has no bathymetry: the lake bed and its surface occupy the same plane. shift_terrain() is a new function that can lower the terrain beneath a lake polygon before you add water, making room for the lake instead of letting the surfaces overlap. It can also raise terrain SimCity 2000-style (no tornados or alien invasions… yet).
Additionally, in render_highquality(), water can now use a rough dielectric material to spread reflections into the broad highlights you expect from a rippled lake. A perfectly smooth dielectric surface behaves like glass: reflected light stays coherent, so lakes and rivers can turn into polished sheets. Real water has small wind-driven ripples, each reflecting light in a slightly different direction. The microfacet material models this give a more realistic appearance to bodies of water, especially when viewed at a low angle.
Rayshader: now streaming!
Streams need to follow the terrain as they wind downhill. render_streams() takes spatial line data, samples the elevation along each path, and builds ribbons of water that hug the surface. Widths can vary by feature, and connected streams can be merged to reduce visible seams in high-quality renders. Put those streams together with lakes and you have a hydrologic scene driven by data.
Load and prepare Mono County terrain, lakes, and streams
library(rayshader)
library(sf)
library(terra)
library(dplyr)
library(tigris)
library(elevatr)
options(tigris_use_cache = TRUE)
target_crs = "EPSG:32611"
dem_z = 12
scene_ll = sf::st_as_sfc(
  sf::st_bbox(
    c(xmin = -119.12, ymin = 37.52, xmax = -118.68, ymax = 37.86),
    crs = sf::st_crs(4326)
  )
) |>
  sf::st_as_sf()
scene = sf::st_transform(scene_ll, target_crs)
water = tigris::area_water(
  state = "CA",
  county = "Mono",
  year = 2024,
  class = "sf"
) |>
  sf::st_make_valid() |>
  sf::st_transform(target_crs) |>
  sf::st_crop(scene) |>
  dplyr::filter(MTFCC %in% c("H2030", "H2040")) |>
  dplyr::mutate(area_m2 = as.numeric(sf::st_area(geometry))) |>
  dplyr::filter(area_m2 >= 5000)
dem_raw = elevatr::get_elev_raster(
  locations = scene,
  z = dem_z,
  src = "aws",
  clip = "bbox"
)
dem = terra::rast(dem_raw) |>
  resize_spatial(scale = 0.5, method_down = "mean")
names(dem) = "elevation_m"
water_level = terra::extract(
  dem,
  terra::vect(water),
  fun = median,
  na.rm = TRUE,
  touches = TRUE
)
water$water_level_m = round(water_level$elevation_m, 1)
water = water[is.finite(water$water_level_m), ]
streams = tigris::linear_water(
  state = "CA",
  county = "Mono",
  year = 2024,
  class = "sf"
) |>
  sf::st_make_valid() |>
  sf::st_transform(target_crs) |>
  sf::st_crop(scene) |>
  sf::st_collection_extract("LINESTRING", warn = FALSE)dem |>
  shift_terrain(
    geometry = water,
    amount = -10
  ) |>
  height_shade() |>
  plot_3d(
    phi = 10,
    zoom = 0.15,
    fov = 29.1,
    shadow = FALSE,
    normals = FALSE
  )
render_water(
  water_input = water,
  water_render_method = "polygon",
  water_edge_extension = 0.25,
  water_color = "dodgerblue",
  water_polygon_failure = "raster"
)
render_streams(
  streams = streams,
  water_color = "dodgerblue",
  width = 1
)
render_highquality(
  camera_location = c(-1752.16, 563.86, 415.55),
  camera_lookat = c(-155.98, -12.60, -246.84),
  fov = 10.5,
  width = 1500,
  height = 500,
  samples = 128,
  water_material = "microfacet",
  water_ior = 1.5,
  iso = 5,
  sky_sun_elevation = 20,
  sky_sun_azimuth = -113,
  sky_args = list(hosek = FALSE)
)
rgl::close3d()
Note that there’s no complex GIS concepts on the rayshader side: all the complexity is related to defining the visual style and appearance. As it should be–rayshader is a visualization package! The remaining complexity is just standard data complexity present in any analysis: get the data loaded, cleaned, and in a form that represents the thing you care about.
The road to believable roads
3D maps might seem like a fun little toy rather than a serious class of data visualization, but the third dimension is often surprisingly important for understanding geospatial data. This becomes less surprising when you realize that the most common mapping tool used by regular people–GPS apps–use 3D quite extensively. When you’re traveling through a city, buildings give you landmarks to match to your surroundings; on a walking or cycling route, the terrain shows where you’ll be climbing; and at a complex highway interchange, seeing which roads pass over one another helps you follow the right ramp and choose the right exit.
I already had surface-hugging polygons working for streams. Swap the water for asphalt and there’s a road! Easy, peasy, right?
No! What’s the issue? We’re spoiled with our GPS apps: we’re used to roads looking like roads. A strip of grey asphalt needs lane markings for someone to know it’s a road. With the help of some fun repeating UV coordinate tricks and our new spatial-first workflow, we can paint properly-sized lines on the road at the cost of a few small textures. And we can use the lane counts supplied in OpenStreetMap data to add the correct number of lanes to each road. Rayshader uses those counts to mesh and texture the road, while the scene’s spatial information keeps the markings correctly sized.
In Figure 11, each dash is 10 feet long and each gap is 30 feet. Those familiar markings do double duty: they improve the picture and act as little scale bars scattered through the scene. Beautiful! Pack it up, put a bow on it, and move on to the next feature, right?
The spacing is configurable for local standards.
No! Our roads are still smooshed together on one layer. At an interchange, that borders on uninterpretable.
OpenStreetMap doesn’t provide a full 3D road model. But it does carry one tiny (but extremely useful!) nugget of vertical information needed to draw roads correctly in 2D: drawing order. Draw layer 0, then layer 1, then layer 2, and the right road appears on top. That tells us which road crosses over which; it doesn’t tell us their heights or how the ramps return to ground level. Is this enough information to fully reconstruct our 3D roads?
The tempting shortcut is to turn each layer into a fixed height: find the crossings, lift each road by a standard overpass height, and ease it back toward the ground with some sort of ad hoc relaxation rule. What could go wrong?
Everything. Everything can go wrong.
Simple hacks? Don’t work here. Turns out the world is filled with little annoying complications like a bridge crossing a sunken highway (the highway is already below ground, so the bridge needs no change in elevation), or short segments in interchanges that are technically not stacked but fall between stacked layers, or places where the road is technically stacked over a traversable water body (which also counts as a layer!), or a thousand other pesky little details.
What are we to do then? How can we implement realistic highways? It’s not like there’s a manual with explicit guidance and standards for how roads should be built in 3D—wait, what is that? There is an explicit manual?
The American Association of State Highway and Transportation Officials (AASHTO) has a design manual for Interstate highways. Two of the things it covers are exactly what our map is missing. How much room does a truck need under a bridge? How steep can the road get on its way up there? Now that rayshader knows the scale of the scene, I can give the solver a clearance in feet and a maximum grade in percent. Here are the default settings I gave the road solver (these are customizable):
- Keeping crossing road surfaces at least 14 feet apart
- Limiting the road grade to 7%
- Ensuring roads default to hugging the ground when not part of an intersection and do not rise unnecessarily
We can turn these requirements into constraints on the road heights. While the rules aren’t guaranteed to generate roads that match the real-world roads exactly, it’s going to be pretty close: excursions from the bare minimum allowable ruleset will usually only increase cost, and we’re talking government contracts here. Around each interchange, we discretize the roads into short segments and solve for their elevations together: maintain the crossing order and clearance, limit the grades, and keep the roads close to the terrain wherever possible.
It’s not like there’s a manual with explicit guidance and standards for how roads should be built in 3D—wait, what is that? There is an explicit manual?
For example, a road can weave over and under several others. Lifting one crossing changes the grades leading into the next, so solving each crossing independently won’t work–we have to solve all the linked constraints at once. We build a graph of the road connections with {igraph}, locate crossings with {sf}, and follow the constraints along connected road segments. Each connected optimization region gets a sparse quadratic problem, assembled with {Matrix} and solved with {osqp}. It turns out, R has everything you need to build and optimize road profiles.
It’s pretty cool how closely a set of road-design rules and OSM’s layer ordering can recreate a complex interchange. The layer tags tell us which road goes over which, and the rules guide how the ramps connect them. Here’s Houston, now modeled in a sane way:
Beautiful. And since I went to Houston for this year’s Posit::conf, I was able to drive over specific intersections I rendered here and confirm that yes: the roads were accurately meshed. Minus the traffic.

Lane markings made the scale of a scene easier to read. Naturally, that led me to the ultimate human-scale feature: humans! But I couldn’t just throw the first set of free human models I found on the internet into the package. I did a fairly extensive search for a suitable pre-made model with both male and female variants, but to no avail. I had some requirements:

I couldn’t find a model that met these requirements with a suitable redistribution license. So I decided this was a great opportunity to learning something new: mesh sculpting in VR!
