articles.title: The 25 best gaming deals we’ve found so far for Black Friday
articles.body:
While deals on consoles and key PC components are in short supply during Black Friday (or simply not good enough to warrant covering), there are numerous fantastic discounts on video games, accessories, and monitors to make up for it. We thought it’d be useful to display all of the deals we think are worth your attention on one page instead of sprinkled here and there in our coverage.
The 25 best gaming deals we’ve found so far for Black Friday
You won’t find deals on most consoles or GTA VI, but we’ve highlighted some Black Friday gems you ought to see.
Below, you’ll find the very best discounts we’ve found for PlayStation, Xbox, Nintendo Switch 2, and PC players to shop. You can filter the table below to display exactly the type of products you’re looking for.
Sony DualSense Edge
Both the white and midnight black versions of the DualSense Edge are discounted. Refurbished versions (with the same warranty as new controllers) are another $25 off.
Nintendo Switch 2 + Mario Kart World Bundle
The Nintendo Switch 2 features a 7.9-inch LCD display, magnetically attached Joy-Con 2 controllers, backward compatibility with most original Switch games, and exclusive titles like Donkey Kong Bananza and The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time. Read our review.
Samsung P9 microSD Express card
The P9 is great if you need more storage for your Nintendo Switch 2. The microSD Express card offers sequential read speeds of up to 800MB/s, but only gadgets with a microSD Express card slot can take full advantage of the highest speeds. That includes certain cameras, tablets, and drones with a microSD USH-I slot.
Donkey Kong Bananza
Donkey Kong Bananza is one of the Switch 2’s first exclusive must-have titles. Its destructible environment allows you to smash your way through each of its 17 levels, and the paths you make will remain intact unless you specifically choose to reset the world. Your companion Pauline’s singing allows you to transform into animals that have abilities that allow you to reach previously inaccessible parts of levels. Read our review.
8BitDo Pro 3 Wireless Controller
The Pro 3 features swappable ABXY face buttons and joystick caps, providing players with a highly customizable experience. It also features new L4 and R4 macro buttons between the triggers and its USB-C charging port, along with more durable and power efficient TMR joysticks.
The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time
Nintendo’s latest Switch 2 exclusive is the best way to relive what is arguably the best Zelda game of all time. The revamped visuals look gorgeous, and while the game’s improved controls might annoy some purists who still cling to the heyday of ’98, we reckon most folks won’t bat an eye.
Elden Ring: Tarnished Edition
The Elden Ring: Tarnished Edition includes both the base game and the “Shadow of the Erdtree” expansion, along with new customization options.
Fractal Scape gaming headset
The Fractal Scape gaming headset has a sleek, refined design, with a 2.4GHz low-latency connection and excellent sound for gaming or music.
Meta Quest 3S
The Meta Quest 3S is a battery-powered standalone VR headset that has the same chipset as the pricier Quest 3, but with the same lenses and screen resolution as the Quest 2. In addition to being able to play many games from the Meta Store, it can also be connected to a gaming PC to play VR games like Half-Life Alyx. Read our review.
Nex Playground
The Nex Playground is a motion-controlled console that connects to your TV and uses a built-in camera and AI to track your movements as you play. Designed for ages five and up, it comes with games like Fruit Ninja and Whac-a-Mole. You can download more games, including titles featuring popular characters like Elmo, with a paid Play Pass subscription.
World of Warcraft Celebration Pass
The World of Warcraft Celebration Pass cuts the price of a 12-month subscription during Black Friday, offering access to World of Modern WoW, WoW: Forever, and WoW: Classic at a discounted rate.
The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt Remastered
The Witcher 3 lets you explore the war-torn Northern Kingdoms as Geralt of Rivia while preparing to face the mysterious Wild Hunt. The recent remaster adds improved visuals, smoother combat, and better movement, cementing the game’s status as one of the best RPGs of all time.
Logitech G Pro X2 Superstrike
Clicking the Superstrike feels like using a regular gaming mouse, which is impressive considering there are no mechanical switches inside. Instead, it uses haptics to emulate the effect (to great effect).
Alienware 32-inch 4K OLED gaming monitor
One of the most affordable Tandem RGB Stripe OLEDs is even cheaper during Black Friday. The AW3226Q monitor has a 165Hz refresh rate, G-Sync compatibility, better-looking text rendering than most other OLED monitors, and unbeatable contrast.
LG B6E OLED TV
Make this the year that the gamer in your life has an OLED TV to play their console games on. Despite being affordable, the B6E doesn’t skimp on features.
A gift for the gamer who already has all the gear they need (and who loves to read about gaming when they’re not gaming). The site focuses on well-researched deep dives and oral histories on classic video games.
Sony PlayStation 27-inch 1440p gaming monitor
The 1440p 240Hz refresh rate screen is sleek, but pretty basic for the price. It stands out, though, thanks to its DualSense-charging cradle that extends from its bottom. This is the first discount.
If you’re seeking out a prettier DualSense, the Chroma series of controllers are just a few bucks more than the standard color schemes.
Star Wars Galactic Racer
No game has delivered more thrills per minute (TPM) this year than Star Wars Galactic Racer. Podracing is back, and it’s better than ever with this title’s stellar sense of speed, plus it has a surprisingly memorable cast of characters.
Nintendo eShop gift cards
Everyone knows gift cards aren’t the best gift, but with such steep discounts happening on Nintendo eShop credit, you can save a lot on a Switch 2, or games and accessories, if you’re alright with jumping through a couple extra hoops.
Halo: Campaign Evolved
Halo: Campaign Evolved lets you revisit the original Halo: Combat Evolved campaign with better graphics, updated controls, and improved sound. The well-crafted remake also adds three new missions starring Master Chief and Sgt. Johnson, which take place before the main campaign. Read our review.
Xreal One Pro AR glasses
USB-C display glasses can make travel (or relaxing on the couch) more fun by putting a huge virtual screen in front of your face. Xreal’s One Pro are some of the best out there at displaying content from your phone, tablet, laptop, or portable handheld.
Pokémon Pokopia
Nintendo’s latest Pokémon spinoff for the Switch 2 is part Pokémon, part Minecraft, and part Animal Crossing. Yet, despite borrowing gameplay mechanics from each, the cozy life sim is more than the sum of its expansive, building-centric parts. It’s breezy and warm-hearted, with enough secrets to keep you occupied for hours on end.
Elgato Stream Deck MK. 2
The MK.2 version of the standard Stream Deck comes with 15 programmable buttons, a swappable faceplate, and a detachable stand.
Resident Evil Requiem
The latest entry in the long-running survival horror series returned in 2026, with two different styles of gameplay (tense first-person and guns-blazing third-person perspectives) via its dual protagonists. Read our review.

articles.title: Jason Arday's research cleared in investigation
articles.body:
Jason Arday research for Queen's University cleared in investigation
Research by academic Jason Arday, who was accused of plagiarism before his death, has been cleared by one of the institutions that was investigating him.
Queen's University Belfast (QUB) began looking into Jason Arday's work after he resigned from his University of Cambridge roles.
The university had published a paper on its academic research site co-authored by Arday and other academics from Queen's.
In a statement, a spokesperson for QUB said: "Having reviewed the matter, we are satisfied that the paper meets the appropriate academic standards and have no concerns regarding its publication."
The paper, published in 2021, was corrected in 2024 to clarify that it used methodologies similar to a previous study Arday had written, which in turn had been based on another research paper published in 2016 by a team of academics at Brighton and Sussex Medical School.
Arday, who became Cambridge's youngest black professor in 2023, was found dead in Battersea on 14 August, having resigned as a professor of sociology of education the week prior.
The 41-year-old's death followed weeks of media coverage over plagiarism allegations and questions about his achievements. He denied the claims. An inquest into his death is under way.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham described the death of the former professor as "a tragedy on so many levels".
Accusations of plagiarism in Arday's work were first voiced by Nathan Cofnas - a US researcher and self-defined "race realist".
Cofnas has previously written that black people are less intelligent than other groups and would "disappear from almost all high-profile positions outside of sports and entertainment" under a meritocratic system.
He claimed on the online publishing platform Substack that he had put Arday's work through a plagiarism detection software, which found that "many passages are lifted with minimal editing, sometimes retaining copy-editing mistakes from the original source".
Following Arday's death, Cofnas was suspended from his post at Ghent University, after it launched an investigation into him "for discriminating against" the former Cambridge professor. He was later handed a three-month teaching ban.
Public figures and friends of Arday had called for a public inquiry into media coverage surrounding the former professor before his death.
Labour MP Diane Abbott and actress Jameela Jamil were among 30,000 signatories of a letter to the prime minister, which claims Arday's death followed "two weeks of relentless harassment".
The University of Cambridge launched a two-part independent review examining the support available to Arday before his death, as well as the wider context of his time at the university.
Liverpool John Moores University - which awarded Arday his PhD in 2015 - concluded that he had not plagiarised work.
Other institutions including Glasgow University, Durham University and Queen's University Belfast all began investigating Arday's work or his appointments to various positions.
Back in August, Queen's University said it was "looking into" a paper, published in 2021, on the impact of what was taught in universities on "Black, Asian and Minority Ethnic (BAME) learners" and "academics of colour".
The paper was called "Attempting to break the chain: Reimaging inclusive pedagogy and decolonising the curriculum within the academy".

articles.title: Buying a laptop right now is rough, but these Black Friday deals help
articles.body:
Laptop prices have been a hot-button topic all year long thanks to RAMageddon. We’ve seen existing models get more expensive and new models arrive at higher prices than last-gen — sometimes with lower specs, too. 2026 in general has been a bad time to buy a computer. But thankfully, Black Friday can offer a tiny bit of respite.
Buying a laptop right now is rough, but these Black Friday deals help
Despite the year’s bevy of price increases, this is the best time to buy a new laptop (if you absolutely need to).
If the computer you currently use is working well for you, good. Happy for you. But if you’re in the market for something more powerful, bigger, smaller, thinner, etc. — and you prefer new over used — you can currently save some decent dough on MacBooks, Windows notebooks, and gaming laptops.
The big, multi-hundred-dollar savings are typically reserved for higher-end models with bigger specs, like Windows models running Nvidia’s new Arm-based RTX Spark platform — which are getting their first major discounts. More budget-friendly laptops are also receiving decent discounts right now, though, including the MacBook Neo. The current $100 discount on Apple’s budget laptop might seem like small potatoes considering it’s just a return to its original price, but it’s the best you can do for now (if you can’t hold out for a rumored new one in 2027).
As always, the deals below are for laptops we’ve reviewed or tested firsthand in some way at The Verge — either that exact model or a similar one we expect to be equally good. There are many laptops out there and myriad deals running now through Cyber Monday, but if any of these fit your needs, you can’t go wrong.
MacBook Neo
Apple’s most affordable laptop uses the same A18 Pro chip found in the iPhone 16 Pro. It features a vibrant 13-inch display, surprisingly good speakers, and 8GB of RAM, making it a solid option for students and anyone who needs a laptop for everyday tasks. Read our review.
Apple MacBook Air (M5)
Apple’s latest MacBook Air features an M5 chip and starts with 512GB of storage, with significantly faster performance than prior generations. It’s still an excellent machine despite the higher base price, especially given the battery life and speakers. Read our review.
Apple MacBook Pro 14 (2026, M6)
Apple gave its base model MacBook Pro an upgrade to a 12-core M6 chip for 2026, and not a whole lot else. Read our review.
Apple MacBook Pro (M5 Pro / Max, 2026)
The non-OLED M5 Pro and M5 Max versions of the MacBook Pro deliver exceptional power and speed, making them ideal for creative work while offering best-in-class battery life. Read our review.
Apple MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display
Apple’s latest (and priciest) MacBook Pro is its first with a touchscreen. The new PROLED models pack familiar M5 Pro and M5 Max chips into a thinner and lighter chassis. Read our review.
Dell XPS 13 (2026)
The best XPS 13 in years. It doesn’t have a headphone jack and starts with only 8GB of RAM, but it’s an excellent thin-and-light with a great screen, a solid Intel chip, and speedy storage.
Dell XPS 14 (2026)
An incredibly nice feeling laptop with great battery life and a love-it-or-hate-it latticeless keyboard. Read our review.
Microsoft Surface Laptop 13-inch (8GB, 2026)
The latest 13-inch Surface Laptop has lower starting specs than the 2025 model, with 8GB of RAM, but it’s still a well put together laptop that now feels better to use after some notable Windows 11 updates. Read our review.
Lenovo IdeaPad Slim 3x
The IdeaPad Slim 3x offers a 15.3-inch touchscreen and a comfortable keyboard. It runs a base Snapdragon X chip, making it well-suited for the basics. The real highlights are battery life and port selection. The speakers, however, are terrible. Read our review.
Lenovo IdeaPad Slim 3i (2026)
One of Lenovo’s new alternatives to the MacBook Neo, with an Intel Wildcat Lake chip, 8GB of RAM, and plenty of ports.
Acer Chromebook Plus Spin 514 (2025)
A great convertible Chromebook with fantastic battery life. Read our review.
Asus Zenbook A16
A 16-inch laptop that’s as light as a 13-inch MacBook Air, packing a powerful Snapdragon X2 Elite Extreme chip and 48GB of RAM.
Asus Zenbook A14
Asus’s Zenbook A14 is a bit of a MacBook Air wannabe, but it’s a compelling alternative if you value a superlight Windows laptop with long battery life. The 2025 model sports an Arm-based Qualcomm Snapdragon X Plus chip, a nice 14-inch OLED display, and a sleek textured beige finish.
Asus Zenbook Duo (2026)
An expensive but excellent dual-screen laptop with a powerful Intel Panther Lake chip. The only thing better than a lovely OLED display is having two of them. Read our review.
HP OmniBook 3 16 (Intel Core 7)
An affordable laptop with a large 16-inch display, plenty of ports, and a solid Intel Core 7 350 chip. Read our review of the Snapdragon model.
HyperX Omen 15 (Intel Core 5 210H, RTX 5050)
The Omen 15 isn’t as affordable as its previous generations, but its upgrade to an RTX 50-series GPU means access to Nvidia’s latest DLSS game enhancements. Read our review.
Asus ROG Zephyrus G14 (2026, Intel)
Our favorite do-it-all gaming laptop for everyday use and portability got a nice upgrade for 2026: a faster Intel chip, better battery life, and a full-size SD card slot. It also got much more expensive than its previous generation. Read our review.
HP OmniBook 5 14 (2025, Snapdragon X Plus)
A nice OLED, 16GB of RAM, and marathon battery life in a travel-friendly laptop with an affordalbe price. Build quality is only okay. Read our review.
Acer Swift Air 14
Acer’s answer to the MacBook Neo, with an Intel Core 5 processor, 8GB of RAM, 120Hz display, and speedy Thunderbolt 4 ports. We’re still testing this one, but it’s showing promise for an affordable choice.
Acer Swift Go 16 AI
One of Acer’s most affordable 16-inch laptops can be had with either Intel or AMD chips. The large display isn’t particularly bright or high resolution but it’s got a smooth 120Hz refresh.
Lenovo Legion 5i 15.3-inch (2025)
Impressive specs with a step-up RTX 5060 GPU and sleek white chassis color for a low-$1,000 price when discounted.
Lenovo Yoga 7i 2-in-1
A good Intel Panther Lake chip, lots of RAM, and an OLED display combined in a 2-in-1 chassis.
Asus ProArt P14 (RTX Spark)
The entry point into RTX Spark laptops, the Asus ProArt is a creator-focused MacBook Pro wannabe with a sleek blacked-out design and lovely OLED display. Read our initial Nvidia RTX Spark hands-on.
Lenovo Yoga Pro 9n
Lenovo’s Yoga Pro 9n with an 18-core RTX Spark chip has a high quality 15.3-inch OLED display and comes with a stylus you can use either on its screen or trackpad. Read our initial Nvidia RTX Spark hands-on.

articles.title: 9/UX: a Macintosh-inspired desktop for 9front
articles.body:
9/UX brings the classic Mac and A/UX desktop (a spatial desktop, a global menu bar, consistent controls and dialogs, icons, and resource-driven presentation) to 9front, built the Plan 9 way: rio and libdraw draw the screen, 9P exposes every application's UI state and commands as files, namespaces define the working environment, the plumber opens documents, and ndb holds human-editable metadata.
Keep the Macintosh's direct-manipulation desktop,
but make every meaningful object, action, and resource visible as a Plan 9 file.
It is not an emulator, a Macintosh ABI, or an A/UX reimplementation. Native 9front programs stay first-class, and existing rio programs (acme, sam, rc windows, nested rio) keep working unchanged beside 9/UX apps.
The pieces:
- rio fork (rio -u): a desktop layer, a global menu bar that follows the focused app, title-bar chrome, and a drag broker, all under /dev/ux. With 9/UX mode off it's stock rio.
- Desktop: volume icons, spatial folder windows, rename, duplicate, Get Info, Trash, remembered layout, and double-click to open documents through the plumber. A remote 9P server works as a volume.
- libux, the Toolbox: windows, menus, dialogs, alerts, and controls, each app serving its control tree over 9P, so echo activate >.../ctl presses a button.
- uxd gathers every app's tree at /mnt/ux with per-app policy; uxmeta keeps associations, volumes and layout in ndb files; resfs serves classic ICN#, icl8, menu, dialog and string resources at /mnt/res; clipd is a typed clipboard kept in step with rio's snarf.
These are real frames, not mockups. The GUI tests embed h9 with a headless screen, inject mouse and keyboard input, and drive the 9P files at the same time.
Macintosh structure, Plan 9 colour: butter title bars from rio's selection yellow, acme's cream and olive, and rio's greygreen for the desktop, so 9/UX windows and legacy rio windows sit together on one screen. Everything reads in one bit, uses a sixteen-colour palette, and is drawn in whole pixels. Every graphic is original to 9/UX; it ships no Apple resources. The mockups below are generated from the same palette and metrics files as the code.
The design document describes 9/UX and its v0.1 acceptance criteria; release.md has where each one stands, the end-to-end demo, and the open issues. Every interface between components is a file protocol in docs/protocols, and the visual design covers the palette, fonts, metrics, chrome, icons and cursors.
The source is on GitHub, under the MIT license. Development runs on h9, which runs 9front's own compilers, mk and rio directly from the host shell, without booting a VM. scripts/h9.sh clones and builds the pinned h9 on its first run:
git clone https://github.com/progrium/9ux
cd 9ux
scripts/h9.sh --rc 'mk'
scripts/h9.sh --gfx rio/7.out -u
scripts/test.sh
Use rio/6.out on amd64. development.md and testing.md have the details.
9/UX is at v0.1 and under active development. Interfaces and behaviour change without notice.
Please report bugs and send questions through GitHub issues.
The 9/UX mark in the menu bar is a pixel-art Glenda by Dan Fessler. Glenda, the Plan 9 bunny, was created by Renée French.

articles.title: Making a 3D fantasy map like a 16th-Century atlas
articles.body:
Making a Fantasy Map Like a 16th-Century Atlas
Hugo -
Over the last few weeks, I worked on a map of various game dev techniques for people to refer to and learn from. Like, a real map! With each town being a technique's home, provided with a concise, illustrated example. And here we are. Today we are diving into the making of The Game Dev Atlas.
That's so 1570, bro.
If you want to pull off a cohesive art direction, you need to spend most of your time learning about your reference materials. No C code, no IDE, no sub-agents doing things. Just explore and wander on Google Images (old-school, I know), Wikipedia, and online museum galleries.
Gather things, ideas, and visuals! You should feel the inspiration (literally, as you inspire fresh air) inflating your mind, and the first scraps of decisions starting to flow through your head, like: I want a bit of that, none of that, this thing specifically for that part etc.
That is the whole work: what do you want? It's on you to set the quality bar and how things should be.
If you don't already know, typography conveys most of the design weight. That's just it.
Example: after some research I stumbled on that Luminari font that was a great fit for what I wanted my map to look like. It is a paid font, and there were plenty of free alternatives, but not quite as right as the Luminari font. Instead of saying "that's ok, this free one is the same vibe", I just paid for the font I found just right. Never concede terrain on your instinct!
A real island.
Claude, please generate a procedural terr...
Just pick an existing, real island. Nowadays we do have precise elevation data for most islands on Earth. If you want a realistic island, well, pick a real one.
Engraving in real time.
Some styles and colourings I've tried (click on the tabs to compare):
Don't be perfect!
Add some imperfections, color blends, etc. Nothing is perfect in real life, and having an eye for imperfections is what makes things look interesting.
Making towns interesting.
The point of the atlas is to showcase game dev techniques, one per town. So I decided two things:
First, I wanted small visual touches on each town's shape reflecting the technique it's about. For instance, the Procedural Legs town shows a crawling house.
Second, I wanted organic town buildings, so I built a small procedural building system to add diversity to buildings. Risky move: I'm a big fan of Houdini, so I could have thrown away the whole thing, and this blog post would be titled "I'm making Houdini, but running in the browser".
Anyway, here's what my small system can build:
60fps on the web.
The map application itself is written in C using the Kaigen engine as a headless C lib. I'm a Rust guy, but I must admit the compile time freaks me out for game dev with Rust. It took me several iterations to reach smooth 60fps in the browser, especially with the night mode (try it!).
But I'm finally happy with how it runs right now, while I'm still tweaking things atm.
The web app is written in Svelte, because I like Svelte. So the shallow routing and anything UI happen as part of the SvelteKit app.
Conclusion
It was a very fun project! At the end of the day, I love the creative process of making things, shaping ideas like a material, refining details. I strongly believe that when artists leverage AI, y'all will be cooked; because they alone know how to touch the human soul and create the surprise.
The Game Dev Atlas
Acknowledgments and tools used
- Sprite Fusion for the pixel art in the techniques
- Svelte and SvelteKit for the web app
- Luminari by Canada Type for the lettering
- EB Garamond Initials by Georg Duffner (SIL Open Font License) for the illuminated initials
- Kaigen for the engine
- NASA Earth Observatory for the photo of Kerguelen (28 October 2016)
- Terrain Tiles on AWS by Mapzen, and the data sources they name, for Kerguelen's elevation

articles.title: The Oura Ring 5 just got its biggest discount ever for Black Friday
articles.body:
If you’ve been curious about smart rings but have been put off by their high price tags, Black Friday is a good time to consider giving one a try. That’s because the Oura Ring 5, which we consider the best smart ring you can buy, has dropped to an all-time low of $299 ($100 off) at Amazon, Best Buy, Walmart, and Oura’s online storefront for Black Friday.
The Oura Ring 5 just got its biggest discount ever for Black Friday
Our favorite smart ring can track your sleep, activity, and more without requiring you to wear a smartwatch.
Compared to the Ring 4, the Oura Ring 5 offers a thinner, lighter, and more durable design that’s more comfortable to wear throughout the day and while sleeping. Like its predecessor, it can track your sleep, activity, heart rate, and other health metrics, giving you insights into your overall well-being without requiring you to constantly check a screen. It also offers roughly the same battery life and sensors as the prior model, though its new charging case supports wireless charging. (Unfortunately, the case is currently sold separately for $99.)
Oura has also introduced several new software features, including Health Radar, which looks for potentially significant changes in your health. You can also import medical lab results, track GLP-1 medications, and access AI-assisted medical guidance through Oura’s partnership with Counsel Health. My colleague Victoria Song appreciated how the latter makes it easier to connect with an actual doctor, though she found it better suited for quick medical questions than more serious health concerns.
However, none of these software features are exclusive to the Ring 5, and you’ll still need a $5.99 monthly Oura membership to access most of its health insights. Given how similar the two generations are, we wouldn’t recommend upgrading if you already own a Ring 4. But if you’re new to smart rings, the current discount makes Oura’s latest model much more attractive, especially since it’s only $50 more than the Ring 4’s starting price.

articles.title: Mozilla Thanks Users For New Features in Firefox 161: Site-Specific VPN and Keyboard Shortcuts
articles.body:
Mozilla Thanks Users For New Features in Firefox 161: Site-Specific VPN and Keyboard Shortcuts (mozilla.org) 10
			
		 	
				Firefox 161 (released Tuesday) promises "A better Firefox, thanks to you.  All of these improvements began with a community request."  In a Thanksgiving-themed message, they wrote "Here's to the passionate people who keep us moving forward."
Choose which sites always open with VPN. Our free built-in VPN just got one of its most requested upgrades. Pick sites where the VPN always turns on, and sites where it stays off because they work better without it.  Bonus: VPN data is unlimited through January. Use it as much as you like until then...
Set your own shortcuts .  Create keyboard shortcuts for what you use most, like opening tabs, saving pages or closing windows.  Type "about:keyboard" in the address bar.
See images appear as they load.  Firefox now supports JPEG XL, an image format that lets you see a preview of the full image before it downloads. 
Neowin notes Firefox is also committing to its redesign:
Mozilla has been trying to win over users from Chromium-based browsers, hoping they pick up Firefox. To do so, aside from still supporting uBlock Origin, the firm made a big design shift this year by introducing Nova, so that users on the other side can feel they are familiar with it, as it brings the more common, modern rounded corner design philosophy, which Google's Chrome has been using for quite a while... However, as is usually the case, not everyone has been on-board with Nova and they are completely fine to feel that way; Mozilla also understands this which is why it offered a way to opt-out of it by tweaking a configuration setting via about:config. However, this week the firm announced that it is going to take that option away.
In a post on its official Mozilla Connect forum, which was shared with us by Neowin forum member ecmram, the Firefox team confirmed that it will remove the config toggle preference for reverting to the old design next month in December. The company says that the rollout of Nova is now complete, and it wants to lock the preference to ensure that Firefox performs as intended and to prevent unexpected browser behavior. As such, anyone who has previously used the browser.nova.enabled preference to disable the redesign will automatically get Nova starting next month, thus wiping the official way to return to the previous UI once the change takes effect. 
On the positive side, Mozilla is not entirely ignoring feedback from users who are unhappy with the redesign. The company says it has introduced several changes based on community feedback, including a new set of Classic Themes with the latest version 161, that offer flat colors without gradients. These can be found under about:addons, and one of them even mimics the older Proton design with a gray appearance.  There is a new Fire toolbar button too that clears history with a single-click.
