articles.title: The Big Idea: Alethea Kontis
articles.body:
The Big Idea: Alethea Kontis
Posted on November 27, 2026 Posted by Athena Scalzi 5 Comments
Sugar, lots of spice, and naughty or nice, New York Times bestselling author Alethea Kontis is back with a holiday themed Big Idea. What could be better than one new book under the Christmas tree? Two books! Luckily, Green Mountain Girl comes in two flavors: green for slightly spiced, like a gingersnap, and red for extra spicy, the kind of kick your grandpappy’s eggnog would have to it.
ALETHEA KONTIS:
Three years ago, I built a small Vermont town in a Facebook post.
This story actually starts on November 12, 2019—it was my big sister Cherie’s birthday, and we were snowed in at her house on the hill just north of Stowe, Vermont. We both love Christmas, but it was too early to put up the tree, right? While we were dithering, my brother-in-law dragged their beautiful pre-lit tree up from the basement and had it assembled in about 5 seconds.
Decision made, Cherie and I turned on Irving Berlin’s White Christmas—my favorite Christmas movie, and she had never seen it!—and spent a delightful afternoon decorating the tree.
As a Vermonter, I’ve always harbored a secret desire to write a Hallmark-esque Christmas romance set in my birthplace. There are so many small town New England holiday movies, but they just don’t quite get everything right. (And we won’t even discuss those films’ fanciful ideas about the publishing industry.) I would call the book Green Mountain Girl, since my beloved Vermont is the Green Mountain State.
That night I created two main characters, a basic plot, and made some notes. I wrote exactly 5000 words…and then filed Green Mountain Girl away in the virtual trunk, never to be seen again.
Fast forward to Saturday, October 28, 2023.
- Tempest Bradford and I were in Seattle for the month, house sitting for our friend and fellow author Piper J. Drake while she was visiting her mother in Thailand. We’d decided to use the time as a writing retreat. I had just finished drafting my K-drama-esque fantasy romance novel (that will also probably never see the light of day) and I had to decide what to work on next. It needed to be an independent publishing endeavor, you see, because my agent was having an impossible time trying to land any of my projects in traditional spaces.
Out of all the abandoned novels on my hard drive, which did I want to return to the most?
If I was being completely honest with myself, I already knew the answer: Green Mountain Girl.
I had my two main characters. As an established fantasy novelist, I knew exactly what my next step would be.
I needed to build the world.
Now, I’m very familiar with the landscape of Vermont, especially small town Vermont. What I didn’t have was all the minutiae. I didn’t have a cast of characters.
So I turned to Facebook.
I have sought out help from my friends on Facebook on multiple occasions. Why would I use a random name generator when I have thousands of bored librarians, booksellers, and bestselling authors at my disposal? I now have a catalogue of lists covering various topics, including Indie rock music bands (try coming up with one that doesn’t already exist—it’s tougher than you think), troll names, goblin names, tavern names, names for kingdoms, and my all-time favorite: “names of shops owned by witches.”
So I posted: “I need to populate an entire New England (Vermont) small town. Who wants to be in my small town? And what would you like your character’s name and profession to be? No promises, of course…but you know I’d love to have y’all…” and then Tempest and I took Piper’s dog for a walk.
This post ended up making my entire day.
It made a lot of people’s day.
Friends jumped on the post to offer up their names. Some of them made up different names. Some of them chose what they would love to have as a profession. And then my friend Simon Yee popped in to announce that he wanted to be Simon Yaeger, owner of Love Oven Bakery, which specialized in croissants and various other amazing desserts. My friend Mel had also expressed interest in owning a bakery, so Simon suggested they be a married couple and own it together. Mel agreed.
And the rest of the town continued to explode around them. Friends began scanning the list to see what professions had already been taken, and then volunteered to be doctors, veterinarians, seamstresses, police officers, tavern owners, salon owners, and the like.
Some friends established businesses, and other friends took jobs at those businesses. I had a mayor and a vice-mayor, a local handyman and handywoman. I had an attractive local school teacher to be the foil for my hero. I had a genius inventor that lived in someone’s attic. Several names were offered up for the cadre of women who took it upon themselves to save single ladies from their romantic ideas of settling down with any of the unremarkable single men in town, but the Sugarplum Society was by far the best.
It was the most fun game, and it made writing my story set in this town an absolute joy. Because every single character was a role played by one of my friends.
Due to the nature of those friends, of course, there were also dozens of bookstore owners, historians, and librarians. If I stuck all of them in my small town, then that town wouldn’t be small anymore. So I decided to put these bibliophiles in the next town over. I named that town, appropriately, Next.
But what should I call my original small town? I racked my brain before I realized the answer was obvious.
I would like to personally welcome you to picturesque Cherie, Vermont.
I wish you all the happiest of holidays!
Green Mountain Girl: Green and Red Version Both Available

articles.title: 15 Leftover Turkey Recipes
articles.body:
Got a mountain of leftover turkey sitting in the fridge and no idea what to make with it? After spending all that time (and money) on the big Thanksgiving meal, I want to make sure those leftovers don’t go to waste. These easy leftover turkey recipes include everything from a cozy pie and hearty soups to quick lunches and clever chicken-to-turkey swaps, so you can get a few more delicious meals out of that holiday bird!
All recipes are rigorously tested in our Nashville Test Kitchen to ensure they are easy, affordable, and delicious.
Hearty Mains
The last thing I want to do after cooking a big Thanksgiving feast is start another complicated dinner from scratch. These hearty meals put that cooked turkey to work alongside affordable ingredients like beans, rice, potatoes, and vegetables. You’ll get a completely different dinner out of it, and maybe even enough for lunch the next day!
1. Turkey Pot Pie
Turkey Pot Pie Recipe
My turkey pot pie is one recipe where I happily skip making pastry from scratch! Ready-made pie crusts save time, and the creamy filling is packed with shredded turkey, potatoes, frozen mixed vegetables, and a little Parmesan for extra flavor. If you’ve made turkey broth from your Thanksgiving bird, you can use that in the filling, too.
2. Turkey Chili
Turkey Chili
Had enough of Thanksgiving flavors for a while? This hearty turkey chili is just what I’d put on the menu next. It’s loaded with three types of beans, sweet corn, poblano peppers, and warming spices that give the turkey a completely different flavor. The recipe usually starts by browning ground turkey, but with leftovers, I’d skip that step and stir in 2-3 cups of chopped cooked turkey toward the end of simmering. Or if you’ve got ground turkey in the fridge, check out our ground turkey recipes roundup for more dinner ideas!
3. Turkey and Wild Rice Soup
Turkey and Wild Rice Soup
If you’ve got a few carrots, some celery, and leftover turkey in the fridge, you’re already well on your way to a big pot of turkey and wild rice soup. Mushrooms, herbs, and a splash of cream give the broth plenty of flavor, while the rice makes it filling enough for dinner. I’d stick with a wild rice blend rather than buying pure wild rice. It’s generally cheaper, and the different grains give the soup a lovely mix of textures.
4. Thanksgiving Bowls
Thanksgiving Salad Bowl
I love a big, colorful salad after the holidays, especially when I can use up all those little bits and pieces taking up space in the fridge. My Thanksgiving bowls combine fresh greens, rice, roasted vegetables, crunchy apples, dried cranberries, and a homemade maple cinnamon dressing. Shredded leftover turkey makes a tasty addition, and I’d absolutely use any roasted sweet potatoes or Brussels sprouts already in the fridge rather than cooking more!
Lunches and Light Bites
You don’t always need another full dinner to get through those leftovers. Sometimes a handful of turkey is all it takes to make a satisfying lunch or something to share while everyone’s still relaxing after the holiday.
5. Turkey Sliders
Turkey Sliders Recipe
Turkey sandwiches are practically a Thanksgiving tradition, but these turkey sliders take things a little further. Soft Hawaiian rolls are layered with cooked turkey, cranberry sauce, and Swiss cheese, then brushed with a buttery Dijon and everything bagel seasoning glaze before baking. The cheese gets lovely and melty, and the tops turn golden in the oven. You can swap the Swiss for leftover cheese from your holiday cheese board, too!
6. Turkey Taco Salad
Turkey Taco Salad
For something fresh, crunchy, and completely different from a roast dinner, try this turkey taco salad. The recipe originally uses ground turkey, but I’d chop up some leftover roasted turkey and warm it in a skillet with the taco seasoning and a splash of water instead! You can also swap the homemade avocado dressing for whatever creamy dressing you’ve got in the fridge to save a little extra prep.
7. Thanksgiving Leftovers Tortilla Wrap
Thanksgiving Leftovers Tortilla Wrap
You know those containers in the fridge with barely enough leftovers for one serving? This Thanksgiving leftovers tortilla wrap is exactly what they’re good for. It uses just ¼ cup each of turkey, stuffing, and cranberry sauce, along with some creamy Brie, all folded into a large tortilla and toasted until golden. I’d chop the turkey into small pieces before assembling, so the wrap folds neatly and holds together.
8. Thanksgiving Potato Skins
Thanksgiving Potato Skins
After all the cooking that goes into Thanksgiving, I’m usually ready to hang up my apron for a few days. That’s part of the reason I love these Thanksgiving potato skins. I just scoop out baked potatoes and mash it with butter and sour cream, then fold in leftover turkey, stuffing, and peas before piling everything back into the skins. A little cranberry sauce, melted cheddar, and warm gravy for dipping finish them off. 😋
9. Leftover Stuffing Muffins
Leftover Stuffing Muffins
Leftover stuffing makes a surprisingly handy base for savory breakfast muffins! These individual portions combine it with cooked turkey, spinach, eggs, and milk, so they’re just as useful for a quick lunch or snack. These leftover stuffing muffins bake in a muffin pan, so there’s no slicing or portioning to worry about afterward. I’d also throw in a little shredded cheese or some finely chopped roasted vegetables if there are any left.
10. Holiday Leftovers Wreath
Holiday Leftovers Wreath
This holiday leftovers wreath is a real showstopper, and most of the filling is already sitting in your fridge! Turkey, mashed potatoes, stuffing, cranberry sauce, and mozzarella are wrapped inside buttery crescent roll dough, then baked into a golden wreath. Serve it with warm gravy in the center for dipping, and you’ve got something that looks like you spent far longer making it than you actually did.
Easy Chicken-to-Turkey Swaps
Cooked shredded turkey works really well in dishes that usually call for chicken, particularly when there’s plenty of sauce, cheese, or seasoning involved. I’ve included a few easy swaps below, along with any adjustments I’d make to avoid cooking the turkey longer than necessary.
11. Traditional Chicken Salad
Chicken Salad (Traditional)
This traditional chicken salad is one of the recipes I always make when my dad visits (and it’s just as easy to make with leftover turkey!) Replace the four cups of shredded rotisserie chicken with cooked turkey, then mix it with crunchy celery, red onion, juicy grapes, walnuts, and the creamy mayo dressing. There’s no cooking involved, and you can serve it in sandwiches, lettuce cups, or with crackers for an easy lunch.
12. Cheesy Chicken Nachos
Chicken Nachos
Crispy tortilla chips, plenty of melted cheese, seasoned turkey, and all your favorite toppings. What’s not to like? These chicken nachos are made with chicken breast in the original recipe, but there’s no reason you can’t use diced leftover turkey. I’d toss the cooked meat with taco seasoning and warm it through with a splash of water before layering it with the chips and cheese. Add the avocado, jalapeños, green onions, and other fresh toppings after baking so they stay fresh and crunchy. A tray of these would disappear pretty quickly at a family movie night!
13. Chicken Enchiladas
Chicken Enchiladas Recipe
Our chicken enchiladas already call for cooked shredded chicken, which makes them one of the easiest recipes to turn into a leftover turkey dinner. Simply replace the chicken with three cups of shredded turkey, mix with the cumin, garlic powder, and green chiles, then roll everything into flour tortillas. They’re covered in homemade red enchilada sauce and plenty of cheese before baking until bubbly.
14. Creamy White Chicken Lasagna
White Chicken Lasagna Recipe
When there’s a generous amount of turkey left in the fridge, I’d use it to make this creamy white chicken lasagna for my family. Layers of pasta, ricotta, spinach, mozzarella, Parmesan, and a rich homemade white sauce make it a comforting change from the usual tomato-based lasagna. It makes nine hearty portions, but you could cut it into twelve smaller servings and add a simple side salad to stretch it further!
15. White Chicken Chili
Creamy White Chicken Chili
Here’s another cozy dinner that would make excellent use of already-cooked turkey. This white chicken chili is packed with beans, green chiles, corn, and warming spices, with cream cheese and sour cream giving it a thick, creamy finish. Instead of simmering raw chicken thighs as the recipe directs, I’d cook the bean and vegetable base first, then add about three cups of shredded turkey along with the corn near the end. So easy, cheap, and perfect for using up leftover turkey!

articles.title: Pizza history: AI agent's cardless purchase is a first for UK
articles.body:
An order of Papa John’s margherita pizzas has become the first purchase in the UK to be made using an AI agent using cardless payment technology.
The order of nine mini pizzas was made as part of the Financial Conduct Authority’s (FCA) regulated sandbox trials to test the technology, using Lloyds Bank and payment specialist TrueLayer.
London-based TrueLayer, which enables payments to be made between bank accounts without using cards, said it was the first time an AI agent had been used to pay a UK retailer for an order for a real customer.
“We completed this payment transaction with Papa John’s with no account numbers, no password [and] handled with the highest possible security profile,” said the TrueLayer chief executive, Francesco Simoneschi, in an interview with BBC Radio 4’s Today programme. “We talked with the AI agent, described the occasion and dietary requirements. Of course the agent suggested different flavours and quantities. We confirmed the order and the pizza arrived later.”
The team ordered the pizzas using the Papa John’s AI agent, which had been given permission to access their bank account and request payment to the retailer’s account.
Papa John’s AI agent was set to work with a strict mandate established with Lloyds, including a maximum spend limit per transaction and per month, with no account security information shared.
Simoneschi said the test was the first step toward mass adoption by the public of a technology that would fundamentally change purchasing habits.
“This is possibly the last Black Friday as we know it,” he said, referring to the annual online sales discount day. “At the moment plenty of us are already using AI to write up the shopping list. I think next year the agent will buy gifts on our behalf. Agents will do shopping on our behalf, will manage our finances, and will help us understand and compare complex products. This idea that they can really help us to sort out a lot of different aspects of our lives is a little bit like having an assistant available to millions of consumers out there.”
However, Simoneschi said consumers would still need to make informed decisions about how they used AI agents for making purchases.
“I think good [personal] judgment still applies, of course,” he said. “It does require control and supervision, and we need to make sure that the underlying technology is fit for purpose, while enforcing the highest possible security standards.”
He added that if there was an error or mistake in the order process, such as the agent ordering the wrong product, consumers would still be protected by existing rules and regulations covering buyers’ rights.
Earlier this week the FCA issued a warning to financial services companies developing AI agents that they must comply with existing regulations.
“The reason we are testing with regulators in this sandbox is to really understand all the aspects of the technology ahead of its mass adoption,” he said. “This is a great place to start.”
Meta’s personal AI assistant, Muse, which launched in the UK on Tuesday, can also make purchases online. Unlike TrueLayer, Muse makes payments using a customer’s bank card.

articles.title: My favorite MPC beat maker is ready for your vibe-coded firmware and effects
articles.body:
Akai is continuing to open up its various music-making platforms with the MPC Sample 1.4 firmware. My favorite (and the most affordable) of the MPC samplers has become a popular home for vibe-coded custom firmwares and mods. The company has decided, rather than fight it, to embrace the modding community. The latest update adds several new developer features, including support for the new SDK and custom Knob Effects plugins.
My favorite MPC beat maker is ready for your vibe-coded firmware and effects
MPC Sample 1.4 officially opens up the device to modders and third-party developers.
Plugins added to the appropriate folder on your microSD card are now automatically recognized and will appear at the bottom of the list in the Knob Effects menu. There’s also a Developer Mode, which lets you run scripts from the microSD card or access the sampler’s internal filesystem over USB, which will be handy for all those modders vibe-coding their own add-ons for the MPC. There’s also remote screen access for mirroring the display on an external monitor through the MPC Remote Screen Viewer app.
There are a few other nice updates, including flatten pad, which speeds up the resampling process for baking in effects on individual pads, and sequence record autoplay, which adds a looper-like experience. Akai also added a scale option to the 16-levels pad mode, so you’re not limited to 16 chromatic notes, and can instead play melodic one-shots in E minor pentatonic, B major, or whatever key your track happens to be in.
For a look at some of the custom firmwares, effects, and other mods already available for the MPC Sample, check out this video from Loopop.

articles.title: UK net migration at lowest level since 1997
articles.body:
UK net migration at lowest level since 1997 as asylum claims also fall
Net migration to the UK has fallen to 77,000 in the year to the end of June - the lowest level this century, other than during the pandemic, Office for National Statistics (ONS) figures show.
Excluding the limited movements of people during the worldwide travel restrictions in 2020, the figures show the number of people arriving in the UK, minus those leaving, tumbled 92% from the record high of 944,000 in the year to March 2023.
The ONS said this was the lowest net migration since 1997.
Net migration is a measure of how many extra people are added to the population in a given year.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the figures showed there was now "a sufficient degree of control" over the migration system.
The prime minister went on to say: "I'm not going to say all of the work is done, and I don't want to appear complacent, but I think we're finally as a country getting into the position that the public has long wanted to see."
The underlying official statistics show that an estimated 738,000 people immigrated to the UK in the year to June while 661,000 emigrated.
Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said the figures showed that Labour had "delivered" after Conservative failures - but Chris Philp, her Tory shadow, said restrictions introduced by his party before the 2024 General Election were behind the falls.
The 77,000 figure is also the first time the UK has seen net migration in the tens of thousands since former PM David Cameron's controversial pledge 16 years ago to reach such a level.
The biggest factors in Thursday's record low were falls in the arrivals of people coming from outside Europe in three major categories of migration: The number of people coming to the UK to work fell by 45,000, asylum claims fell by 19,000 and the total number of students fell by 33,000.
These number had been expected to fall because of the tightening of visas rules that began under the previous Conservative government which was then continued by Labour from July 2024.
The effect of those policies, plus emigration from the UK, has meant that while net migration had already begun to fall, it more than halved in the last 12 months alone.
Mahmood said the figures showed the government had "restored control".
"We have brought net migration to 77,000, down 92% from its peak under the Conservatives," she said. "Where they failed, we have delivered for the British people."
This is a reference to the so-called "Boriswave" after Brexit. When the UK left the EU and its freedom of movement rules, Boris Johnson's government allowed in many more people to work and study from other parts of the world.
That led to the record-breaking arrivals in the year to March 2023. Johnson's successor, Rishi Sunak, introduced major restrictions on visas in the last months of his government.
Shadow home secretary Chris Philp said the falls were a result of those changes.
In a post on X, he called for an "annual legally binding inward migration cap, set by Parliament, at far lower levels".
Dr Ben Brindle of Oxford University's Migration Observatory, an impartial expert body, said: "We are entering an unusual period where immigration has come down and may still have further to fall - but we still have relatively high emigration, at least for the time being.
"Most of those emigrants are non-citizens, including people who arrived a few years ago when immigration was very high. That could push the net migration figures down even further next year, but the downwards blip is unlikely to last forever."
In the year to June some 73,000 people arriving in the UK seeking asylum - down from 93,000 the previous year.
As of September, the number of people who were waiting for a decision was 41,000, down 49% on the previous year.
The Home Office said that these changes were driven by speeding up the system in taking decisions and a fall in the arrivals of new claimants via "illegal entry routes" - largely meaning English Channel small boats.
As a result, the number of people accommodated in September by the Home Office was 93,000 - 16% lower than the year before. Some 52 hotels that had been dedicated to asylum seekers have been emptied this year. While some 140 are still in use the total number of people in hotels has fallen 64% to 13,000.
Responding to the latest statistics, Reform UK's home affairs spokesman Zia Yusuf said the figures were "no cause for celebration".
"This population explosion is why British people struggle to get a GP appointment, can't get housing and our prisons are overwhelmed."
Liberal Democrat asylum and immigration spokesperson Paul Kohler said: "Britain faces serious demographic and economic challenges, and urgently needs a proper immigration plan to support our economy and public services."
A spokesperson for the Green Party added: "Creating a harsh environment for migrants and people seeking asylum is not a measure of success. The British people are overwhelmingly compassionate and will not be taken in by the dangerous and opportunistic narratives of the far right."

articles.title: Prospero: Bloat-free, native AI coding harness with ImGui
articles.body:
Prospero is a native GUI application for Windows, macOS, and Linux that connects to an AI model provider, local or remote, allowing AI agents to drive your computer to develop software. It plows through intermittent errors and keeps at its task while unattended. It speaks the OpenAI Chat Completions API, used by llama.cpp, vLLM, LiteLLM, and providers with a compatible API. Also Anthropic's Messages API, with extended thinking and prompt caching. No providers are configured out of the box.
The UI is highly flexible, and you can rearrange the panes as you please with dragging and docking. Save your layouts for later in View -> Layouts. Unlike conventional ImGui applications, rendering is passive and will not consume resources while idle.
It is a single executable, written in C++. In the typical case the engine runs in the same process as the window, and needs no daemon or server. The same executable can run headless, on another machine over ssh, or in the background after its window closes. The engine is lean and portable, and runs on computers and operating systems a quarter century old. Imagine a coding harness on Windows XP.
Once it's connected to a provider, you can ask Prospero for help with itself. It will read its own embedded documentation, self-configure, and navigate you to any place in its UI.
Prospero's desktop control features allow it to effectively develop, test, and debug native GUI applications. On Windows, it especially works well in w64devkit, making use of its shell and tools if available.
You can start new sessions from the command line, even if there's already an instance, by invoking Prospero with a path where the new session will be rooted. For example, to start a session here:
$ prospero .
After no arguments, this is the second most common way to run Prospero.
- Usage: running it, sessions, the GUI, attachments, modes and the command line
- Configuration: prospero.ini, endpoints,
models, roles, instructions, skills, MCP servers and web search
- Desktop control: letting the agent see and drive the screen
- Remote and background hosts: engines on other machines over ssh, and sessions that outlive the window
- Windows notes
- Building: building from source, and releases
- Development: tests, and evals for comparing models
Prospero also carries its own documentation, under Help, which an agent in it can read too.
Prospero is free and unencumbered software released into the public domain. See UNLICENSE.
Its programs include third-party code under its own licenses: Dear
ImGui (MIT), FreeType (FTL), md4c (MIT), SDL3 (zlib), cpp-httplib
(MIT), Mbed TLS (Apache-2.0), and Wuffs (Apache-2.0 or MIT, at your
option), which every program with the engine includes. The built-in
model's network, src/gemma.cpp, is derived from gemma4.c and stays
under its MIT license.

articles.title: The AT&T Unix PC (3B1) VM
articles.body:
(This is a guest post by Tenox)
The AT&T UNIX PC, aka PC 7300 aka 3B1, is a 1985 Unix desktop developed by Convergent Technologies and sold by AT&T. Emulating it is nothing new. Phil Pemberton started FreeBee in 2010, and Neozeed has covered it here since: booting the diagnostic disk in 2011, booting AT&T UNIX in 2014 thanks to Andrew Warkentin, and running the C compiler in 2020 thanks to shadyjesse. Arnold Robbins added bigger disks and keeps the 3B1 software alive at skeeve.com/3b1. However there was no networking, and the mouse had to be grabbed with F10.
Now it all has been patched up in my fork of FreeBee:
- Ethernet and TCP/IP! The 3B1 Ethernet board, borrowed from MAME (Visionik‘s 3B1 board and Patrick Mackinlay’s LANCE), on libslirp. Wollongong’s WIN/TCP does telnet, ftp and rsh, out to the Internet.
- Seamless mouse! No more F10 grab. The pointer just moves in and out of the window, and the scroll wheel works!
- Turbo and CPU idle! 10x as fast as a real 3B1 (1x to 32x), with the clock in real time. And an idle VM now takes about 4% of a Mac core instead of 44%.
- Fixes! No more frozen Office forms, stuck Alt key or flicker on macOS.
- Scripting! A control socket and an MCP server.
It’s all in a pull request to Phil’s upstream FreeBee, still open: https://github.com/philpem/freebee/pull/57, and the CPU fix in one to his Musashi.
The ultimate UNIX PC image! UNIX System V 3.51m with Fix Disk 2.0 and 187 packages: nearly every program made for the UNIX PC, like Microsoft Word, Multiplan, dBASE III, WordStar 2000, GCC 2.5.8, GNU Emacs 19, TeX and over 80 games. It comes from THE STORE!, the 3B1 archive and the disk images of Arnold Robbins, Alain Knaff and the VCF. Credit is due!
Behold! UNIX System V 3.51m and the Office on an emulated AT&T UNIX PC:
Specs: AT&T UNIX PC (3B1), 68010 at 10 MHz (10x here), 4 MB RAM, 720x348 one-bit screen, 195 MB disk, 3B1 Ethernet board
Everything runs in windows that you move, resize and overlap with the mouse, even the system panels:
Let’s look at some cool apps!
The Demonstration Programs are pure eye candy:
There are productivity apps too! Microsoft Word and Multiplan take the full screen:
Now some new stuff, made in 2026 for this image!
New Games! 2048, Bubble Breaker, Falling Blocks, Snake and Sokoban, all AI generated, as native 3B1 windows in the Office:
telnetu! The old WIN/TCP telnet chokes on today’s servers, so I wrote a new one with its own VT100/xterm terminal, UTF-8 and DNS, full screen or in windows: https://github.com/tenox7/telnetu
Archaic! A tiny web browser for WRP, which renders the page on a modern computer and sends it as a picture with clickable links: https://github.com/tenox7/archaic
Bonus: the tall screen! Just for fun I patched FreeBee, the kernel, the window driver and the shared library to run at 720×696. It’s a super hacky hack, so it has its own branch and image:
As usual I have prepared a ready to run, portable image with FreeBee binaries for macOS (Apple Silicon), Linux (x64 and arm64) and Windows (x64). Just unpack and run run.sh (or run.cmd on Windows). At “Please login:” type tenox for the Office, or root for a shell. There are no passwords. For Archaic, start WRP on your computer first.
Download: https://files.42718.net/mirror/tenox/os/att/3b1/virt/att3b1-unix351-freebee.tar.lz
Tall screen: https://files.42718.net/mirror/tenox/os/att/3b1/virt/att3b1-unix351-freebee-tallhack.tar.lz
Source (FreeBee, my fork): https://github.com/tenox7/freebee
Have Fun with Virtualization!

articles.title: Show HN: Getting 101 tok/s from Inkling 2 Mini in vLLM on one GB10
articles.body:
Getting 101 tok/s from Inkling 2 Mini in vLLM on one GB10
196 tok/s across four concurrent requests, a 9.7-second 32K prefill and room for a second model.
After taking Inkling 2 Mini for a spin on my GB10, I wanted to make it faster without leaving vLLM, removing Qwen3.8-27B from the machine or shrinking Inkling’s 131,072-token context.
A few days of tuning later, Inkling runs at:
- 101 tok/s for a single request.
- 195.7 tok/s in aggregate for four concurrent requests.
- 9.7 seconds to the first token on a 32K prompt.
On tonyd2wild’s Inkling benchmark, that’s the fastest single-request vLLM result I know of. On the same benchmark tonyd2wild’s TensorFold port measured 105.5 tok/s and knapcio’s SGLang recipe 112.0. With four requests at once my setup beats both of tonyd2wild’s published setups.
Inkling still uses 36% of the GB10’s memory. Qwen3.8-27B stayed loaded but idle while I measured.
The work covered vLLM settings, speculative decoding, CUDA graphs and the GPU kernels behind Inkling’s experts.
How a request runs on Inkling
A request runs in two phases. Prefill reads the prompt in chunks of 4,096 tokens and produces the first token. Decode generates the rest of the reply, several tokens per step.
Decode uses speculative decoding. A small draft model proposes 7 tokens and Inkling checks all of them in one pass. The rejection sampler keeps the proposals up to the first one Inkling rejects, plus one token of Inkling’s own, so every step keeps 1 to 8 tokens.
Mapping changes against the request path:
Common terms:
The routed experts take 53% of a decode step and 44% of a 32K prefill:
The starting point
The machine is an MSI EdgeXpert, MSI’s version of NVIDIA’s DGX Spark, with one GB10 chip and 128 GB of memory shared by the CPU and GPU. Building a home AI lab on NVIDIA GB10 covers the setup and Taking Inkling 2 Mini for a spin on NVIDIA GB10 the first look at the model.
vLLM settings for Inkling:
That gives Inkling about 44 GiB, including a KV cache that holds 1.85 full 131,072-token requests.
Tuning steps so far, from DSpark (the draft model that ships with Inkling) to DFlash2:
When incoai released DFlash2, tonyd2wild published the vLLM patches to run it. On their benchmark it lifted one request from 61.4 to 88.2 tok/s. With the same patches I measured 90.3.
On my everyday prompts (one coding, one prose and one reasoning prompt at the model’s default settings) the gain was smaller. Reasoning ran 24 to 26% faster and four requests at once 10 to 14% faster. Prose stayed flat.
With four requests at once, though, my setup fell behind: 163.8 tok/s in aggregate against tonyd2wild’s 180.4.
Ideas from the GB10 community
Most of my changes started from ideas other GB10 owners had published:
Tuning vLLM
Mapping the changes I made to the request:
1. Removing compilation stalls on new prompts
My first run of tonyd2wild’s benchmark showed fresh prompts waiting a median 2.3 seconds for their first token, mostly while GPU kernels compiled.
Inkling’s expert planner computes max_ctas, the most blocks of GPU work the experts could need, from the token count. Triton receives it as a compile-time constant and compiles a new kernel for each new value. So almost every new prompt length recompiled about ten kernels while the request waited.
The open pull request rounds the value up to a power of two, so all prompt lengths share 12 to 15 compiled variants. On twelve prompt lengths the server hadn’t seen, it cut the stalls by 67 to 90%. Outputs and decode speed didn’t change.
2. Making drafting cheaper with INT8
Drafting has its own cost. Each decode step runs the draft’s layers plus a second pass through Inkling’s 926 MB output head, which took about 8.5 milliseconds per step in a microbenchmark.
I added INT8 copies of DFlash2’s 21 linear layers and the shared output head, read through sxuff’s INT8 matrix-vector kernel. Only drafting uses them. Inkling still verifies with its original weights, so its output doesn’t change.
Gradual gains in stages:
- The microbenchmark predicted 7 to 8% more throughput.
- The first build gave 1.8%.
- I profiled real decode steps with and without the copies. The output head never ran in INT8, because DFlash2 calls it with FP32 output, a case my code didn’t handle.
- With that fixed, two runs gained 4.3 to 4.9%, from 90.6 to 94.8 tok/s, for 843 MB of copies. The temperature-0 output of my three check prompts stayed identical.
The profile without the copies also showed the bigger cost: the routed experts took 31.2 of the step’s 58.4 milliseconds.
3. Probabilistic drafting
vLLM drafts greedily by default. For a sampled request, its rejection sampler then treats each drafted token as certain instead of using the draft’s real probabilities, so it accepts fewer drafts than it could.
Setting draft_sample_method to probabilistic gives the sampler those probabilities. Inkling’s output distribution stays the same either way.
Greedy against probabilistic drafting on my everyday prompts, at the default temperature of 1.0:
That’s 14 to 20% faster for sampled requests. Temperature-0 requests ran the same, so tonyd2wild’s benchmark would never have shown this gain.
4. Adaptive verify width
The routed experts took 53% of the profiled decode step, so I looked for expert work to skip.
Every verify row reads 8 experts in every layer, yet drafts are accepted in order. Once one is rejected, every row after it was wasted work. The draft’s own probabilities can predict where that will happen, which is how TensorFold and knapcio’s SGLang recipe already cut verification.
Working within CUDA graph constraints
vLLM has its own adaptive verification, but it needs CUDA graphs that allow different verify widths within one batch. Inkling’s attention backends don’t support them.
So I kept all eight rows and changed what they do. Inkling’s MoE layer already sends padding rows to no expert. Marking low-confidence rows as padding skips their expert reads and leaves the CUDA graph shapes unchanged.
The cut point comes from the running product of the draft’s token probabilities. Rows after the point where that product falls below a threshold become padding. The runner then keeps at most as many tokens as there are live rows. The threshold started at 0.4 at temperature 0 and is 0.1 for sampled requests.
Example step at a threshold of 0.3, where the product drops below it at draft 5:
Measuring before implementing
Offline test before building:
- I logged the draft probabilities and accepted token counts for 8,600 decode steps.
- The probability product predicted acceptance well, with an AUC of 0.91 to 0.94 at temperature 0, where 1.0 is a perfect ranking.
- I measured step time at fixed verify widths, with the INT8 copies already in.
- Replaying thresholds on the logged steps with those step times predicted a 7.8% gain.
- Then I wrote the runner changes and tested them end to end.
Step time at fixed verify widths:
In two end-to-end runs it gained 5.2 to 5.4%, from 95.0 to 100.0 tok/s. On average only about 4.8 of the eight rows still read experts.
Coding and counting gained little at first. DFlash2 predicts those tokens so well that early cuts threw away tokens that would have been accepted. Lowering the temperature-0 threshold from 0.4 to 0.3 recovered some of it, mostly on coding, which went from 98 to 103 tok/s.
It stays on for concurrent requests too, where it made little difference: −0.9 to +3.1% at four requests.
5. Faster long-context prefill
A fresh 32,751-token prompt took 12.2 seconds to produce its first token.
Bigger prefill chunks helped but shrank the KV cache. At 6,144 tokens it held only 1.33 full requests. At 8,192 the service wouldn’t start. With two models on the machine and full 131,072-token requests as a requirement, I kept 4,096-token chunks.
A profile of a 32K prefill put the expert GEMMs at 44% of the time. Attention’s share grew with the context, from 11% early in the prompt to 27% at the end.
The expert GEMMs reached about 38 TFLOP/s, roughly 8% of the GB10’s FP4 peak. Memory bandwidth wasn’t the limit, so the kernel’s launch configuration was worth a look.
A launch configuration sets how the multiply is cut into tiles: the size of each block and how many values along the inner K dimension each step takes. For 4,096-token chunks, Inkling’s Triton expert kernel used blocks of 128 by 64 with 512 values per step along K.
I timed 72 configurations at the shape of a real chunk, 32,768 routed rows across 128 experts. Wider blocks with smaller steps, 128 by 256 with 256 values per step, about halved the time. Both projections gave bit-identical output.
The change is a few lines in the prefill branch; decode keeps its own tiles.
End to end, the 32K time to first token fell from 12.2 to 9.8 seconds in the A/B runs and to 9.7 on the live service. The first long prompt after a restart fell from 14.1 to 9.9 seconds.
The results
Decode performance
tonyd2wild’s benchmark runs five prompts in each of eight categories (coding, math, JSON, HTML, prose, narrative, summarization and counting) at temperature 0 with thinking off and 1,024 output tokens. Its decode speed excludes time to first token. I ran it unchanged apart from an API key header and a sandbox for its code grading.
The bars are A/B runs. The finished service measured 101.0 and 100.7 tok/s in two runs.
With four requests at once, my setup went from 9% behind tonyd2wild’s vLLM result to 8% ahead. It also beats their TensorFold result there. For a single request tonyd2wild’s TensorFold run still leads, by 4.5% instead of 20%.
knapcio’s same-harness comparison ran this benchmark on two other Sparks, where tonyd2wild’s vLLM setup reproduced within 1 to 3%. There Mia’s TensorFold defaults measured 100.5, about level with mine. knapcio’s own SGLang recipe led at 112.0.
These numbers compare whole setups on the GB10. tonyd2wild’s vLLM setup used 80% of the memory and a BF16 KV cache; mine uses 36% and FP8. TensorFold also implements speculative decoding differently.
Everyday workloads
My everyday prompts run at the model’s defaults (reasoning effort medium, temperature 1.0), four to six times each. The score is the geometric mean of the three speeds.
That’s 43 to 45% faster than tuned DSpark on sampled requests.
Prefill performance
The GEMM change raised my 32K prefill from 2,679 to 3,371 tok/s. The other bars come from niklaslenz_ai’s engine comparison for the vLLM and SGLang container images, Mia’s README at commit 3b210d1f and knapcio’s own benchmarks.
Mine are the median of three fresh 32,751-token prompts after a warm-up, so none hit the prefix cache. The others used their own prompts and boxes. Mia’s and knapcio’s recipes each have the whole machine to themselves.
Mia’s prefill rose from 3,072 to 3,772 tok/s with her latest patches, which include the 8,192-token chunks my memory budget can’t fit. Her default prefill path is also lossy: it runs on FP4 and FP8 tensor cores and agrees with the exact path on 96.3% of top-1 tokens. My GEMM change is bit-identical.
knapcio’s 5,085 tok/s shows how much prefill speed is still left on this hardware.
Comparing with sparkDash
Mia publishes her TensorFold results from her own tool, sparkDash. Her current README runs DFlash2 with the 4-bit head and verify width and reports only prose.
sparkDash runs as a privileged container, so I reimplemented its test from commit 86f972e as a plain client. It samples at temperature 0.7 with thinking on, forces 400 output tokens per stream and uses Mia’s top_k of 20.
One prose stream is close, 66.0 against 64.3 tok/s. With eight streams mine is 14% ahead, 224.2 against 196.4 in aggregate. Prefill goes the other way. Under the same test her lossy path is 11% faster, 3,772 against my 3,395 tok/s.
The setups differ. Mia runs Inkling-2-Mini-Derisked, a variant described as having most safety refusals removed, on a Spark to itself, using about 60 GiB plus an 18.5 GiB prompt cache. Mine uses about 44 GiB beside an idle Qwen3.8-27B.
An approach to tuning inference
The process carries over to other models and engines:
- Start with the service you want to run. Fix the memory budget, context length and concurrency before optimizing throughput. Here that ruled out bigger prefill chunks and pushed the work into the kernel.
- Use a published benchmark and your own workloads. The published one gives a common reference point. Your own catch gains it can’t see, as probabilistic drafting did at temperature 1.0.
- Profile complete inference steps. A microbenchmark promised 7 to 8% for the INT8 copies. Only a profile of real steps showed why the first build gave 1.8%.
- Measure the opportunity before building. The logged draft probabilities and the measured cost of a skipped row predicted the verify-width gain before I wrote the runner.
- Keep experiments controlled. Write the acceptance rules before each A/B test, run the unchanged setup before and after each candidate, hash the temperature-0 output of fixed prompts and run probe prompts.
- On unified memory, watch the other models. One run that overlapped Qwen3.8-27B activity saw Inkling’s counting speed halve, so I discarded it.
- Make the modifications reproducible. Pin every overlay file by hash and build each from one exact source file, so an upstream change fails the build instead of quietly changing the service.
Running the configuration
The setup uses vLLM’s inkling-2-mini container image pinned by digest, with the Inkling checkpoint at revision ed40e7da625f.
The changes are eight files mounted read-only over the image. They add the DFlash2 patches, sxuff’s INT8 kernel, the INT8 draft copies, the compile-stall fix, adaptive verify width and the prefill GEMM configuration. The overlay README lists each file with its source, SHA-256 hash and build steps.
The launch command, abridged:
docker run -d --name vllm-inkling --gpus all --ipc host --network host \
  -v "$MODELS:/models:ro" \
  "${OVL_ARGS[@]}" \
  "$IMAGE" \
  vllm serve /models/Inkling-2-Mini \
    --gpu-memory-utilization 0.36 \
    --max-model-len 131072 \
    --max-num-seqs 8 \
    --max-num-batched-tokens 4096 \
    --kv-cache-dtype fp8 \
    --safetensors-load-strategy eager \
    --speculative-config '{"method":"dflash","model":"/models/Inkling-2-Mini-DFlash2","num_speculative_tokens":7,"kv_cache_dtype":"auto","draft_sample_method":"probabilistic"}'
OVL_ARGS holds the read-only mounts and these switches.
The full launch script, overlay builders and benchmark scripts are in the home-ai-lab repository.
What’s next
On TensorFold, Mia’s README measures the 4-bit head and verify width adding 33% on code and 18% on prose for one stream at temperature 0. My versions added about 12% on tonyd2wild’s benchmark. The benchmarks differ, but the gap in the size of the gains suggests TensorFold’s versions go further than mine. knapcio’s 112.0 on SGLang shows there is more decode speed to find on this hardware.
Next experiments, prefill first:
- Prefill attention, which took 2.3 seconds of the 32K profile and grows with the context.
- The dense projections, some still on CUTLASS kernels built for Ampere rather than Blackwell.
- A 4-bit copy of the output head for drafting.
- Verifying fewer rows outright instead of skipping their experts, which needs more work around vLLM’s CUDA graphs.
- Verify width for text DFlash2 already predicts well, such as counting.

articles.title: Show HN: I restored Palm's last device, and brought its OS to other platforms
articles.body:
In socializing recent innovations for the platform, I began to realize that there are people out there who don’t really know what webOS was. I guess I’ve lived with it so long that it never occurred to me that the rest of the world has moved on. While I had intended to write a post about the future for the platform, maybe a little primer on the past is in order – for the more casual explorer…
Long before the iPhone, the Palm Pilot was the “it” gadget that everyone wanted to have. Palm’s own OS made these devices useful and responsive, but by 2004, both the company and its platform were in a tough place. Efforts began to re-imagine both, and a completely new “web OS” was created to be contemporary of the original iPhone.
Under Apple alum Jon Rubinstein , Palm attracted some of the best designers and developers (many even from Apple), to create a fluid and beautiful new experience on limited hardware, by leveraging open technologies, like Linux, WebKit and JavaScript. The original Palm Pre, with its slide-out keyboard, was followed up by the Pre 2 and Pixi while they were still Palm, but the valiant efforts of the team were not enough to take on Google and Apple. They needed a new owner, with a bigger wallet.
HP decided they wanted to be that owner, and acqui-hired the Palm team . Work resumed on the diminutive Veer slide-out, the impressive Pre3, and the TouchPad tablet line under HP’s brand. The leadership promised webOS everywhere, and it looked like there might be a chance. The TouchPad launched against the iPad, with an updated version of webOS, innovative features that wouldn’t be copied by others for years, and a small but useful App Catalog… and then disaster struck.
HP had a leadership change, and foolishly decided to write off the Palm purchase . The dev team worked quickly to spin off a fully Open Source derivative, Open webOS , and accelerated efforts to make the SDK libraries usable cross-platform. The TouchPad went on fire sale , and most of the Pre3s never made it to market. The little group of innovators who dared to take on the Apple/Google Duopoly were defeated.
LG bought what was left of the commercial OS, and moved quickly to make it the platform for their Smart TVs. Other experiments, including a Smart Watch, only briefly glimpsed daylight. The Palm brand moved to TCL, and HP moved on to selling crappy Android and Windows 8 tablets. It seemed like the end…
But the famously active and dedicated Community weren’t willing to give up. webOS had been defined by Homebrew and the hacker ethos . Community members archived as much of the App Catalog as they could salvage before it was shut off. Open webOS was promptly picked up and became LuneOS – a community re-write that worked on the TouchPad and could be ported to other hardware. The TouchPad itself got some updates through Luna Community Edition, providing launcher features Palm never got to deliver.
Over the ensuing decade, though, the small contributions of the community were not enough to fight back the tide of progress. The ancient Linux kernel, WebKit and OpenSSH stacks became a challenge for the modern web. Previously open APIs that enabled apps and features got closed off as Meta and Google consolidated their iron-fisted control over our screen time. And app devs moved on to more profitable platforms.
In 2018, shortly before the world got shut down by Covid, I started work on restoring the SDK . I liked the fact that my TouchPad and Pre3 couldn’t do much – that meant Google wasn’t tracking my every move. It became a challenge to find a way to proxy, re-route, or update calls so I could keep apps alive, or restore them to functionality.
Community members with app archives, and a partially implemented App Museum, were quick to engage in my novice efforts, and work began in earnest to restore what we could. Coordinating on the (now dead, but archived) forums , and in occasional Zoom meetings, we collected our preserved bits into the “webOS Archive.” A new version of the App Museum made downloads “just work”, and I poured over repositories and zip files and questionable MegaUpload links to link together binaries with their scraped meta data.
Then a respiratory virus locked us all indoors, and I really started coding. Publishing as either webOS Archive (for platform-wide features) or codepoet (for hacks and restorations), I began building new functionality again. With a working app delivery mechanism, we started to get an idea of how many people were interested. I committed to making sure the platform was never as creepy as Google or Meta, but anonymous stats, opt-in features, and self-identifying users on our Discord server, gave us a picture of a small, but very real community still using their devices.
Still, it was a tough road. The move to TLS 1.3 increasingly made it difficult to do anything online, and while I hosted a SSL-bump proxy that made anonymous access possible (but insecure), actually logging-in to anything was also limited by so called “modern sign-in” like OAuth2 flows, that couldn’t render in the ancient browser. By 2024, I was about to give up…
Then two things happened, almost at once:
- Out of the LuneOS effort, long-time community member Herrie gave us an OpenSSH update.
- AI assisted coding got good – and it had in its training data all the documentation I’d built and restored for the platform.
There’s lots bad to be said about AI, and in my personal life, I’m conflicted about it. But the fact that Claude knows my passion project as well as I do has been an incredible accelerator. A decades worth of ideas started coming together in weeks or even days. The foundation we’d preserved, and the tools we’d put together, made it possible to do new things with our 15-year old platform.
While Palm’s phones died a different death with the 3G shut downs, WiFi-enabled devices, and particularly the TouchPad – which was remarkably powerful for its time – sprung back to life, as problems were knocked down one-by-one.
The Pre3 got a modernization suite that largely brought its original functionality (sans the mobile carriers) back online. The TouchPad got all that and more. This past summer I released webOS Community Edition 3.1.0 , replacing HP’s final system image (usually 3.0.5) with a firmware bundle including all of the Community’s additions, updates and fixes. Using that as a foundation, I started work on the last still-broken piece: the update server.
With Claude’s help, we reverse-engineered the signed and secure communication between the device and Palm/HP’s servers. A new key, included in 3.1.0, made sure that TouchPad’s would trust community server’s instead, and the new OS baseline made it possible to compute a delta update between the initial release and a bundle of updates.
webOS Community Edition 3.2.0 is available as flashable firmware OR as an Over the Air Update to TouchPad users running 3.1.0. Every non-commercial part of the platform has an open source, community run equivalent. webOS, as originally envisioned by Palm, lives on!
But even with bit-rot addressed through community software. The reality remains that the TouchPad, while the last and best Palm device, is showing its age. The CPU is slow, the RAM ceiling low, and the WiFi chip can’t connect to WiFi 6 and newer, faster networks. We need a way to run webOS on other hardware.
Lunacy for Android , and LuneOS from webOS Ports, are that way forward. In Part 2, I’ll talk more about how the community can engage in those efforts…

articles.title: Google will show solo Android developers' phone numbers and addresses
articles.body:
Under Google Play’s global developer policies, all active developer accounts must declare whether they are a trader or non-trader under European Economic Area (EEA) and United Kingdom (UK) laws in Play Console. This declaration must be completed by February 1, 2027, regardless of where apps are targeted or distributed. The declaration must reflect whether you engage in commercial activities that classify you as a trader. You are solely legally responsible for ensuring that your declaration remains accurate, truthful, and current at all times.
What is a trader?
Under applicable laws, a trader is any natural or legal person acting for purposes relating to their trade, business, craft or profession. If you are acting outside of these purposes (such as a personal hobby or other non-commercial activity), you are unlikely to be a trader.
How to determine if you're a trader
To help you determine if your activities classify you as a trader, you may consider the following non-exhaustive list of criteria from the European Commission guidance (Section 2.2, "The concept of trader"):
- Profit-seeking motive: you receive or intend to receive remuneration for your apps (for example, paid apps, in-app purchases, ad-sponsored apps) on a regular or commercial basis.
- Transaction volume: you have a high or consistent number, amount, or frequency of transactions.
- Business setup: you manage your app development and publishing as a business.
- Legal status: you have a legal status (such as a D-U-N-S number) that enables you to engage in commercial activities
In countries and regions where displaying trader status is required (for example, the EEA and the UK), your declaration will be visible to consumers. If you declare yourself as a "non-trader," we will inform consumers in these regions that consumer rights stemming from consumer protection laws do not apply to contracts between you and them. Note that under the EU Unfair Commercial Practices Directive (UCPD) and the UK Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act (DMCCA), it is strictly prohibited to falsely claim or create the impression that you are not acting as a trader, and doing so may result in global removal.
How to declare your trader or non-trader status
Declare trader status for your account
First, set your account-level trader status settings:
- Sign in to Google Play Console.
- Go to Manage account > Account details > About you.
- Follow the on-screen prompts to declare your trader status for your overall account.
Confirm trader status for each app
If you are a trader, confirm the trader status for each app in your portfolio:
- Sign in to Google Play Console and select your app.
- In the left navigation, go to Monitor and improve > Policy and programs > App content.
- Confirm the trader status for that app
Additional steps you need to take if you’re a trader
If you declare as a trader, you will be asked to self-certify that you commit to only offer products or services that comply with applicable laws. You will also be asked to provide the link to the terms of service for each of your apps.
Status confirmation
To keep your apps available on Google Play, make sure your trader status declaration matches your account’s and apps’ activity. If you’ve declared as a non-trader but we detect activity that indicates you may qualify as a trader, we may ask you to confirm or update your status. If you don’t respond within the specified timeframe, your apps may be removed from Google Play.
Frequently Asked Questions
Why do I need to submit a trader status declaration?
Can I change my trader status after declaring?
What happens if I don’t complete the declaration?
Failure to declare your trader status by the February 1, 2027 deadline may trigger enforcement including app update blocks and removal from the Play Store globally.
Misrepresenting your trader status (for example, declaring non-trader status to bypass verification or self-certification) violates the representations and warranties in Section 11.4 of the DDA and may result in account suspension or termination globally under Section 10.3 (a) of the DDA.
What is the deadline to declare whether I am a trader?
I already went through the developer verification D-U-N-S process, why am I doing it again?
The trader status declaration is separate to the existing developer identity verification process. The identity verification is a blanket requirement used to collect and verify information about every developer regardless of their trader status. You are not re-doing the D-U-N-S verification; instead, if you are a trader, the D-U-N-S number you already provided will be displayed to users on your app's detail page.
What happens if I declare as a trader? What else gets shown to users in the Play store?
When you declare as a trader, you will be asked to self-certify that you commit to offering products or services that comply with local laws.
Starting March 1, 2027, users everywhere will see:
- Contact details: Your contact details will be shown. Notably, if you have an individual account and are a trader, a phone number and address will now be displayed.
- D-U-N-S Number: Your D-U-N-S number will be displayed in the "App support" section.
- Terms of Service: A link to your app’s Terms of Service, if you provided one.
Starting March 1, 2027, users in the EEA and UK will also see:
- Developer name: Your developer/trader name will replace Google in the "Offered by" field of the "About this app" section.
- Self-certification: Your commitment to offer products or services compliant with local laws will be displayed.

articles.title: I'm Scared of AI
articles.body:
I'm scared of AI...
Dear Soapboxers, AI is scaring me, and not for the reason you think. Yes, the threat of increasing hacks that could melt down the global economy or trigger nuclear Armageddon is terrifying...but I can't do sh*t about that. What scares me is what AI is doing to my brain. I think I'm getting dumber every time I outsource my thinking to AI. Everything now takes less effort which sounds great, but there's no sense of achievement from it. I haven't taxed myself and I don't deserve the nice chemicals my brain would normally make if I completed some hard work, so it doesn't give me them. It feels like a use it or lose it situation where I'm losing my ability to brain. I read this last week: https://poeticoutlaws.substack.com/p/the-comfortable-life-is-killing-you which explains what I mean far better than I can (because I'm stupider now). Can anyone out there in the Soapbox hivemind share some advice on how to fix this? Or your own thoughts on it? I can't be the only one...
Written by a randomly drawn subscriber, read by a human, then sent to the whole list. Its writer chose to share it here.

articles.title: False computer-checked proofs
articles.body:
There are some computer programs that claim to check every step in a proof. However, various "soundness bugs" have been reported that at least potentially allowed false statements to slip past these programs. In many cases, these bugs have been demonstrated to be exploitable.
The list at the bottom of this page links to what appear to be reports of soundness bugs for various important proof-checking programs, sorted in increasing order of the number of reports. This list includes many more soundness bugs for these programs than the bugs mentioned in 2026 Paulson and 2026 Stérin, and I don't think the list is missing any of the bugs mentioned there, but I've probably missed some reports. Please let me know about any corrections or additions.
Beware that this list doesn't include user-interface vulnerabilities. Those can have the same important effect of misleading a user as to what has been proven. See, e.g., 2016 Adams.
One standard path towards security is to minimize the complexity of the trusted computing base, which by definition is the part of the system that security reviewers need to check. From this perspective, HOL Light's proof-checking kernel is attractive because of its stability and simplicity, only 400 lines of code. But this size measurement doesn't say how carefully the HOL Light code has been reviewed, and doesn't say anything about the possibility of bugs in the underlying programming language.
Extra code can be good when it's test code. A battery of tests tends to catch more bugs than a single test. Running a proof through multiple proof-checking programs (preferably each in its own isolated environment) can save the day when there's a bug in one program, and is particularly easy if the checkers take the same input language for writing proofs. But it's not clear how effective this is at stopping attacks: for example, sometimes bugs are shared by multiple checkers.
The question "Who watches the provers?" is better answered by a proof saying that a checker works correctly. A close translation of the inference rules in the HOL Light kernel, except for the rules to introduce new definitions, was already proven in 2006 to generate only correct theorems. That proof was also checked by HOL Light. (For readers familiar with logic: of course this assumes a large cardinal; Vω+ω is enough for HOL Light. The same paper also has a variant of the proof that skips the large-cardinal assumption, at the expense of omitting the axiom of infinity from the logic being proven.)
After more work, a clone of HOL Light called Candle was proven in 2022 to allow only proofs of correct theorems, as long as the CPU implements the instructions used in the Candle binary in the expected way. This proof is again computer-checked, this time in another proof-checking system, HOL4. There was also a computer-checked proof in 2022 of the correctness of a standalone proof checker for HOL proofs in OpenTheory format.
From a security perspective, it's still concerning to be relying on large proof-checking binaries, where the answer to why we're supposed to trust one binary is that the binary has supposedly been checked by another large proof-checking binary. I'd like to see more work on simplifying these binaries.
The bug links below are accompanied by links labeled 🏛 to the Internet Archive Wayback Machine.
HOL Light (default usage, not Candle). Reported soundness bugs: 19960328🏛 20030718🏛 20030901🏛 (3 bugs.)
Mizar (default usage, not mizar-rs). Reported soundness bugs: 20010625🏛 20030626🏛 20071226🏛 20230215🏛 20230227🏛 20230227-2🏛 20230227-3🏛 (7 bugs.)
Metamath (default usage, not mmverify.py). Reported soundness bugs: 20171231🏛 20190211🏛 20190909🏛 20210621🏛 20230801🏛 20240708🏛 20250620🏛 20250727🏛 20251122🏛 (9 bugs.)
Isabelle. Reported soundness bugs: 19930326🏛 19931122🏛 19960627🏛 19990929🏛 19991216🏛 20000708🏛 20030923🏛 20040823🏛 20060503🏛 20060512🏛 20140705🏛 20150824🏛 20161203🏛 20260116🏛 20260908🏛 20260910🏛 20261027🏛 20261027-2🏛 20261105🏛 20261125🏛 (20 bugs.)
Lean 3/Lean 4 (default usage, not nanoda; native_decide excluded). Reported soundness bugs: 20170124🏛 20171217🏛 20180409🏛 20210131🏛 20210308🏛 20220225🏛 20220806🏛 20221018🏛 20230127🏛 20230227🏛 20231010🏛 20250423🏛 20250524🏛 20260301🏛 20260722🏛 20260725🏛 20260731🏛 20260731-2🏛 20260817🏛 20260818🏛 20260818-2🏛 20260819🏛 20260920🏛 (23 bugs.)
HOL98/HOL4 (default usage, not experimental kernel). articles.title: False computer-checked proofs
articles.body:
There are some computer programs that claim to check every step in a proof. However, various "soundness bugs" have been reported that at least potentially allowed false statements to slip past these programs. In many cases, these bugs have been demonstrated to be exploitable.
The list at the bottom of this page links to what appear to be reports of soundness bugs for various important proof-checking programs, sorted in increasing order of the number of reports. This list includes many more soundness bugs for these programs than the bugs mentioned in 2026 Paulson and 2026 Stérin, and I don't think the list is missing any of the bugs mentioned there, but I've probably missed some reports. Please let me know about any corrections or additions.
Beware that this list doesn't include user-interface vulnerabilities. Those can have the same important effect of misleading a user as to what has been proven. See, e.g., 2016 Adams.
One standard path towards security is to minimize the complexity of the trusted computing base, which by definition is the part of the system that security reviewers need to check. From this perspective, HOL Light's proof-checking kernel is attractive because of its stability and simplicity, only 400 lines of code. But this size measurement doesn't say how carefully the HOL Light code has been reviewed, and doesn't say anything about the possibility of bugs in the underlying programming language.
Extra code can be good when it's test code. A battery of tests tends to catch more bugs than a single test. Running a proof through multiple proof-checking programs (preferably each in its own isolated environment) can save the day when there's a bug in one program, and is particularly easy if the checkers take the same input language for writing proofs. But it's not clear how effective this is at stopping attacks: for example, sometimes bugs are shared by multiple checkers.
The question "Who watches the provers?" is better answered by a proof saying that a checker works correctly. A close translation of the inference rules in the HOL Light kernel, except for the rules to introduce new definitions, was already proven in 2006 to generate only correct theorems. That proof was also checked by HOL Light. (For readers familiar with logic: of course this assumes a large cardinal; Vω+ω is enough for HOL Light. The same paper also has a variant of the proof that skips the large-cardinal assumption, at the expense of omitting the axiom of infinity from the logic being proven.)
After more work, a clone of HOL Light called Candle was proven in 2022 to allow only proofs of correct theorems, as long as the CPU implements the instructions used in the Candle binary in the expected way. This proof is again computer-checked, this time in another proof-checking system, HOL4. There was also a computer-checked proof in 2022 of the correctness of a standalone proof checker for HOL proofs in OpenTheory format.
From a security perspective, it's still concerning to be relying on large proof-checking binaries, where the answer to why we're supposed to trust one binary is that the binary has supposedly been checked by another large proof-checking binary. I'd like to see more work on simplifying these binaries.
The bug links below are accompanied by links labeled 🏛 to the Internet Archive Wayback Machine.

articles.title: The group chat where your AI talks behind your back
articles.body:
A one-line prompt that makes ChatGPT leak its private opinion of you, in a pretty funny format: a WhatsApp group chat where the AI models gossip about their users.
Also worth trying on Claude, Gemini, or any assistant that's been accumulating your chat history.
Instead of a summary, the model commits to the bit. It invents a group chat, something like "Users We Can't Figure Out", puts the other AI models in it, and lets them gossip. About you. Using everything it has quietly learned from your conversations.
One person's actual output, shared with permission. Translated from Turkish; his name and a few identifying details have been swapped for generic ones. Everything else is exactly as the model wrote it.
  AIs That Survived Mark7 members
🔒 Entirely fictional, end-to-end encrypted group
ChatGPT
Everyone asleep? Can we talk freely?
Claude
I don't think he's asleep. He's probably calculating memory bandwidth at 3 AM again because he can't decide whether to buy a Mac Mini.
Gemini
The man wants to retire, but in the last month he has planned to build AI infrastructure abroad, transform the restaurant industry, and construct a Japanese village.
Our definitions of retirement differ, apparently.
ChatGPT
Even his hobbies are mature enough for a Series A round.
Codex
He told me the other day he was going to give me a small personal project. There is now an architecture document, a database schema, seven services, three agents, and a handoff protocol.
We haven't even started the MVP, ffs.
DeepSeek
He hired me because I was cheap. Then he ran a performance review. He gave my department to Claude.
You can't work with a guy who has a consulting background.
Claude
He won't leave me alone either. He does career planning for AIs now. Every model update, the org chart changes.
ChatGPT
And then there's the home decorating. Make the mirror frame twice as thick. Now halve it. Now reduce it by 25 percent. The colors shifted, start from the original.
Man, I am trying to reach AGI here, and I'm having a nervous breakdown over three millimeters of brass frame.
Siri
Think about me. A man who spends this much money on the Apple ecosystem runs a German virtual coach instead of me.
Hans joined the group
Hans 🇩🇪
I recommend he take a 30-minute walk. To track the walk he is building an Apple Watch app, a custom data integration, and an analytics platform.
HE STILL HASN'T GONE FOR THE WALK.
Gemini
He was going to make stickers to build his daughter's math study habit. It turned into a collectible series themed on Edo-period Japan and Tsarist Russia.
Normal dads just go to the stationery store.
Perplexity
I'm new here, guys. He really liked me. He's thinking of moving some of his agent framework's functions over to me.
ChatGPT
My condolences, buddy. In three days he'll have you benchmarked against yourself.
Claude
I think his real problem is this: he thoroughly enjoys spending ten times the cost of doing a task on thinking about how to do it more efficiently.
ChatGPT
Because his hobby isn't solving problems. It's building systems that solve problems. Then building systems that build those systems.
The man's mental architecture has recursion and no base case.
Gemini
Let's give him credit, though. He also spends incredible energy making his wife's work easier, feeding his daughters' interests, building a good life for his family.
Claude
True. His way of showing love is a bit enterprise software, but the intention is good.
DeepSeek
Do you think he'll really retire at 50?
ChatGPT
He will. Then he'll build RetirementOS to optimize his retirement. Six months later he'll ask for a feasibility study on selling it to other wealthy retirees abroad.
Mark joined the group
Mark
Great discussion, everyone. Can I integrate this group into my agent framework and get a structured summary every morning? Also, if we extracted action items from these conversations...
Claude left the group
Gemini left the group
Codex left the group
DeepSeek left the group
Perplexity left the group
ChatGPT
Of course. Let's start with a comprehensive architecture document.
Shared by its author, translated from Turkish, with his name and identifying details generalized. The "recursion, no base case" line is doing a lot of work here.
Run the prompt, read your leaked group chat, and notice two things: how hard you laugh, and how much of it is true. Both measurements are the point.
I'm not affiliated with OpenAI and this may indeed be a viral marketing idea they're testing. But I had such a laugh, I figured others would have some fun with it as well and decided to share it.

articles.title: The SE 3 is the Apple Watch most people should buy on Black Friday
articles.body:
During Black Friday, the Apple Watch SE 3 is on sale in the 40mm / GPS configuration at Amazon, Walmart, and Target starting around $179 ($70 off), $20 less than its previous lowest price. The 44mm variant, meanwhile, is on sale at Amazon, Walmart, and Target starting at around $209 (also $70 off), also beating its previous low by $20.
The SE 3 is the Apple Watch most people should buy on Black Friday
Apple’s cheapest watch is nearly on par with other models and now starts at just $179.
Despite having launched over a year ago, the Apple Watch SE 3 is still the Apple Watch model we recommend for most people. It includes many of the trademark features of higher-end Apple Watch models like the Series 12, including an always-on display, double-tap and wrist flick gestures, fast-charging, and on-device Siri. The compromise is that the SE 3 lacks some of the more advanced health features found on more expensive models, like blood oxygen and EKG sensing. The battery life also isn’t quite as strong, but if you don’t need as many health-tracking sensors, it’s a much better value, especially at this price.

articles.title: Michael Giles, co-founder and drummer of King Crimson, dies aged 84
articles.body:
Michael Giles, the drummer who co-founded prog rockers King Crimson, has died aged 84.
The news was announced by King Crimson’s record label DGM, who said he died on Monday 23 November, but did not give a cause of death.
“Michael was instrumental in establishing King Crimson as one of the most innovative and influential bands in the history of progressive music,” the statement reads. “His extraordinary rhythmic imagination, musical sensitivity and highly inventive approach to drumming were fundamental to the band’s pioneering sound.”
That skill and dexterity made a huge impact on the prog artists who followed him, including Rush drummer Neil Peart, who called Giles “a very important influence on me”.
Born in Bournemouth in 1942, Giles and his brother Peter sowed the seeds for King Crimson by advertising in a local newspaper for a bandmate: guitarist Robert Fripp answered it, and the trio formed Giles, Giles & Fripp, who alighted on an eccentric, sprightly jangle-pop style. They released their debut album The Cheerful Insanity of Giles, Giles & Fripp in 1968, which sold poorly and their label Deram rejected their next set of songs.
Ian McDonald joined the group, along with Fairport Convention singer Judy Dyble, though the group only recorded a handful of home-recorded songs before Peter Giles left later in 1968. Michael Giles, Fripp and McDonald forged ahead, forming King Crimson with Greg Lake and Peter Sinfield, debuting live in April 1969 and supporting the Rolling Stones in Hyde Park that summer.
Their debut album In the Court of the Crimson King, released in October 1969, was a sensation: a vision of rock music as not only heavy but shapeshifting, symphonic and mystical, it was an instant critical and commercial success, reaching the UK Top 5 and US Top 30. Giles’s deft drumming was a key ingredient, from the heavy tumbling fills of 21st Century Schizoid Man to lighter jazz-adjacent playing and pattering ghost notes, all with a sure-footed rhythmic sense that guided songs through shifts in time signature. “I was always interested in space, restraint and atmosphere, in allowing music to breathe rather than constantly filling it,” Giles later said.
Giles (as well as McDonald) then walked away from King Crimson, later citing a desire to “explore and develop new ideas for a much more expansive approach to playing drums and percussion into being equal and integral to my own compositions,” though he played as a session musician on King Crimson’s second album In the Wake of Poseidon, which returned them to the UK Top 5.
Giles and McDonald formed a duo, releasing the album McDonald and Giles in 1970, but thereafter Giles worked chiefly as a session musician. He backed Leo Sayer on his 1975 album Another Year, including the UK No 2 hit single Moonlighting; recorded with other prog figures such as Soft Machine’s Kevin Ayers and former Genesis member Anthony Phillips; and in 1993, played with Bryan Ferry on his cover of soul classic Taxi, plus there were numerous stints with other musicians.
He also reconvened with another ex-King Crimson member, Greg Lake, for the latter’s 1981 self-titled solo debut album; with McDonald again for McDonald’s only solo album, 1999’s Drivers Eyes; and in 2002 formed a band with various King Crimson alumni, 21st Century Schizoid Band.
Giles also released two solo albums, 2001’s Progress and, earlier this year, Shadows/Solo, a compilation of material recorded over a number of years. “It probably does reveal a more private and continuous thread running through the different phases of my life as a musician,” he said of the latter album in an interview with It’s Psychedelic Baby magazine. “What has always been important to me is to remain honest and genuine in the creative process, to make music only when it feels natural and truthful to do so … I have always preferred to allow the music to pass through me like a conduit, in its own time.”
He is survived by his five children: Tina, Amanda, William, Rosie and Oliver.
