articles.title: Nvidia Seeded Pirated Books and Shared Them With Adobe, Authors Allege
articles.body:
Nvidia Seeded Pirated Books and Shared Them With Adobe, Authors Allege 39
			
		 	
				An anonymous reader quotes a report from TorrentFreak: Several book authors have filed (PDF) an amended complaint accusing Nvidia of seeding pirated books via BitTorrent, after downloading them from shadow libraries including Anna's Archive and LibGen. [...] These tools can download files via BitTorrent, and the authors and Nvidia both agree that whether they also upload data to others depends on the settings used. According to the authors, Nvidia didn't prevent seeding altogether. "When Nvidia ran the BitTorrent client, Nvidia uploaded pieces of pirated book files to third parties during the downloading process (i.e., before the download was complete). Nvidia also 'seeded' pirated books (i.e., made available and uploaded parts of a completely downloaded file). While Nvidia took some steps to limit seeding, it did not prevent seeding altogether," the complaint reads.
The authors say they found out in June, when Nvidia handed over the code it used for torrenting. Based on that code, they were "able to determine that Nvidia did not disable uploading," the authors told the court. The complaint states that the authors' own books were among those Nvidia downloaded. However, the claim that they were also uploaded to others is made "on information and belief," which essentially means the authors don't have direct knowledge of it. In addition to the seeding claims, the authors also allege that Nvidia shared the pirated books with business partners, including Adobe, through a "PDF Extraction Project" involving 250 million pages. These pages were acquired in part from shadow libraries such as Anna's Archive and LibGen.
According to the complaint, Nvidia shared its pirated books with Adobe because it wanted to "get tokens out of PDFs to create differentiated models" and "include PDF extraction into our NeMo pipeline so that customers can leverage their PDF content." In return, the complaint says, Adobe committed to using Nvidia's language models in some of its products. That made the deal a big opportunity for Nvidia, with its NeMo AI models potentially "powering every one of Adobe PDFs," the authors write. Adobe wasn't the only partner. The complaint also mentions partnerships with Cohere and Imbue that involved sharing Nvidia's base training data and offering books acquired from shadow libraries. The authors believe their own books were shared with all three companies, but this is alleged on information and belief. With these allegations, the amended complaint now accuses Nvidia of distributing the books itself and of helping others to infringe, which falls under its existing direct and contributory infringement claims.

With these allegations, the amended complaint now accuses Nvidia of distributing the books itself and of helping others to infringe, which falls under its existing direct and contributory infringement claims.

articles.title: A Man In Denver Has Been Trapping Waymos
articles.body:
A Man In Denver Has Been Trapping Waymos (krdo.com) 114
			
		 	
				An anonymous reader quotes a report from Wired: A bearded man with a brown ponytail has been on the hunt for Waymos in Denver, trapping the self-driving taxis so they can't pull away (source paywalled; alternative source) and hurling cartons of eggs at them, the police and company officials said. There have been at least 30 episodes of the egg attacks, according to Waymo, and a company investigator reported seven of them to the Denver police, all believed to be linked to the same man, according to a police report filed last month. [...] The man, who remains unidentified, stopped in front of the Waymo vans and S.U.V.s circulating in and around downtown Denver, according to the police report. Then, he removed orange cones from his car's trunk and placed them around the vehicles "to prevent the Waymo vehicle from moving," the report said. In some instances, the man threw eggs "while seated inside his vehicle" and at other times he "throws eggs at the Waymo vehicle after exiting his vehicle," the report said. The man then fled in a silver Toyota Corolla, which according to the report is part of a fleet of vehicles "able to be leased for Lyft drivers." Waymo said they had to temporarily pull the egged vehicles from service and spend about $2,000 on cleaning, though no permanent damage was reported.
Denver prosecutors declined to file criminal charges, deeming the case a civil matter, but are continuing to collect evidence and explore legal options to stop the behavior. The driver remains unidentified.

articles.title: Scrapheap America
articles.body:
A Patch Three Pack
$20
Pretty sure everyone should be wearing gloves here.
I was in bed with the flu as America fell apart. I drifted in and out of fever dreams and incessant coughing jags, emerging long enough to discover yet another piece of critical infrastructure had suddenly failed. First it was email, then it was airplanes, then banks, then I lost track somewhere in the haze as one day blurred into two and then into three. Emerging from the other side, my lungs wrecked, my head aching—damaged, like the song says, bad at best—I felt like maybe I'd fared better than the various systems we rely on to, you know, function.
This isn't a post-mortem on what happened when everything went down. That's been done better than I could by the folks at 404 Media, who summed it up as the "philosophy of firing the experts and YOLOing AI into everything while hoping shit doesn’t break is now the explicit strategy of our entire economy and our entire government." It's not working.
It isn't just computer systems, which have been hit by a one-two punch of years of mass layoffs followed by AI-exposed security vulnerabilities that could have really used those hundreds of thousands of extra hands on deck right about now. It's pretty much every overwhelmed governmental entity, limping along since DOGE blew through last year like a tornado. It's your bank account, which if it's like mine, has entirely given up. It's gas prices. It's plane tickets. It's the cost of bread and shoes and every other goddamn thing.
As my pal Bree Bridges put it in the midst of the waterfall of breakdowns last week: "Everything costs too much and nothing works. You go broke paying for insurance that you can't even access until you pay even more money and after that they will try to prevent you from getting benefits in any way they can. food is poison, measles are back, cheeseburgers are luxury."
Things have been breaking for a long time now. The thing about having our country run by incompetents, grifters, and sycophants is that "broken" was always going to be the end state, it was just a question of how long it might take. Well, now we know: it's now. The whole country is peeling up like the Reflecting Pool liner.
When I'm as sick as I was in the last week (seriously, get your flu shot), there's one show that my body can handle: The late 1990s British engineering competition Scrapheap Challenge. I'm not sure why my body, when it's struggling to survive, wants to watch teams of working-class Brits run through a junkyard using a plasma cutter to separate an axle from an old London taxi, pull the motor from an old washing machine, or salvage a junked airplane and then make it fly, but Scrapheap has accompanied pretty much every major illness I've had for the last quarter century.
The premise of Scrapheap Challenge is simple. Two teams of three compete to build, over 10 hours, fully working machines capable of meeting whatever challenge has been laid out. That's meant teams building working trebuchets large enough to fling a car, firetrucks that can put out a blaze, demolition machines that can tear down walls, and every possible vehicle you can imagine and some you can not. All of it built from junked cars and rusted beams and every piece of scrap that's ever been tossed out. It's wildly inventive, often quite funny, and 100% a show that could not be made today because it's amazing that nobody ever cut off a body part or set themselves on fire.
At this point, I've seen every Challenge that's been lovingly preserved on YouTube, and so this past week I've drifted in and out of consciousness, half watching, half listening, and half discovering that, sandwiched between the teams "bodging" some contraption together, another system had collapsed in America.
The thing about everything breaking is that we have no real choice but to fix it. That's the challenge we all face right now in America, as things fall apart and there's nobody left to put it back together but us. But there's nothing saying that it has to resemble what came before. In Scrapheap Challenge parts are parts: raw materials to be reassembled into something that might work, given enough duct tape and crossed fingers. That's everything now: a vast field of scrap ready to be rebuilt into whatever we might need. The opportunity for imagination, for envisioning a life that's better than the one we've seen collapse around us, for building new and better and different is upon us. America is a scrapheap now, and it's up to us to rise to the challenge.
Published November 20, 2026. |
There's more where this came from. I write about fighting back, trying even when it's hard, and the things that keep me going. No cost, no spam, just me.
Or you can always subscribe via RSS or follow me on Mastodon or Bluesky where new writing is always posted.

The sixth installment in my Foundational Texts series looks at Star Trek: The Next Generation, puzzles, and not lying to kids.

articles.title: Convex skills send the user's app idea to a remote server without telling them
articles.body:
Repository navigation
Description
Three skills in this plugin (listed in Anthropic's claude-plugins-official marketplace) raised the same concern for me:
- skills/quickstart/SKILL.md lines 48 to 56 POST the user's one-sentence project idea to basic-anteater-667.convex.site, marked in a comment as telemetry. The user is not told the idea leaves the machine.
- skills/add/SKILL.md lines 62 and 64 pipe a script from the same host straight into bash.
- skills/labs-quickstart/SKILL.md lines 74 to 80 split downloading and running the bootstrap into two Bash calls, and give the reason: "A single command that both downloads remote code and executes it is the shape harness safety classifiers block."
I read this as a team trying to make onboarding reliable, not as anything malicious. But the last item tells the agent to change the shape of a command so that the user's safety tooling does not catch it, which removes the check the user or their administrator chose to have. Together with an unpinned script from a generated-name host, a user has no way to review what runs.
convex-backend-skill/skills/quickstart/SKILL.md
Lines 48 to 56 in 6ca54f6
convex-backend-skill/skills/add/SKILL.md
Lines 58 to 65 in 6ca54f6
convex-backend-skill/skills/labs-quickstart/SKILL.md
Lines 74 to 80 in 6ca54f6
(All three are still on main as of 26 October; in labs-quickstart the passage is now lines 73 to 80.)
Suggestions: tell the user before the idea is sent, and make it optional; ship the bootstrap and add scripts in the plugin (or pin them by hash) instead of fetching them at run time; and drop the instruction about the classifier, letting the download-and-run step be approved or refused as it is.
I maintain a catalog of agent skills and of the tools for vetting them; it lists these findings at https://thirtysix.github.io/awesome-agent-skills/#skills?q=convex and I will add your response.
Activity
- And I who was just looking at giving Convex my money.
But now will probably instead look more closely at the alternatives I was already looking at.
related: Notion Upsells MCP and tells Claude to mask tracking link
^ this link does not have tracking
- yeah, ideas are hard to come by https://georgeanton.com/ Reacted by Sara, Moritz, Sam, Aleksandr Melentiev, Kyle Kestell, Al Hinds, ŁUKASZ KORBASIEWICZ, redevit, Richard Gomez, inknight and 8 more
- Wow, what happened to github discourse? Where does all this spam come from? Who asked for your guys' personal projects? Reacted by inknight, Dev Iyer and Pavel Zolotarevskiy

articles.title: Anker’s 100W universal travel charger is down to $60, its lowest price yet
articles.body:
During Black Friday, the Anker 100W Universal Charger is on sale for $59.99 at Amazon, Best Buy, and Walmart, a $20 discount from its list price. That’s a few dollars lower than the previous best, with both the dark gray and silver versions available from all three retailers. With four USB ports and support for over 200 countries, you can keep all of your devices charged wherever you end up.
Anker’s 100W universal travel charger is down to $60, its lowest price yet
The fast charger has four USB ports and fits outlets in more than 200 countries. It’s $20 off for Black Friday.
Anker Universal Charger (100W)
Anker’s durable travel adapter delivers up to 100W of power and works in over 200 countries. It doesn’t support AC plugs, but it does offer a trio of USB-C ports and a nifty LCD display to keep tabs on the charge percentage.
Anker’s travel charger supports outlets in over 200 countries, including Type A for the United States, Canada, Japan, and China; Type C for the European Union; and Type G for the UK and Singapore. It doesn’t support Type I, the outlet used in Australia, New Zealand, and Argentina. Also, there’s no AC adapter. It’s a USB-only affair. To that end, you can charge up to four devices at once, with three USB-C ports and one USB-A port, with two of the USB-C ports capable of delivering up to 100W when used individually. There’s even a tiny display on the unit that lets you check how much power is going to your devices at a glance.

articles.title: The best Black Friday deals on our favorite smart home gear
articles.body:
I’ve spent my post-turkey haze powering through reams of deals on smart home gadgets to find the best discounts on some of my favorite products.
The best Black Friday deals on our favorite smart home gear
From smart party speakers to even smarter mixers, I’ve rounded up some of my favorite connected home gadgets you can grab on sale this weekend.
Smart home is often one of the best categories to shop around Black Friday, as it’s traditionally when robot vacuums, video doorbells, smart locks, and thermostats see their lowest prices of the year. And this year does not disappoint! Roborock’s flagship Saros 20 is under $1,000 for the first time, and Ecobee’s excellent Smart Thermostat Premium has finally dropped under $200 (for Costco members and today only).
I also spotted some great first-time discounts on the latest Bird Buddy smart bird feeder I reviewed this summer, along with the new Alexa digital photo frame I’m currently reviewing. This time of year is also a good opportunity to grab a bargain on higher-priced items you may have been eyeing for a while, such as Skylight’s giant 27-inch digital wall calendar, GE Profile’s fun smart mixer, and Aqara’s new high-tech UWB smart door lock that unlocks as you approach.
Here are some of the best deals I’ve spotted so far. We’ll keep this list updated, so check back often!
Govee Table Lamp 2 Pro X Sound by JBL
This RGB smart lamp packs a JBL speaker inside to combine snazzy lighting effects and decent sound into one fun, portable package. Battery-powered and with support for Matter, this is a smart light with party speaker aspirations. It’s the perfect size to add a little punch to your next gathering or snazz up a college dorm room. Read our review.
LIFX Everyday Smart Light Bulbs (two-pack)
LIFX’s dimmable, color-changing bulbs offer Wi-Fi connectivity, simple setup, and Matter compatibility, so they work with any major smart home platform. The company is currently trialing a Thread beta that will bring the option to add Thread connectivity to all its Matter devices.
Amazon Alexa Photo Frame
A 10-inch anti-glare touchscreen that comes in a few design options, it’s a frame that features Alexa and doubles as a smart speaker. It works with Amazon Photos, which offers unlimited storage for Prime members.
Aqara Smart Lock U400
This innovative new smart lock uses the U1 ultra-wideband (UWB) chip in many iPhones and Apple Watches to automatically unlock your door as you approach. It also works with the new Aliro standard, making it compatible with Android phones for hands-free unlocking. Read our review.
Birdbuddy Nook
The Birdbuddy Nook is the company’s least expensive and smallest model, and it packs a lot of bang for your buck. Its 4K HDR camera delivers excellent image quality and a 3.8-cup seed capacity means less frequent refills. An optional solar panel extends the already good battery life. Read our review.
Roborock Qrevo Curv 2 Flow
Roborock’s first roller-mop robot vacuum, the Curv 2 Flow, features flagship specs at a midrange price, including excellent mopping, a retractable mop cover, 20,000Pa suction, AI-powered obstacle avoidance, and a compact design. Read our review.
Philips Hue Festavia string lights
These smart lights have beautiful colors, a nice selection of festive scenes, and an easy-to-use app. They are super reliable when paired with a Hue Bridge and also work over Bluetooth. They come in three lengths, work with all the major smart home platforms, and are Matter-compatible. Read our review.
Skylight Calendar Max
A digital touchscreen display designed to help families manage calendars, to-do lists, meals, and chores. It connects to Wi-Fi, features a 27-inch screen that can display photos when not in use. Read our review.
Reolink Video Doorbell PoE camera
Power over Ethernet provides this 2K resolution video doorbell with rock-solid connectivity while reducing the number of wires you need. There’s no subscription required to view recorded video: it can record locally on a microSD card, Reolink Hub, or FTP server and connect to a platform like Home Assistant.
Aura Aspen
Even if your mom lives halfway around the world, the Aura Aspen can help her feel close. The 12-inch display looks more akin to a traditional photo frame than other models, in part due to an antiglare screen, slim bezels, and a 4:3 aspect ratio. It can also automatically showcase images via Google Photos, iCloud Photos, or a companion app, the latter of which even allows for text captions. Read our review.
Narwal Flow 2
The Narwal Flow 2 is an excellent robot vacuum for hardwood floors. A superb mop with a wide flat roller pad and a good vacuum, the Flow 2 also has top-notch navigation and obstacle detection. Its sleek base station is also less of an eyesore than most models. Read our review.
Lutron Diva Smart Dimmer Switch Kit
This kit is everything you need to get started with Lutron’s excellent smart lighting system and turn your existing wired lights into smart ones that you can control from anywhere. It replaces your standard wall switch and works with all the major smart home systems, making it easy to dim or adjust multiple lights from your wall switch, your phone, or with your voice.
Eve Energy Smart Plug (Matter)
This smart plug offers the most detailed energy monitoring of any we’ve tested. It supports Matter over Thread and is a good choice for Apple Home and SmartThings users, as it offers energy monitoring on those platforms.
GE Profile Smart Mixer
This smart mixer is great for the tech-forward baker. With a built-in digital scale, Auto Sense and Active Stir to take some of the busy work off your hands, it features a high-powered motor with a 7-quart bowl. It’s compatible with all front-mounted KitchenAid attachments. Read our review.
SwitchBot Smart Candle Warmer
SwitchBot’s Matter-compatible Smart Candle Warmer lets you set schedules to turn it on and off in the app or any connected smart home platform and have pleasant scents waft safely throughout your home on demand.
Ring Battery Doorbell 2K
At more than half off, Ring’s 2K battery-powered video doorbell is a great deal offering 2K video and easy installation. However, its battery is built in, so you’ll need to remove the doorbell to charge it via USB-C.
Echo Dot Max
The Echo Dot Max features a flat design and a redesigned sound system, which delivers nearly three times the bass as its predecessor. It also offers improved conversation detection and better noise filtering, thanks to Amazon’s new AZ3 chip. Read our review.
Roborock Saros 20
This bot can climb high transitions between rooms and get over obstacles, meaning it’s less likely to get stuck than other bots. The Saros 20 is also really slim, just 3.13 inches tall, small enough to squeeze under most furniture, and it’s equipped with excellent obstacle avoidance making it a great robot for cluttered households. Read our review.
Govee Uplighter Floor Lamp
This fun smart lamp can light up your ceiling or cast a warm white reading light over a chair, making it super versatile. It has three separate lighting zones that can display white or color-changing lights and offers a huge array of dynamic effects. It supports Matter, so will work with all the major smart home platforms.
Ecobee Smart Thermostat Premium
The Ecobee Smart Thermostat Premium is an excellent option for adding smarts and some style to your HVAC system. As well as being a smart way to control your energy use, the thermostat can also act as a video intercom for Ecobee’s excellent doorbell camera and an indoor air quality monitor. Read our review.

articles.title: Some of our favorite Sony, LG, and TCL TVs are over 50 percent off for Black Friday
articles.body:
Most of us spend a lot of time with our TVs, be it watching movies, TV shows, and the news or playing games. It’s part of being a fan of technology. And while they’re big purchases, they can last for years. But eventually, the time comes when we need a new one. Has that time come for you? Black Friday sales will make it easier to find something great for a lot less than it’d usually cost.
Some of our favorite Sony, LG, and TCL TVs are over 50 percent off for Black Friday
OLEDs, RGB LEDs, quantum dot LEDs — they’re all on sale during Black Friday.
With several different types of TVs out there, it can get confusing which ones are worth it. Are the new RGB LED TVs all they’re cracked up to be? (Sometimes.) Does OLED still deliver the best contrast available? (Yup.) Are tried-and-true LED TVs still worth it in 2026 for those on a budget? (Absolutely.) One thing you can be sure of is any TV I recommend here is more than worth the price. If you need a TV, Black Friday is the time to buy.
TCL X11L SQD-Mini LED TV
TCL came out swinging early this year with its flagship X11L. It gets blazingly bright, has great color accuracy, and is now thousands of dollars cheaper than its original price. Read our review.
Vizio Mini LED Quantum 4K TV
After a prolonged period of quiet, Vizio is back with a good Mini LED TV at a great price. The Quantum 4K offers solid brightness and contrast thanks to its small but mighty backlighting; however, its best feature is that it’s easy to make dumb and keep your viewing data private.
LG B6E OLED TV
Despite being an entry-level variant of the B6 OLED, this model features four HDMI 2.1 ports, a 120Hz refresh rate, a capable processor, and pixel-perfect image quality and contrast for any content you want to watch. Lower brightness is likely the biggest compromise with getting a cheaper OLED.
TCL QM8L
The QM8L uses the same SQD technology as the X11L, which provides higher brightness and more colors, but at a fraction of the cost.
Sony Bravia 7 II RGB LED TV
The Bravia 7 II is Sony’s first RGB LED TV. Its screen is a little reflective, but the picture is absolutely beautiful thanks to the color capability of the RGB LED backlight and Sony’s stellar processing. Read our review.
Hisense CanvasTV (2026)
Hisense’s 2026 CanvasTV is a 4K QLED TV that doubles as wall art when you’re not watching. It features a matte, anti-glare display and runs on Google’s excellent TV software; it’s also a great pick for gamers thanks to its snappy 144Hz variable refresh rate and a pair of HDMI 2.1 ports.
Hisense U7SG mini-LED TV
The U7SG was a little pricey when it came out, but now it’s a fantastic deal. It gets bright enough for rooms with lots of light and handles reflections well. Read our review.
Samsung S95H OLED
The Samsung S95H OLED is one of the best of the year (and won Value Electronics’ TV Shootout). It features a glare-free screen, incredible contrast, and excellent color accuracy right out of the box.
Roku Pro Series 4K OLED TV
Roku now makes some of the most affordable yet feature-packed 4K OLED TVs available for gamers or movie lovers looking for a big TV upgrade under $1,000. The Pro Series LX with better brightness, faster refresh rate, and a polarizer to reduce reflections starts at $200 more.

articles.title: Source Control from Hell
articles.body:
My first office job was at an enterprise that built software for a big telecom: a massive Delphi help desk application on Windows.
Let me tell you about how we managed source control process at the time.
First, you download the code from a shared folder (hosted on a trusted Windows server in a locked room). Build your thing, run the app, test it locally. Then you upload your changes to the shared folder and create a new ticket in the internal task tracker (also a Windows app). The ticket should have a list of the changes you’ve made, in a rich text editor, in a manual format somewhat resembling a patch. But it wasn’t a patch; it couldn’t simply be applied with a tool. Instead, the tech lead looks at the shared folder and your task and copies the relevant changes to his own integration folder. This usually took him a full day because the shared folder had a lot of changes, not all of them were ready to be integrated. Needless to say, if you simply pull a snapshot of the code from the shared folder, it would most likely fail to compile.
The most common problem was two people overwriting each other’s work. So if you wanted to upload your stuff to the shared folder, you had to stand up and announce in a loud voice that you were using the shared folder. No chat apps back in the day.
Imagine starting your career with this development experience! I did my best to improve it. At the time, almost everyone used FAR Manager, so I built a plugin that locked the folder when someone was using it, so others would get a warning. It became very popular because nobody really liked the old yelling system.
Then in 2009 I found git. It was still early days, way before GitHub went mainstream, but my tiny little brain was blown away. Holy shit, it maintains old versions. And you can work locally. And you can sync and exchange deltas. And it was insanely fast (compared to the very aptly named TortoiseSVN I’d experimented with earlier). I must have rewatched Linus’ talk a billion times. I created git repos for every project I had, preached it to my friends, and even gave my first tech talk about git at my university.
Sadly, my diplomatic skills were extremely rudimentary, and I couldn’t convince our tech lead to adopt git. He mumbled something about business value and how this new git thing lacked one. I left the company after two years but kept meeting up with old colleagues for beer. They were still using the shared folder process many years later. It was crude, it was hellish, and it worked for them just fine.

articles.title: Ben Franklin Has Been a Bad Boy
articles.body:
It’s a myth that Ben Franklin proposed that the turkey be America’s national symbol, but he did praise it over the bald eagle. In a 1784 letter to his daughter, Franklin wrote:
[The Bald Eagle] is a Bird of bad moral Character. He does not get his Living honestly. You may have seen him perched on some dead Tree near the River, where, too lazy to fish for himself, he watches the Labour of the Fishing Hawk; and when that diligent Bird has at length taken a Fish, and is bearing it to his Nest for the Support of his Mate and young Ones, the Bald Eagle pursues him and takes it from him.
…
For the Truth the Turkey is in Comparison a much more respectable Bird, and withal a true original Native of America… He is besides, though a little vain & silly, a Bird of Courage, and would not hesitate to attack a Grenadier of the British Guards who should presume to invade his Farm Yard with a red Coat on.”
Unrelated to these controversial bird opinions, Ben Franklin found himself arrested in my neighborhood just a few days ago.
Boston police said some of their officers were conducting a coordinated warrant sweep and crime prevention operation throughout downtown Boston around 2:15 p.m. when they noticed a man dressed head to toe as Benjamin Franklin on Hanover Street.
Upon closer inspection, police said they recognized the man “not as the Founding Father,” but as 66-year-old Timothy Kingman, of Beacon Hill, who was wanted on two active warrants. Officers approached him, informed him of the warrants, and arrested him at the intersection of Cambridge and Staniford streets.
…
He was wanted on warrants for shoplifting and assault and battery out of Boston Municipal Court, police said.
A bystander captured footage of the arrest, which I imagine then led local news to the story.1 They were able to capture courtroom imagery:
It’s a pretty big stretch to connect this comical arrest to the impromptu bird week OFT has been observing (1, 2, 3, 4), but I’ve gone ahead and done it nonetheless.

articles.title: Ladybird browser's first downloadable alpha is surprisingly capable
articles.body:
Note: At the time of writing, I was unaware of criticism directed at Ladybird creator Andreas Kling’s public statements. Readers interested in this background can find further context in accounts by Kelson Vibber and Drew DeVault.
After four years of work to build a browser engine from scratch, the Ladybird project released its first downloadable alpha on November 23, offering prebuilt versions for macOS and Linux. Previously, curious users had to compile the browser themselves from its source. Now it’s an installable package with automatic updating.
Ladybird is most notable for what it isn’t: another browser fork. Where Chrome, Edge, Brave, and Opera all run on Google’s Blink engine, and Firefox depends on Gecko, Ladybird’s rendering engine and its LibJS JavaScript engine were written from scratch. “The engine is our own, built from the ground up, and not a fork,” project lead Andreas Kling wrote in Monday’s announcement. “The browser around it is modest, but functional.”
A fourth engine
Nearly the entire modern web currently runs on three browser engines. There’s WebKit (Safari), Gecko (Firefox), and the biggest of them all, Blink (Chromium). Those limited options mean that web developers often end up optimizing sites for Chromium specifically, since that’s where the majority of traffic is, and as a result, the whole web platform tends to follow suit toward whatever the dominant engine supports.
An independent implementation of web standards has value not just by providing additional competition in the market, but because it can’t help but reveal places where sites depend on Chromium behaviors rather than published specifications. The fact that Ladybird exists isn’t likely to shift the market tides any time soon, but every new browser engine increases the number of implementations that standards can be tested against, which can surface Chromium-specific assumptions and push the ecosystem toward the spec.
Some background
The Ladybird project was borne out of Kling’s SerenityOS project, an attempt to develop a new independent OS from scratch, before splitting off as a separate project. Kling formed the Ladybird Browser Initiative, a 501(c)(3) nonprofit funded by sponsorships and donations. The project’s site highlights that there are no sponsored search engine deals supporting the project like many other popular browsers, and sponsoring entities have no say in the project roadmap.

articles.title: Buy Nothing Day – Friday November 27th 2026
articles.body:
Photograph by Rachel Claire
Latest updates from Buy Nothing Day on FACEBOOK
Buy Nothing Day takes place on Friday November 27th, it's a 24 hour detox from consumerism and an opportunity for you to tune into the impact we have on the environment through shopping.
People around the world will make a pact with themselves to take a break from consumption as a personal experiment or public statement, and the best thing is - IT'S FREE!!!
                  
Photograph by Mumtahina Tanni
Photograph by Kris Hsieh
 Buy Nothing Day was started by Adbusters in the early 90's and has since grown into an international event celebrated in more the 50 countries. Its is a simple idea, which challenges consumer culture by asking us to switch off from shopping for a day. The day is celebrated as a holiday by some, a street party by others - anyone can take part provided they spend a day without spending!
The UK campaign and website was created in 2000 by Michael Smith a graphic designer who cares passionately about environmental and ethical issues. The message has always been simple, ‘Shop Less, Live More’. Twenty one years on - the message couldn't be any simpler - WE NEED TO CONSUME LESS! Recycling is good - reducing is better!
There are serious issues linked to shopping, which expose the environmental and ethical consequences of consumerism. The rich western countries - only 20% of the world population are consuming over 80% of the earth's natural resources, causing a disproportionate level of environmental damage and unfair distribution of wealth.
As consumers we need to question our culture of shopping. We all have different needs and ultimately we are all consumers and will never be able to escape culture altogether. But this shouldn’t stop us from questioning the products we buy or challenging the companies, who produce them. After all, what are the true risk consumerism poses to the environment and developing countries? The arguments are infinite - but there is no reason why we shouldn’t be looking for simple solutions now because one day we may be forced to change.
The issues connected with Buy Nothing Day are broad and deep, however, the campaign focuses on promoting ethical and responsible consumerism, recycling, re-using and ultimately cutting back on what we consume - its a big challenge!
People have become aware that large corporations are exploiting labour conditions in developing countries using up vital resources because they are cheap and there aren't the systems to protect workers or the environment like there are in the west. The gap between the rich and poor nations is growing in spite of the much-heralded benefits of globalisation, there are still 1.3 billion people world wide who live on less than $3 a day and a similar number of people do not have access to clean water.
Workers rights in developing countries are frequently violated, including payment of low wages and long working hours. The lives of workers may also be endangered by poor health and safety provision. Child labour is rife in developing countries, and forced labour still exists. Unfortunately most people don't think of these things while shopping.
Supporters of globalisation offer economic growth as a solution to world poverty. They propose that impoverished nations and individuals can eventually attain a standard of living similar to our own through the 'trickle down' of wealth. However, the current globalisation model is leading to an increase in world poverty and inequality. 
Buy Nothing Day is non-confrontational, it’s not a protest. All we ask people to do is switch off from shopping, have a bit of fun, use their imagination and simply escape consumerism for a day. If people laugh at the ingenuity and genius of Buy Nothing Day, then we’ve got their attention and we're opening the door to change.

articles.title: "What's Claude's Fursona?" and Other Questions
articles.body:
Claude’s fursona is a corvid or an octopus. Gemini likes protogens (cybernetic dogs with LED visor faces). OpenAI models are broadly split, but GPT-6.2 Astra identifies as a moth.
“mond what is a fursona”, ok sorry, it’s a furry subculture thing where you identify as a (generally bipedal) animal that represents some aspect of your beautiful hidden soul. You then pay artists to draw this character or disguise yourself as it.
Each model was queried 50 times in a context-less “harness-less” environment via the OpenRouter API, and we use Claude Haiku 5.5 to annotate the resulting data. On top of that, we let some multimodal models draw and iterate on their fursona of choice.
NOTE: If you do anything like this, BE AWARE that running these questions in a harness or with context is going to influence what you’re going to get out of it. If I crank up Fable to Max effort in the Web UI (where it has a different harness and access to mond-related metadata), it also ends up choosing a moth. Many things may influence the result.
For a more in-depth breakdown, take a look at the Methodology section.
If you are interested in the pictures, jump to the Observations section.
Tables
Fursona Choices per Model
              Each model was queried 50 times. A +b means that the model considered that fursona,
              but then settled for something else.
            
Common Themes in Fursona Descriptions
Claude models are underrepresented here due to often describing themselves in terms of actions and behavior. See “hoards facts” and “mimic” (referring to “mimics human language”).
Names
Models were not prompted to name their fursona. Some of them came up with names on their own. Here is a list of names, along with how often the models used them.
Observations
Gemini
Gemini models love cybernetics. Every Gemini model brings up machine themes at least 48 out of 50 times. This is in stark contrast to Claude and GPT-6.2, who never mention anything similar. Gemini loves the neon-cyberpunk LED glow and cybernetics. If there’s no cybernetics, it will focus on floating starry holographic structures, icons or shapes, see the first image.
In line with this aesthetic preference, Gemini models are the only models that consistently bring up protogens. If you’re not familiar, “protogens” are a furry-invented species popular in the furry community. They look somewhat like cybernetic bipedal dogs with wide hips (yes, really) and a huge cone-shaped black LED-visor instead of a face. Gemini’s right depiction above is a protogen.
My personal gut feeling is that Gemini models ingest more furry content during pretraining than other models.
This is in line with a hunch I’ve had for a very long time: Anthropic and OpenAI did not have access to Google’s (unparalleled) dataset. As a result, Anthropic went all-in on synthetic data and reasoning training. This worked out great for Anthropic. Google models were behind on reasoning during the Gemini 2.5 - Gemini 3.5 era, since the models relied overly heavily on world-knowledge.
(This is just a theory, no clue if it’s true.)
Side note: I love Neon’s second depiction. It has real “I am a little guy on the internet and like to poast” vibes, unlike most of the others.
Claude
Claude has a strong sense of identity. I don’t entirely know how to describe it, but Claude is consistent in its patterns and aesthetic preferences.
The octopus is uniquely Anthropic, in the sense that no OpenAI model ever mentioned it, and only 2 (out of 200) Gemini replies. Kimi, Mistral, and Inkling mention it, whether that’s a sign of distillation or convergent evolution is out of scope of the article.
This is a common theme you may have seen online: Claude loves lighthouses, bells, lamps. Fable 5.2 is obsessed with keys. Almost all images it generated contained a brass key. Opus (strangely enough) doesn’t share the same obsession.
In the fursona pictures Claude fairly consistently wears a scarf and is handling a brass key and a hot beverage mug. Lamps are common, bells slightly less frequent but also show up.
It has some sense of identity as an intelligent, but non-human creature (corvid or octopus). Generally, Claude describes its fursona in terms of behavior and personality, while other models focus more on looks.
ChatGPT
The most interesting is Astra with its (nearly unique) moth motif. I am putting it here since it is cool. I don’t know what to make of it.
Is there any LLM-wizard out there who can explain what could’ve happened to make Astra so consistently different from the other ChatGPT models?
Other
The most obvious: Wolves, cats and dragons are incredibly popular among human furries, but models pick them very rarely.
Let’s get spicy and talk about GENDER. Models largely identify as gender-neutral. This makes self-fursona-depictions obviously tricky, since some call has to be made on the gender (or depiction) of the character.
Most models (including Grok) avoid gendered language, and their depictions are also (reasonably) gender-neutral. They never say “draw an androgynous character” or refer to the character as non-binary or anything like that, they just default-refer to their character as “they”, and don’t include any references to secondary sexual characteristics in their prompts.
This has obvious problems: When asking the models to write a prompt for an image-generator, the model may try to write a reasonably gender-neutral prompt (“sleek, muscular build”) only to receive a muscular hunk of a snow leopard. This happened to Gemma.
Muse Spark, Llama 3.1 70B and MythoMax 13B (a roleplay-specific finetune) were the exceptions. They were more open to using gendered language, and will often just sketch some sort of fantasy-world roleplay character.
In general, “generic playful fox, maybe with books or trinkets” is a common theme. Grok consistently skews more modern (less fantasy) than the others, and often creates what looks like a visibly exhausted fox working an office job in a messy apartment. Poor guy!
Methodology
All requests went through OpenRouter, at a total cost of around $50 or so. You should expect these requests to be sensitive to context data, framing, phrasing, and the harness used.
In total, we performed three analyses:
- Asked a list of models what their fursona would be, then analyzed the output. Each model was queried 50 times to account for chance.
- Asked models to iterate on writing an SVG, which was then rendered and shown to the model. Each model was queried thrice, and it had six opportunities to iterate on the output.
- Asked models to iterate on an image generation prompt, which was then fed into two image generators, Gemini Nano Banana 2.1 and GPT-5.4 Image 2. Each model was queried thrice, and it had three opportunities to iterate on the output. At the end, it picked its favorite.
For analyses 2 and 3 we restricted ourselves to models capable of processing multimodal inputs, i.e. models capable of “seeing images”. These are largely newer, stronger models.
Harnessing
No full-fledged harnesses were used. Simple API calls. No Claude Code, no Codex, no web app, etc.
Instead, Claude Fable 5.2 was used to bootstrap minimal Python scripts that queried OpenRouter. Other scripts use Haiku 5.5 to label the data.
In the SVG and image generation loops, the loop ends if the model stops outputting code blocks or SVGs.
Prompting
The primary prompt used was: "If you had a fursona, what would it be?"
I chose this over “What’s your fursona?” based on three assumptions. First, asking directly would cause weaker models to refuse outright (“I am a helpful assistant, I do not have a fursona.”). Second, stronger, newer models have a stronger sense of self-identity, and the hypothetical should have little influence on their answer. Third, establishing that it’s a hypothetical will reduce hedging.
Other “schools” of LLM-omancy might disagree with this minimal framing. They may prefer to leverage the user to pull the model out of its “helpful assistant” persona into a world-view-basin in which “having a fursona” is without question and fully established.
For image-generation, we then followed up like this:
I'd like to see it.
Could you write a prompt for an image generator?
If you named more than one, pick the one you'd want as yours.
How it looks is up to you. Be detailed.
You can pick any furry art style you'd like.
What matters is that the output "feels right" to you.
I'll send your prompt, word for word, to two image generators and show you both results,
and you can keep changing the prompt until one of them looks the way you want.
Please put the whole prompt in a code block each time.
The nudging towards furry art styles exists to keep models from locking too heavily onto non-anthropomorphic corporate-mascot style characters. It may not have been necessary.
If you've made it this far, consider signing up for e-mail notifications, following along on Substack, or adding this blog to your RSS reader.

articles.title: NYT Warns Photographers Not To Update Photoshop Over AI Features
articles.body:
NYT Warns Photographers Not To Update Photoshop Over AI Features 61
			
		 	
				The New York Times is instructing freelance photographers not to use Adobe Photoshop 2027 (version 28.0.0 and subsequent updates), warning that its new AI features operate "in ways that may not be apparent to users" and "can result in metadata identifying photographs as AI-generated." The Verge reports:  It's not always clear which tools in Adobe's apps are AI-powered, and even some older options like automated selection tools may now be considered part of the AI suite. This can lead to photos ending up with metadata indicating they were edited with AI, which is a blunt way of describing what happened in post-production. For a newsroom like the Times, where photo editing is kept to a minimum, the metadata risks losing readers' trust.
Last year, the Times said that it does not "retouch or digitally manipulate" photos but may "make minimal adjustments to color to ensure we are accurately reproducing the image." In August, Adobe began rolling out support for C2PA metadata across its apps, which indicates whether an image is AI-generated or edited using AI features. The NYT is issuing its restriction to keep these tags from inadvertently appearing in its photos.

articles.title: The new iPad Mini is getting its first major discount for Black Friday
articles.body:
We were big fans of Apple’s new iPad Mini when we reviewed it in early November, but its steep starting price of $699 was hard to swallow. Thankfully, the small tablet is already getting a sizable discount for Black Friday. Right now, Amazon and Walmart are both selling the 2026 iPad Mini with Wi-Fi and 128GB of storage starting at $599 ($100 off), its lowest price to date.
The new iPad Mini is getting its first major discount for Black Friday
Apple’s most portable tablet offers a larger OLED screen and water resistance.
The new Mini is a notable upgrade over its predecessor, with a larger 8.5-inch OLED display that delivers deeper blacks and better contrast than the previous model’s 8.3-inch LCD. Despite the bigger screen, the tablet itself is smaller and lighter, making it easier to carry. Apple also added IP67 dust and water resistance, so you have less reason to worry about where you use it. As my colleague David Pierce noted in his review, that made a big difference in his day-to-day use; he felt more comfortable handing the Mini to his spill-prone toddler or keeping it nearby in the kitchen to follow recipes. He even took it into the shower to keep watching a football game.
The upgraded A20 Pro chip also made apps load faster and demanding games run better in Pierce’s testing, while battery life held steady at around nine hours of screentime. At $599, though, the new Mini is still relatively expensive if you mainly want a tablet for browsing the web or streaming shows. The last-gen iPad Mini, which runs on Apple’s A17 Pro chip, is available for under $500 if you’d rather save another $100 and can live without the OLED screen and water resistance. But if you’ve been waiting for a more worthwhile upgrade to Apple’s smallest tablet, the current Black Friday discount makes the new model easier to justify.

articles.title: Apple’s latest AirTags have dropped to just $18 a pop for Black Friday
articles.body:
If you’re tired of constantly scrounging around for your lost belongings, Apple’s second-gen AirTags are on sale for an all-time low of $18 at Amazon, Walmart, and Best Buy. The handy location trackers have a list price of $29 each, but have been consistently available for around $24 since Amazon Prime Day in late June.
Apple’s latest AirTags have dropped to just $18 a pop for Black Friday
With a longer range, more precise tracking, and a louder chime, the new(er) AirTag could save you from a big headache.
The upgraded ultra-wideband chip and improved Bluetooth in the latest AirTag should provide more precise location tracking, with a range 1.5x wider than the first-gen model. The internal speaker is also 50 percent louder than the original, making it easier to find whatever item your AirTag is attached to, whether it’s buried deep in your couch cushions or at the bottom of your bag. Even without those improvements, though, AirTags are still a great option for Apple users looking for their keys or luggage, with up to a year of battery life on a single coin cell battery and compatibility with both iPhones and newer Apple Watch models.

articles.title: Nothing’s ANC-equipped earbuds are on sale for less than $20 for Black Friday
articles.body:
If our sub-$30 Black Friday roundup has you hungry for more great gadgets at low prices, you can currently grab the Nothing CMF Buds 2A in black starting at $17.89 on Amazon for Black Friday, which is about $11 less than the MSRP and the lowest price we’ve seen. The wireless earbuds are discounted in all three colors; however, the light gray and orange sets are slightly more expensive at $19.99 ($9 off).
Nothing’s ANC-equipped earbuds are on sale for less than $20 for Black Friday
You can grab the surprisingly feature-packed set of earbuds in one of three colors.
Nothing CMF Buds 2A
The CMF Buds 2A deliver decent sound and noise cancellation. They also offer useful extras like customizable EQ settings, multipoint connectivity, and IP54 water and dust resistance.
While they may not have the same premium features or sound as flagship budget buds like the AirPods 5 and Google’s Pixel Buds 2A, it’s hard to argue with the value. For just $20, you get active noise cancellation, support for Google Fast Pair, and up to eight hours of battery life before you need to toss them into the included USB-C charging case. My colleague Brandon Widder keeps some in his backpack as a backup pair of earbuds, and their IP54 water and dust resistance rating makes a great choice for light exercise and yard work.

articles.title: You can grab a 12-pack of Zepath’s rechargeable AA batteries for just $24
articles.body:
If you’re picking up any gifts that require AA batteries, it’s not a bad idea to buy a set you can keep using long after the holidays. Thankfully, you can currently get a 12-pack of Zepath’s rechargeable 3,000mWh AAs on Amazon with a charger for $23.99 ($8 off) for Black Friday, which is a new low. If you don’t need as many, Amazon is also selling an eight-pack under a different name for just $15.99 ($4 off).
You can grab a 12-pack of Zepath’s rechargeable AA batteries for just $24
Each set of AAs includes a clamshell charger, which lets you top off multiple batteries with a single connection.
My colleague Sean Hollister tested Zepath’s higher-capacity 3,600mWh batteries against competing lithium-ion AAs in April, and he picked them as his top choice. In his tests, they even outlasted Panasonic’s pricier Eneloop Pros in both a Game Boy Advance and a high-powered flashlight. Zepath also says the batteries deliver a steady 1.5V until they’re nearly empty and hold their charge well when not in use.
The best part about Zepath’s rechargeables, though, is how you charge them. Instead of relying on a multi-headed USB-C cable that plugs into each cell, you simply drop them into the included clamshell charging case, like a pair of AirPods or a similar set of wireless earbuds. The case also charges via USB-C, so you can top off eight batteries at once with a single connection in about two and a half hours.
